events.title: AI companies scraped the web. Now they want to learn how you work.
events.summary: An office in action before the rise of generative AI. Kirn Vintage Stock/Corbis via Getty Images A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . AI companies have already scraped much of the web. Now they're chasing something even more valuable: data that shows how humans actually work. That's the focus of Business Insider's new series, The AI Data Grab . This week, we published three stories showing how the race for workplace data is accelerating. One piece, from Charles Rollet, Tom Carter, and Stephen Council, examines the booming market for company records . AI firms are offering businesses six- and even seven-figure sums for anonymized Slack messages, emails, presentations, and internal documents. The goal is to teach AI systems how people solve problems, collaborate, make decisions, and complete long, multi-step tasks. Those real-world workflows are becoming the fuel for the next generation of AI agents. Another story, from Melia Robinson, explores how law firms are building AI systems around decades of legal knowledge , turning their own experience into a competitive advantage rather than relying solely on off-the-shelf AI models and tools. A third piece, by Rya Jetha, reveals how AI companies pay people to record real-world work , such as cooking dinners and packing warehouses, to teach robots how humans perform everyday physical tasks. Together, these stories point to a major shift in AI development. The first wave of generative AI was mostly about bigger models and faster chips. The next chapter is about machines understanding how work gets done, so AI can help us do it better and quicker. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . events.title: The bloated workweek is coming for Sundays—as some embrace flexibility, others worry about job security
events.summary: Work AI is making a mess of how humans interact at work Psychology and Relationships What we lose when kids can't connect, IRL Work Tech reporter Joanna Stern asked AI to do 'almost everything' for a year—the No. 1 tool she'll keep using Work Forcing workers to use AI can be counterproductive—3 tips for a better approach Work 'Doomjobbing’ can hurt your job search and worsen anxiety, experts say: Why it happens and how to avoid it Alessia Montanaro is just about to close her second busy season of the year. Since September she's been logging up to 60 hours of work per week, sometimes going as late as 11 p.m., and making a habit of working Sundays from her home office. The 30-year-old works in public accounting in Austin, Texas, and has gotten used to these sprints around tax season. She's not the only weekend work warrior. For many office workers, Sundays have become the unofficial new start to their workweek: Nearly half of workers often clock in on Sundays, according to a recent report from Owl Labs , the video-conferencing technology company, which surveyed 2,000 people in July with a margin of error of 2%. Some 21% of people surveyed say they work the whole or nearly the whole day, and another 24% say they often do a few hours of work. Of the remaining set of workers, 11% say they quickly check messages but don't really work, 18% say they rarely do any work on Sundays, and 26% say they never do. It's been six years since work for many moved home during the Covid-19 pandemic, opening the possibilities of logging hours anytime and anywhere there's Wi-Fi. While some people deprioritized work and put up strict boundaries to protect their personal time, tech use data shows that many years later, working time has bled into every hour of every day. Chat messages sent outside of the standard Monday through Friday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. workweek rose 15% year-over-year, now up to an average 58 messages per user, according to Microsoft's 2025 research on what it calls the rise of the " infinite workday ." Among those working on the weekends, nearly 20% check their email before noon on a Saturday and Sunday, and over 5% are in their inboxes on Sunday nights, per Microsoft. As far as these online habits show, the sanctity of Sundays off may be vanishing as an always-on work culture takes over. Daytime distractions push work to the weekend Some Sunday workers say working weekends or after hours is the only way to get focused work done. During the workweek, "I get pulled in five different directions" with messages or requests from associates and higher-ups, Montanaro of Austin says. Working a distraction-free Sunday can help workers get more done, says Frank Weishaupt, CEO of Owl Labs. But it can also be a signal that the typical Monday-through-Friday is overloaded with busywork. The work of getting work done can be disruptive: Employees are interrupted roughly every two minutes during core work hours with meetings, emails or chat messages, according to Microsoft data . Some 38% of workers say they have meeting fatigue, with the most common gripes being that meetings are too long and there are too many of them, according to Owl Labs . Workers carve out flexibility where they can Weishaupt says Sunday work periods could be seen as a good thing "as it relates to the employee's desire for flexibility" and a growing interest in " microshifting ," a term Owl Labs coined to mean working outside of a traditional Monday through Friday 9-to-5 time block. Microshifting can be especially helpful to moms, caregivers and anyone who might need to duck out for a few hours on workdays. Kylie Gonzalez, 29, says she'll clock into her account manager job from home on a Sunday if she took some time during the week for doctor's appointments, school pickup for her kids or other events. But she's wary of spending more than an hour or so working on the weekend, or making a habit of it. "Some companies may take advantage of that fact and add more to your plate because they see so much is being done," she says. Job anxiety fuels the Sunday scaries In 2019, the norm was going into the office on a Monday and getting settled for the week ahead, Weishaupt says. That prep work is now shifting to Sundays. "My Sunday evening feels awful because I'm just thinking about Monday and all the work that I didn't finish on Friday," says Tobi Collins, 28, a strategy consultant in Dallas. Her weekend work helps her curb the Sunday scaries, she says: "If I just get ahead of it, I'm not as nervous about the week." Dina Otero, 42, of Philadelphia, says she used to regularly log weekend hours, even spending her Sundays back from vacation catching up on emails before her actual return to work. Working a little extra at the start of the week would help her get ahead, she told herself. Really, it was just anxiety and "my own way of thinking that I had control over things that I really did not," she says.

events.title: I spent a 4-day Amtrak trip working remotely so I wouldn't waste any PTO. I underestimated how difficult it would be.
events.summary: Working remotely on an Amtrak train wasn't easy, but I would do it again. Laura Gio Carroll This summer, I took a four-day Amtrak trip with my spouse, and worked remotely the entire journey. I loved working in the café car while taking in views of the Mississippi River and the Great Plains. Even though the internet wasn't reliable, it was a great experience that I can't wait to do again. This summer, my spouse and I decided to take the longest Amtrak trip we've ever taken — three trains from Washington, DC, to Vancouver over four days. My partner, who is a teacher, had a break between the school year and the summer program, so this adventure was the perfect excuse to relax, disconnect from the world, and enjoy the train's views. That was, unfortunately, not the case for me. Since I have an office job with limited vacation time, I decided I would work remotely throughout the entire trip. Even though I had my boss's permission to work on the train and had packed all my essentials, I still wondered how successful this endeavor would be. Turns out, it was more challenging than I anticipated, but still worth the hassle. I made sure to prepare for any WiFi outages and pack accordingly. Laura Gio Carroll Before the trip, I researched whether the trains would have WiFi, but found that it could vary by route. Since I wasn't sure how reliable my internet options would be on board, I made sure to download the most important documents onto my computer instead of just relying on the cloud. This way, even if there was an unstable connection, I'd still be able to access them. Additionally, I made sure to have my phone's hotspot at the ready for whenever there wasn't WiFi on the train. And just as an extra precaution, I made a point of scheduling any important calls for either before or after our train rides , so that I wouldn't risk losing signal while speaking with my team. To prevent any other hiccups, I packed everything I could think of that I might need: my work laptop, my portable monitor , all the appropriate cords and chargers, and my planner for anything I needed to do on paper. The roomette's privacy was great, but it didn't have enough outlets. Laura Gio Carroll On two of our three train rides, we booked a roomette , a small bedroom with two seats facing each other that would convert into bunks at night. The internet was spotty in there, but I was still able to wrap up the last emails of the day without any problems. On the first train ride from DC to Chicago, the roomette had two power outlets, but on our journey from Chicago to Seattle, it had only one — forcing my spouse and me to take turns charging our devices. I loved working in the café car. Laura Gio Carroll Sometimes, the roomette felt pretty cramped, so I took my work setup to the café car as often as I could. Not only was there plenty of room for me to spread out with my laptop and second screen, but I could also witness amazing views — like the Mississippi River or the Great Plains — from the window. However, since there weren't any power outlets in the café car, I was only able to be productive for as long as my computer and phone batteries lasted, which was about 2 hours. Then, once everything had run out of power, I had to return to the roomette and plug everything in, which disrupted my workflow. I didn't think about how my hotspot wouldn't be reliable in rural areas. Laura Gio Carroll Since there was only stable WiFi on one of our three trains, I was relying heavily on my hotspot for most of the trip. But by the third day, the cellular signal kept getting spotty as we entered more rural areas of the country, making my hotspot less reliable. Because of the weak connection, I couldn't access my team's folders, so I had to email my boss a report instead of uploading it to SharePoint. I panicked a little, since we're not supposed to save documents directly to our computers, but this was my only option without a consistent signal. When we sat in coach, I could barely get any work done. Laura Gio Carroll For the last leg of our trip from Seattle to Vancouver, we sat in coach instead of reserving a roomette. We were able to sit at a small table, but it was too cramped to take out my laptop, and there wasn't any space to work in my seat either. This was the only portion of the trip where it was impossible to do any work, and it really made me miss my roomette. Even though working on the train was challenging, the station lounges were perfect. Laura Gio Carroll Whenever we had train delays, I would work at the Amtrak stations , which were great places to be productive. The station in DC had a place to stash our suitcases, decent WiFi, and various tables and chairs. The one in Chicago was also a great size, was well-lit, and had a strong internet connection and plenty of seating. Similarly, the upper level of the Amtrak station in Seattle had a small art gallery and sitting area — a perfectly comfortable space for me to do my job. It wasn't the easiest way to work, but I'd do it again. Laura Gio Carroll Although working on these trains wasn't always smooth, I still had a great experience and would definitely love to do it again. Next time, though, I would pack a power bank to charge my phone and monitor without needing an outlet, and overprepare for a lack of WiFi. Overall, even though working remotely on Amtrak trains had its challenges, I loved the stunning views and the chance to see new sights rather than just sitting at my desk. events.summary: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said the country's military has prepared a response to any new attacks by the U.S. and Israel. Rezaei said the new operational plan would not follow "rules with which they are familiar." The British Navy-affiliated United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported attacks on vessels operating near Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the United Arab Emirates. A senior Iranian security official warned Sunday that Tehran has prepared a new response plan for any renewed U.S.-Israeli attack, as maritime authorities reported several separate attacks on commercial vessels around the Arabian Peninsula. "Iran's armed forces have prepared a response to any new act of adventurism that would be far more devastating than the 12-day and 40-day wars," Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said in a post on X, referring to attacks by Israel in June 2025, and the conflict triggered by the U.S. and Israel in February. "Iran's new operational plan will not follow the rules with which they are familiar," Rezaei said in comments translated by Google. President Donald Trump said last week that he does not intend to use nuclear weapons against Iran or foresee deploying ground troops in the country. Speaking in an interview with Newsmax, broadcast Thursday evening, he said: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world." The right-wing cable outlet asked Trump about reports that Washington was considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, widely known as the "Mother of All Bombs." Iranian state media agency IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as saying that while Iran would not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure, it remains ready for dialogue. Meanwhile, shipping vessels operating in waters around the Arabian Peninsula reported coming under fire in recent days. The British Navy-affiliated UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a tug traveling south northeast of the United Arab Emirates was hit by two unknown projectiles on Sunday. On Saturday, a master of a liquefied natural gas tanker southwest of Yemen reported "being approached by a small skiff with seven persons onboard," UKMTO said . The skiff fired twice, and the tanker's security team responded with two warning shots, it said. Another tanker northeast of Saudi Arabia reported being hit by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat on Friday. Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday amid rising tensions in the Middle East, while Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries. Brent futures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to settle at $109.86, a 3.7% gain. U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% last week while Brent advanced nearly 5%. Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, a military spokesman said. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said. Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia last week. The kingdom's energy ministry said oil giant Aramco came under attack when militants hit one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran on Tuesday.

events.title: Why have France’s school protests become a wider political crisis?
events.summary: France’s school protests have united students and ‘yellow vest’ supporters, exposing deeper anger over living standards. Protests are sweeping France as anger over conditions in schools meets frustration with high living costs and a government accused of doing little to address problems facing people. About 550,000 people demonstrated nationwide on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry. Most marched peacefully, while a small minority attacked buildings, looted shops and clashed with police, who fired tear gas and charged protesters. list 1 of 4 Fighting intensifies across Yemen as humanitarian crisis deepens list 2 of 4 Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill list 3 of 4 Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’ list 4 of 4 South African rugby player Hyron Andrews remembered in emotional tribute Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were injured. Behind the confrontations lies a political crisis, fuelled by anger at deteriorating services and overstretched household budgets, and compounded by a sense that France’s political institutions offer little hope of change. Here is how school blockades became a nationwide movement – and what that means for President Emmanuel Macron. How have the protests spread, what are protesters demanding? The movement began last month in high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where students protested against teacher shortages and poor facilities. School blockades and demonstrations later spread to cities including Bordeaux, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Lille and Marseille. Saturday brought together students and trade unions, alongside supporters of the “yellow vest” movement that emerged in 2018 to challenge rising living costs and economic inequality. Emile Chabal, a professor of contemporary history at the University of Edinburgh, told Al Jazeera the demonstrations were “the logical outcome of a series of protests” stretching back to the yellow vests. That movement was driven by financial pressures and resentment at “the French presidential system”, he told Al Jazeera, alluding to a structure which often leads to the election of a centrist candidate, such as President Emmanuel Macron. Saturday combined those longstanding grievances with students’ anger at deteriorating state schools. The yellow vests had demanded better public services. Bringing students’ grievances together with wider social demands, therefore, represented “the worst possible outcome for the French government”, Chabal said. Students’ immediate demands concern conditions in France’s lycees (public high schools), which generally educate pupils aged 15 to 18. They want smaller classes, enough teachers, better buildings and less exhausting timetables. Their complaints also reflect broader concerns about whether the state can provide the education and opportunities young people need. But for workers, including school staff, the dispute also concerns wages and the resources available to deliver public services. The school protests coincided with a nationwide public sector strike against the government’s budget plans. Bringing all these concerns together under one umbrella represented “the worst possible outcome for the French government”, Chabal said. It comes as the proposed 2027 budget includes a 54 billion euro ($60.8bn) package of cost-cutting and tax measures, which the government says is necessary to reduce France’s deficit. The proposals include freezing the pay scale used to calculate civil servants’ basic salaries, which unions say would be the fourth consecutive annual freeze. Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, said students were inspiring wider mobilisation around inequality, cuts to public investment and democratic rights, with demands for social welfare spending rather than militarisation. “They do not want to fight wars; they want a different future,” she told Al Jazeera. She also linked the movement to young people’s mobilisation over Gaza, with Palestinian flags appearing at demonstrations across several European countries. The government has focused its immediate response on public order, with President Macron saying those responsible for violence would be “prosecuted and punished”. His comments came as a fire largely destroyed the historic town hall in the city of Limoges, while public buildings and shops were attacked elsewhere. But those involved in violence represent only a small minority of the much larger mobilisation. Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, has accused the government of repressing school students and allowing the confrontation to intensify. His argument reflects a wider political dispute about whether the government treats the protests chiefly as a security problem or addresses the grievances that have brought different groups together.

events.title: I've studied over 200 kids—parents who raise resilient, successful children teach them these 6 lessons early on
events.summary: Psychology and Relationships 2 red flags of a big ego and 5 signs someone is truly secure: ‘It’s easy to get hoodwinked,’ says psychologist Raising Successful Kids Stop telling kids they can do anything—what parents can say instead to raise successful kids, says psychologist Raising Successful Kids Harvard- and Stanford-trained child psychiatrist: 5 habits of parents who raise highly resilient kids Raising Successful Kids Pediatric surgeon: This is the 'essential' AI-proof skill kids need right now Psychology and Relationships People in the strongest relationships ask 7 questions in the evening, says therapist—instead of 'How was work today? When we talk about raising successful kids, we tend to talk about what they can do. Are they getting good grades? Are they going to basketball practices and winning games? Did they clean their rooms and set the table? Are they motivated? Responsible? Social? Can they solve problems, make good choices and eventually become independent adults? But after years spent working with more than 200 families, I've seen that some of the most important lessons children need to live successful, happy and fulfilling lives — and to build healthy relationships — have very little to do with action or achievement. Children absorb crucial messages in ordinary moments based on how we respond when they struggle, fail, disagree with us, disappoint us or simply become someone different from who we imagined they would be. In my experience, there are six things parents of the most successful, confident, resilient and well-adjusted kids teach them early on that have nothing to do with accomplishments. 1. Failure doesn't change who they are to you Children notice what happens between you when something goes wrong. They see your face when the grade comes back. They notice whether you seem prouder after the win and more distant after the loss. A child should be able to fail without feeling they have fallen in your eyes. For example, instead of immediately asking "Why didn't you study more?" try "I know you wanted a different result. How are you feeling about it?" When children know a bad result won't change how we see them, they don't have to be so afraid of getting things wrong. Failure can become something they learn from instead of something they feel they need to hide. 2. Disappointing someone doesn't always mean they did something wrong If being "good" means pleasing other people, someone else's disappointment can start to feel like proof a child did something wrong. They may learn to read the room before they learn to read themselves. We can show them a different way. You might say: "Someone else can be disappointed in your choice, and it can still be the right choice for you." Your child needs to know that you can disagree with them and they can still trust themselves. That matters later, too, with friends, partners and bosses. 3. What they're good at isn't who they are Even positive labels can feel like pressure. If adults keep saying: A child can quietly start to hear: This is who I have to keep being. Then a B isn't just a B. Getting cut from the team isn't just disappointing. Struggling can start to feel like losing a piece of who they are. Instead of making the achievement their identity, notice what went into it . You might say: "You kept going even when that got difficult." When we separate what children accomplish from who they are, we give them room to become more than whatever they happen to be good at today. 4. They can disagree or be upset with someone and still be loved Children need to disagree with us sometimes and discover that the relationship is still okay. That doesn't mean they make every decision. We are still the parents. We can hold a boundary with our kids and stay connected to them at the same time. You might say: "You're allowed to be angry with my decision. The answer is still no, and we're still okay." A child shouldn't have to choose between having a voice and feeling close to us. If they feel like they have to give up their voice to stay connected at home, saying no can become much harder everywhere else too. 5. Uncomfortable feelings don't need to be fixed right away Our instinct as parents is often to make our children feel better. We fix, reassure, distract or tell them everything will be fine. Sometimes they need something simpler: "This is hard. I'm here." Children need to learn that feeling bad doesn't mean something has gone wrong. They can be embarrassed and get through it. They can be nervous and still walk into the room. We don't have to rescue children from every uncomfortable feeling. Sometimes staying beside them as they experience those feelings is how they discover: I can handle this . 6. Home is the one place they don't have to impress anyone Children already live in a world that measures them: grades, teams, rankings, likes and eventually college admissions, job offers and performance reviews.

events.title: Roth conversions: When the ‘juice isn't really worth the squeeze,’ according to a top-ranked advisor
events.summary: Roth individual retirement account conversions can potentially reduce lifetime taxes and kick-start tax-free growth. But the move increases current-year income, which can include an up-front tax bill and other consequences. The choice to convert has become more complex after President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill" and other tax law changes. Roth individual retirement account conversions can potentially reduce lifetime taxes . But the strategy isn't right for everyone, and the choice is now more complex amid updates from President Donald Trump 's "big beautiful bill" and other changes. Roth conversions transfer pretax or nondeductible IRA funds into a Roth IRA, which kick-starts tax-free growth. The trade-off is that they can trigger more income in the year of the conversion. The move can be attractive if you have large pretax retirement balances and you expect higher tax rates when it's time to withdraw the funds , experts say. At year-end 2025, IRA-owning households in the U.S. had $15.9 trillion in assets in traditional IRAs, compared with $2.4 trillion in after-tax Roth IRAs, according to a 2026 report from the Investment Company Institute, an investing trade organization. More from CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors: CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor for 2026 takes a family-office approach CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 FAQ: Who is eligible and how rankings work Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations How to navigate new tax rules in year-end planning, according to top-ranked advisors Weighing Roth conversions, or partial Roth conversions, is "a strategy that continues to be very popular year-over-year," said Charissa Anderson, a certified financial planner who is an executive vice president at Ferguson Wellman Capital Management in Portland, Oregon. Her firm ranked No. 52 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026. As of March 31, Roth conversions were up 41% this year compared with the same period in 2025, according to the latest Fidelity data , based on an analysis of 19.6 million IRA accounts. But experts say the strategy isn't right for everyone. "There are just so many variables" when analyzing a possible Roth conversion, said Tommy Lucas, a CFP at Moisand Fitzgerald Tamayo in Orlando, Florida. His firm is ranked No. 44 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026. These could include when you claim Social Security , your life expectancy and legacy goals , among other factors, he said. Depending on your tax bracket, "sometimes the juice isn't really worth the squeeze," said Lucas. "And we're going to have to squeeze every single year" because multiple factors can change the analysis. If you're eyeing a Roth conversion before year-end, here are some key things to consider. Roth conversions impact tax benefits When deciding on a Roth conversion, projections should include the current year's taxes, along with an analysis of future years, financial advisors say. "The [tax] bracket you see isn't always the rate you pay," because more income could phase out, or reduce, other tax benefits, according to CFP Tommy Blackburn, senior financial planner and partner at Mason and Associates in Newport News, Virginia. He is also a certified public accountant. As an example, Blackburn pointed to a client in the 22% tax bracket with a child in college. Income from a conversion could trigger taxes above 30% because the client would lose an education tax credit , which is subtracted from their taxes owed, he said. By comparison, a client in the 10% tax bracket could convert a limited amount under their standard deduction without owing additional taxes for the current year, he said. More income could also impact temporary tax deductions enacted via Trump's "big beautiful bill," which have varying income phaseouts. These could include the bigger federal deduction limit for state and local taxes , known as SALT, worth up to $40,400 for 2026, or the $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction , among others. Retirees should also consider income-related monthly adjustment amounts, or IRMAAs, which increase Medicare Part B and Part D premiums once income exceeds a certain level. The surcharge is based on modified adjusted gross income from two years prior. ACA enrollees should 'proceed with caution' Boosting your AGI with Roth conversions can also reduce the premium tax credit , which makes Affordable Care Act marketplace health insurance less expensive. Earning even $1 more than a certain income limit can threaten eligibility for the credit — known as the "ACA cliff" — and enrollees could owe full premiums for health coverage. The cliff affects ACA enrollees when household income exceeds 400% of the federal poverty line, which varies by family size.

events.title: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?
events.summary: The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the year Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about. Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each. In addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort. “It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort. “I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be.” The damage of such “AI worms” could be astonishingly large. Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet. That legacy includes the Morris worm of 1988, which arrived before the mainstream consumer internet, when a graduate student released a program that took advantage of various software flaws and weak passwords, copying itself so rapidly that many infected machines slowed to a stop. The US and Israel brought worms into international espionage with the stealthy Stuxnet in the lat 2000s, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges. Other worms like the Russian NotPetya and North Korean-attributed WannaCry have caused tens of billions of dollars’ worth of damage worldwide. Many of the world’s most destructive worms have depended on known vulnerabilities that device owners have not patched, sometimes months after patches became available. The Anthropic team predicted that a worm like theirs could function in the same way and be harder to stop, because smart devices receive patches less often than phones or laptops. Worse, they theorized that an AI worm could keep adapting to other types of hardware by researching newly disclosed vulnerabilities. What differentiates AI worms from typical reproducing viruses is that AI models can learn as they go, said Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early security expert at OpenAI who now runs AI security startup RunSybil. Existing cybersecurity infrastructure is not ready for the proliferation of such threats, Herbert-Voss said. “We need to better enable our security teams. We need to be giving them more resources to fix problems.” Worms could also be used for benevolent purposes, suggested Chris Inglis, a former deputy director of the National Security Agency who served as National Cyber Director in the Biden White House. “The question of whether AI worms are plausible has been settled by several breakout events over the past six months,” Inglis said by digital message. “The better question is how we will employ them, counter them, and/or combine them with other emerging technologies.” Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end. Their research follows a paper published by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm. “The capabilities have been developing very rapidly,” said co-author and Toronto PhD student Jonas Guan. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Guan and other experts said that, as a practical matter, an AI worm should not top anyone’s list of AI fears. The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers. Basic security hygiene, including requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication, would stop most worms and other hacking, experts said. “Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, vice-president of research at security firm SentinelOne.

events.title: Tim Cook says late Apple cofounder Steve Jobs gave him this unforgettable advice before handing over the reins as CEO: ‘Never ask what I would do’
events.summary: Many companies are inextricably tied to their iconic founders—from Mark Zuckerberg being the face of Meta , to Warren Buffett leading Berkshire Hathaway for decades. But when it came time for Tim Cook to take the reins of Apple , the brand’s late cofounder Steve Jobs instructed him to forge his own path at the now-$5 trillion trillion giant. The advice continues to inspire the tech company’s leaders 15 years after Jobs’ passing. “[Jobs’] advice to me was ‘Never ask what I would do, just do the right thing,’” Cook told CBS Sunday Morning in an interview earlier this year .  It was a lesson that Jobs had learned while working with Disney —the Apple cofounder was also one of the three founding fathers of Pixar Animation Studios , purchasing the group from LucasFilm in 1986. Entertainment behemoth Disney later acquired Pixar in 2006, and during his work at the company, Jobs picked up on a trend. “He had watched Disney go through this paralysis of sitting around and talking about what Walt [Disney] would do,” Cook explained. “And he did not want that for Apple.” The former Apple CEO explained that at the time, the business had never had a “professional transition” at the chief executive level; the previous successions were always done in a time of “panic.” However, Jobs wanted to do things differently this time. So he called Cook over to his house and offered him the CEO job—with no pressure to emulate his leadership style.  “I’ll never forget that and it was such a gift for me, because he took off of my shoulder this question of, ‘What would Steve do?’” Cook continued. “I just put my head down and thought, ‘I’m going to be the best version of myself.’” Cook brought his own flair, but stuck to these core principles Cook first joined Apple in 1998 after stints at PC-maker Compaq and IBM , less than one year after Jobs had returned as interim CEO. From 2000 onwards, Jobs would lead as the permanent CEO, while Cook worked his way up to high-level positions, becoming the COO in 2005. At the start of September this year, he stepped down from CEO role, and John Ternus took his place in the top job . Over Cook’s nearly three decades at the company, working under Jobs until his passing in October 2011, he learned what principles are essential to the “DNA” of the company. While Jobs advised the current CEO, Ternus, to do his own thing, the cofounder imparted some everlasting fundamentals that will always be core to Apple.  “[Jobs] had the vision that the collaboration was something that would produce great results. That one plus one is equal to three, not two. That if you share an idea and debate it, it gets bigger and better,” Cook explained in the CBS interview . “If you care enough that you call somebody at 10 at night because you just had an idea, that incredible things can come out of that.” Cook said the strategy to “argue and debate everything” at Apple meetings, breeding bigger and better ideas, dates back to the origin of the business. He spoke on different strengths he’s harnessed within the business, particularly around accessibility, privacy, and education. But he’s sticking with the collaboration culture that Jobs popularized through his decades of leadership.  “[Jobs] had an idea of focus that you say ‘no’ to a thousand things to say ‘yes’ to the one that’s truly important,” Cook continued. “And that when you do something, you should do it at an excellence level where good isn’t good enough: it has to be insanely great.” The advice other business leaders have received from Jobs Throughout his career, Jobs has advised many on how to step into their own success—from college graduates to leaders of billion-dollar companies.  Marc Benioff, the CEO of Salesforce , said on Lenny’s Podcast in 2024 that Jobs helped him overcome “entrepreneurs block.” The Apple cofounder instructed him to do three things: grow your business 10 times larger in two years, get a big customer for the Salesforce automation product, and build an application economy.  Benioff believed Jobs wanted him to build an app store, so he created AppExchange, later gifting Apple the App Store trademark and the appstore.com domain for Jobs’ help. That advice “dramatically influenced me in my career and my whole life,” Benioff said.  Former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz also received some tough love from Jobs that ultimately led him on the path for success. It was 2008, and the coffee chain was in a crisis. After confiding to Jobs about the company’s issues, Schultz was advised to fire his entire leadership team—reasoning they’ll all be gone within nine months anyways. The then-Starbucks CEO found the idea to be preposterous, but said Jobs was ultimately right in the end: all of the team left, except for one. Jobs also imparted some critical advice for young job-seekers aspiring for greatness: Do the work you love. It’s a learning lesson that kept the tech pioneer going after being ousted from the company he had built, and weathering crises like Apple’s near-bankruptcy. “Your work is going to fill a large part of your life, and the only way to be truly satisfied is to do what you believe is great work. And the only way to do great work is to love what you do,” Jobs said during his 2005 Stanford University commencement speech.  “If you haven’t found it yet, keep looking—and don’t settle. As with all matters of the heart, you’ll know when you find it.” A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on March 11, 2026. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Gaza families fear food shortages as Israel halts commercial shipments
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Gaza residents report rising prices after commercial shipments stopped, while families unable to afford extra supplies fear further shortages if the closure continues. Gaza City, Gaza — Prices of basic goods are rising daily in Gaza, as Israeli restrictions on the import of commercial goods entered their fifth consecutive day. Families already suffering from the siege on the enclave have started stocking up on goods they can still find, for fear of imminent shortages and continued price increases. list 1 of 3 UN warns nearly 1 million in Gaza face flood risks as winter approaches list 2 of 3 What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’? list 3 of 3 Maps show how Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ keeps squeezing Palestinians in Gaza The cost of flour, eggs, onions and other staples has sharply increased since Wednesday, when Israel said that commercial goods would no longer enter Gaza. This comes amid a dispute over fees involving Palestinian merchants and Hamas, which still has some authority in the strip. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been plunged into poverty since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023. The price of basic goods has soared, as incomes have shrunk due to the war and Israel’s tightened siege. Residents without the means to buy in bulk will have to continue to purchase food when they can. They will be worst hit by the daily price rises if the border remains closed. The impact of the Israeli import restrictions is playing out in marketplaces, which are slightly busier than usual. Ismail al-Barawi, 52, from Jabalia in northern Gaza, noticed a significant rise in prices within two or three days of the crossings being closed on Wednesday. He described a recurring cycle of uncertainty in Gaza over the status of the crossings, which is usually followed by higher prices. Al-Barawi said a carton of eggs that had cost 35 shekels ($11.34) was now selling for between 60 and 70 shekels ($18 to $21). The price of a kilogramme of onions had risen from five or six shekels ($1.50–$1.80) to between eight and 10 shekels ($2.40–$3), while a kilogramme of avocados had increased from seven or eight shekels ($2.10–$2.40) to around 15 shekels ($4.50). “These increases happened in just two or three days,” he said, voicing concern about what prices would be if the crossings remain closed for another 10 to 15 days. The increases have forced him to buy smaller quantities of what he needs. Instead of a full carton of 30 eggs, he might buy only four or five. “Today, everyone is trading at the expense of the people. There is no mercy,” he said. He expressed frustration at traders, saying they raise prices as soon as they hear that crossings may remain closed, adding to the problem of real shortages. Al-Barawi predicted that a 50 kg sack of flour could end up costing 200 or even 300 shekels ($60–$90), if the crossings remained closed. Al-Barawi is responsible for providing food to his extended family of about 11 or 12 people, including his married daughters and their children. Whenever he has money, he prioritises basic goods such as flour, rice, cooking oil, onions and potatoes. Given the uncertainty, it makes sense for Palestinians to stock up now before prices increase further. But many families in Gaza have no money to spare, he added. “Some people cannot even afford to feed themselves for a day. How much can they save or store when they have no money?” he said. But stockpiling also has its limits. Fresh vegetables can spoil within days, he said. Unreliable electricity supplies make it difficult to store meat for more than a brief period. Gaza’s Government Media Office on Thursday rejected Israel’s explanation for the suspension, denying that authorities in the territory had imposed taxes or government fees on commercial trucks. The office said the 10,000-shekel ($3,242) amount cited by Israel was linked to a voluntary community fund intended to support vulnerable families and financial relief projects. It also said measures requiring a 30 percent rate for cash transactions had been introduced in agreement with the Chamber of Commerce to address a shortage of cash liquidity and the circulation of worn-out banknotes. The office accused Israel of using the dispute to impose further restrictions on supplies entering Gaza, which has been under an Israeli blockade since 2007. Gaza authorities were not to blame for the reduction of trucks entering the enclave, it said, and called on mediators and international parties to push for the entry of 600 trucks a day , in line with existing agreements with Israel. The office warned that continued restrictions would worsen the humanitarian and economic crisis in Gaza. Food remains unaffordable for many households in Gaza.

events.title: Boomers are buying into the promise of monthly income from options ETFs, but there's a tax catch
events.summary: Covered call ETFs have risen in popularity in recent years with older investors, particularly retirees, willing to give up some market upside for a monthly income stream. ETFs are generally tax-efficient investment vehicles, but because these funds distribute income in various forms, the potential tax hit is easy for investors to miss until IRS form 1099-DIV arrives. Covered call ETFs have gained a following for their ability to generate monthly cash flow. But a tax surprise could be lurking for many investors. These actively managed funds have different underlying assets and strategies. But the premise is generally the same. Covered call funds hold equities and sell call options or use related derivatives to generate income. Investors receive attractive income yields in exchange for limited capital upside. The tax piece is more complicated, however. A fund that realizes option premiums, short-term gains or other income still has taxable amounts to distribute. The tax hit can be easy — and costly — for investors to miss, especially since ETFs are typically understood to be tax-efficient investment vehicles, and especially since most investors aren't looking at the tax implications until they receive a 1099-DIV at tax time, the IRS tax document issued by financial services companies to report dividends and related distributions paid to investors during a tax year. Even if a fund has good returns and a favorable 30-day SEC yield — which measures the net investment income of bond funds or equity funds and is annualized to reflect the yield an investor would expect to earn over the course of a full year — investors need to look under the hood and understand the tax implications of covered call ETFs. "The after-tax net total return might fall below your expectations," said Matthew Smart, chief investment officer at WWM Investments in Chicago. Here's what investors need to know about covered call ETFs and taxes: Not all income distributions are created equal Distributions from covered call funds come in several forms: dividends, capital gain distributions, or non-dividend distributions. The distribution mix can vary by fund and change year to year. Non-dividend distributions are commonly known as return of capital — payment or distribution from a portion of an investor's original principal rather than an economic profit, capital gain, or dividend earnings. And this is where it can get confusing for investors because ROC distributions aren't treated as current income. Instead, they reduce the investment's cost basis by the distribution amount, so they are tax-deferred until shares are sold. Covered call ETFs take different approaches to distributions. "Some covered call strategies make distributions characterized only as ordinary dividends. Other strategies make distributions that may include all three types. And since investors' individual tax rates vary significantly, there can be a large difference between what investors receive in fund distributions on a pre-tax basis, and what they keep after paying taxes," ProShares wrote in a blog on covered call strategy and tax efficiency. Investors surprised by cost-basis and delayed taxes Some covered call ETF investors are surprised at tax time by the magnitude of the qualified dividends and ordinary income, said Edwin Retter, senior wealth advisor in the Melbourne, Florida, office of Mission Wealth. They are also confused by the ROC concept. While it seems favorable from a distribution standpoint in the short term, it's investors' own money coming back to them, which reduces the cost basis. Having a lower cost basis generally increases the investor's capital gains tax liability at the time of sale. "You're not avoiding the taxes; you're just delaying it until you sell," said Aaron Brachman, wealth manager at the Washington Wealth Group of Steward Partners in Washington, D.C. Use of tax-deferred accounts is recommended Investors who decide to purchase a covered call ETF should ideally do so within a tax-deferred account such as a traditional IRA, Retter said. "I don't know how many investors give so much thought to that. They just find out at tax time that they've put it in a less tax-desirable account." By investing in a covered call ETF through a traditional IRA, investors don't have to worry about taxes until they pull money out of the account. "You can really save a lot of time and taxes by putting it in the right account structure," Retter said. Tax-cost ratio is a key measure to evaluate Investors who want to better understand how taxes come into play in a covered call ETF can use a measurement known as the tax-cost ratio . The Morningstar Tax Cost Ratio measures how much a fund's annualized return is reduced by the taxes investors pay on distributions. Investors can type in the ticker of the fund they are researching on Morningstar.com, click on the price tab, and scroll down to see the tax-cost ratio.

events.title: Paris left reeling as student-led protests turn chaotic
events.summary: Some 1,800 people arrested and hundreds injured during nationwide demonstrations attended by hundreds of thousands. Paris residents tell Al Jazeera they’re dismayed by protest damage Paris, France – France is counting the cost of a day of unrest after hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets nationwide, in the largest mobilisation since protests over education reforms and the cost of living began last month. At Place de la Republique, in the heart of the French capital, people on Sunday surveyed the previous day’s destruction in dismay: smashed windows, gutted buildings, looted shops. “I find it unacceptable – absolutely unacceptable,” said Rabah, who has been living in Paris for more than 70 years. “Back in the day, we also demonstrated, but peacefully,” he said. Staring at the burned skeleton of what used to be a newspaper stand, 56-year-old Claire was also shaken. “I love Paris so much, and seeing it like this makes me furious,” she said. “It’s absolutely appalling. I’m actually quite overcome with emotion.” Nearby, the statue of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic, was covered in graffiti. “Those who sow misery reap anger,” read one inscription. The student-led protests began in mid-September, caused by grievances ranging from overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages to systemic inequality and a lack of opportunity. The movement quickly spilled out of the schoolyards and into the streets, tapping into broader social and economic anxieties. On Saturday, these complaints converged in a mobilisation that saw a nationwide turnout of 550,000 people, according to authorities; unions and organisers put the estimate at 800,000. But while the vast majority of demonstrators rallied peacefully, the scale of the violent unrest threatened to eclipse their message. In Paris, there was also heavy use of tear gas and stun grenades by the police, including before the start of the march, which set the tone for a tense day. “I marched from the 10th arrondissement town hall to Place de Clichy. I was there from start to finish, and it was very peaceful – just all kinds of people, all of them nonviolent,” said Stephanie, a 23-year-old Parisian student. “But once again, the violence was so spectacular that the actual message – the reasons behind the protesters’ grievances – was never conveyed,” she said. French President Emmanuel Macron, whose second and final term ends next year, will give a televised address to the nation at 18:00 GMT on Sunday after meeting government ministers, his office announced. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said nearly 1,800 people had been arrested – almost half of them in Paris – and more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters had been injured in the unrest. “Protesting is a fundamental right. Causing disorder through violence and in a concerted manner is not,” he said on Sunday. During Saturday’s protest in Paris, Al Jazeera saw groups of black-clad, masked young men smashing shop windows with what appeared to be golf clubs before fleeing with bags of stolen goods. In Marseille, France’s second-largest city, dozens of shops were looted and a group of people broke into the city hall before being forced out. “Students and others have real claims they want to air which no one is listening to now because idiots are smashing everything,” said Benoit Payan, the city’s mayor. In Limoges, footage showed flames engulfing the city hall as the fire spread through the historic building. Public buildings were also damaged in Bordeaux and other cities. Police conduct has also come under scrutiny. France’s police inspectorate, the IGPN, had opened 36 investigations into alleged police violence since the high-school protests began, according to figures released by the Ministry of the Interior on October 13. The figure predates Saturday’s demonstrations. Human rights lawyers have described some of their clients’ injuries as comparable to those seen in conflict zones. These include a minor who has lost his hand, another with his jaw smashed and a third pupil who lost sight in one eye. “There is an increasingly systematic use of crowd-control measures that would normally be reserved for much more serious situations,” said Christophe Calvao, president of the Paris Young Lawyers’ Union. “This only serves to inflame tensions and make people even angrier.” The government now faces the challenge of responding to widespread social discontent while trying to pass a budget aimed at bringing France’s public finances under control. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wants to reduce the country’s deficit through spending restraint and tax measures – a move that will likely deepen public anger. Cuts to France’s generous welfare system have traditionally faced strong public resistance. All of this takes place in a highly toxic political environment as parties harden their positions ahead of next year’s presidential election.

events.title: The next ayahuasca? Gabon fights to protect sacred plant from US drug companies
events.summary: Iboga root, central to several Gabonese ritual traditions, is believed to have huge potential for use in treating addiction and some mental illnesses T he temple is dark, its sandy floor edged with candles. People sit shoulder to shoulder beneath palm fronds hung from the rafters. Through the night, they swallow what they have come here for: a bitter root bark called iboga. Tabernanthe iboga is a slow-growing central African rainforest shrub, the root bark of which has long been used in several Gabonese ritual traditions. In Gabon’s villages and forests, iboga is cultivated and sometimes gathered from wild populations, often collected under ritual conditions. But nothing in its cultural usage, at sites such as this temple on the outskirts of Libreville, is comparable to the potential wave of demand fast approaching from abroad. A US executive order has turned a spotlight on ibogaine, a drug made from the plant , which pharmaceutical companies believe has huge potential for use in addiction treatment. In the Bwiti (also known as Bwété) spiritual tradition, iboga is used in many different ways. Apollon Obolo, a practitioner of Misoko Bwiti, a branch concerned with healing and divination, describes the ceremony taking place that night, called Mubindu, as a way of lifting the burden carried by relatives and friends after a death. But, he stresses, iboga is only one part of the practice. “In Gabon , we don’t talk about iboga. We talk about Bwiti. Iboga is just an element,” he says. “For me, Misoko is like a microscope to see clearly about details in the life of someone.” Obolo believes it can “restructure” a person and resolve what ordinary medicine cannot. In Misoko, Obolo says, knowledge of iboga is received “from generation to generation”, and accumulated “time after time”. A 2012 report by Yann Guignon, an intercultural and sustainable development consultant and president of the NGO Blessings of the Forest, records practitioners describing wild iboga as something that must be considered in relation to the whole forest, including by following animals that eat the fruit. This stands in contrast to the interest now being taken by pharmaceutical companies. Ibogaine has a fast-developing reputation in addiction treatment, with early observational studies reporting sharp reductions in opioid withdrawal and craving after a single treatment. In a study published in 2024 , 30 male US special operations veterans, most of whom were diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury, received ibogaine combined with magnesium. A month later, average PTSD, depression and anxiety scores had fallen by at least 81%, while disability scores moved from mild-to-moderate impairment into the “no disability” range. The study was small, uncontrolled and included complementary therapies, meaning it could not establish eﬃcacy. Its authors have called for further controlled trials. The former Texas governor Rick Perry has become one of ibogaine’s most visible political champions. Texas has granted $50m (£38m) for a multicentre trial , and on 18 April, the US president, Donald Trump, signed an executive order specifically naming “ ibogaine compounds” and directing federal agencies to create a treatment pathway for eligible patients. A therapeutic economy already exists elsewhere: Beond, a clinic in Cancún, lists programmes costing from $13,500 to $19,500. B eyond the last paved streets in Libreville, Gabon’s capital, up a rutted hill and behind a concrete compound, stands the temple of Madame Djédjé Stéphanie Djoungounda, known as Maman Djédjé. The temple’s entrance is guarded by a painted mermaid. Djédjé specialises in Mbomba Ossoundo, a branch of the Mbomayano, which she describes as concerned with rebirth and restoration. It involves a plant she calls ikasô alongside small amounts of iboga administered during vigils. “We don’t heal only with ibogaine,” she says, standing among the iboga plants growing at her temple. “We heal with the whole iboga: the flower, the leaf, the bark, the trunk, the roots.” Not every dose of ibogaine abroad comes from Gabonese iboga. The molecule can be made semi-synthetically from voacangine, found in the related African tree Voacanga africana . But the iboga root bark is particularly in demand for ceremonial use, and for the manufacture of extracts containing several of its alkaloids. Even before the US announced its interest, demand had already begun to pose an ecological problem. Small amounts of root bark can be removed without uprooting the shrub, according to Guignon’s report. But commercial extraction can incentivise something faster: taking the entire root system, which yields more bark at once but kills the shrub. The report documents collectors doing exactly that – without replanting. Recognising the danger, Guignon’s organisation has worked with communities on iboga cultivation and conservation since 2015.

events.title: My family moved from a small country town to a big city this year. There are plenty of things we like, but a few we miss.
events.summary: The author and her family moved to the Gold Coast this year. Courtesy of Melissa Noble My family of five moved from a small country town to a city earlier this year. I wanted to spend more time with my parents, and there is plenty to love about the city. However, I miss the slower pace of life and the close-knit community. I've always been a city mouse, so when we decided to move from Melbourne, Australia, to Bright in country Victoria in 2021, I wasn't sure how long I'd last. Our family ended up falling in love with the slower pace of life and the people, and spent four years in the small alpine town at the foothills of the Victorian Alps. But in January, we moved from Bright to the Gold Coast, where I grew up. My parents' health was declining, and I wanted to spend quality time with them before it was too late. Moving from a small regional town of fewer than 3,000 people to a city of almost 700,000 was a profound lifestyle shift for our family of five. We had to make new friends , learn how to navigate a traffic light again (joking!), and get used to the buzzing city life. Overall, we've gained a lot from moving to the city, and I feel it's been especially beneficial to our kids, as it's helped build resilience. But there are definitely things about country life that I do miss, if I'm being honest. Life is full of trade-offs, and we've definitely made a few. We've gained convenience and accessibility In country Victoria, our nearest major retailer was an hour's drive away. If the kids needed new shoes or I needed new underwear, off we'd drive to the nearest major town. It often felt like a mission just to access simple amenities. Nowadays, everything we need is at our fingertips. If we want to eat Italian one night and Nepalese the next, we can. The Gold Coast has all the amenities we need, and a good mix of beaches, hinterland hikes, nightlife, festivals, and an up-and-coming food scene. There are more career and education opportunities Cities generally offer better career and education opportunities , without a doubt. In our family, my husband has probably benefited the most in that regard. When we moved here in January, he expanded his Muscle Freedom remedial massage and myotherapy business and started a clinic on the Gold Coast. Since then, the opportunities have been incredible, and he's treated some of Australia's biggest sporting identities. That would likely never have happened in country Victoria (unless they were holidaying there). Likewise, our kids seem to be thriving at school and in their extra-curricular activities, many of which were unavailable where we used to live. I enjoy the anonymity, and the diversity here is also a big plus When I was having a bad mental health day in Bright, there was no escaping friends and family (bless them). Once, at the supermarket, I was weeping in the bread aisle, only to be greeted by my husband's cheerful colleague, who was keen to chat about the weather. I wanted to scream and run away. In the city, I quite enjoy the anonymity and being a number in the crowd, especially on harder days. I also love having access to a diverse range of art, music, entertainment, and food on the Gold Coast. After four years living in the country, I began to feel a bit starved of culture. My kids are also mingling with children from different backgrounds and walks of life, which I am really happy about. However, we miss having nature at our doorstep, and wide open spaces Bright is surrounded by mountains, forests, rivers, and cycling trails, with gorgeous national parks a short drive away. It really is a smorgasbord of activities for outdoor enthusiasts. The Gold Coast has plenty of sunshine and offers some spectacular natural scenery, but you do have to drive to access it. I've actually put on a few kilos living in the city , and I think it's mainly because I'm not walking or cycling as much. When we recently returned to Bright for a family holiday, I realized how much I've missed those wide open spaces. The air seems to feel fresher there. Living in suburbia on the Gold Coast, the blocks are tighter, and some areas feel like the properties are on top of each other. Even as I write this, I can overhear the next-door neighbor arguing with her husband about his messy household habits. I also miss the close-knit community and slower pace I've been lucky enough to make some wonderful friends on the Gold Coast. The kind who check in on us when we're sick or offer to babysit if my husband and I need a night out. But it also seems that people are busier in the city, and get-togethers happen less often. In a small town like Bright, it's easier to catch up with people because everyone lives close by. I found that living in the country helped me form deeper connections with friends. That brought a sense of security, knowing that someone always has your back. Since moving to the city, life has felt frantic. For the first six months, every weekend was jam-packed with catch-ups with family and new and old friends. In a small country town, the pace of life was much slower. Recently, while we were holidaying in Bright, I felt my shoulders relax, and my stress levels decrease. There's something to be said for a simple life. What our next chapter holds We'd intended to give the Gold Coast 12 months and then make a call about where to base ourselves long-term. But now that we're almost at that mark, we've realized it's too soon to make a decision. And so, we'll be spending 2027 here, then reassessing our options late next year. Part of me craves the open skies, fresh mountain air, and the stillness I took for granted in the country, but I'm also  enjoying having Aldi  a kilometer away and more choices overall. I suppose at the end of the day, there's no perfect place to live, just places that suit you at different life stages. For now, the Gold Coast is giving us convenience, variety, and time with my folks, and I intend to enjoy the best of what city life has to offer. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions, Zelenskyy condemns it as 'wrong'
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump invoked the Graham Act’s national-interest waiver to suspend new duties on Russian goods and major Russian energy buyers. The moves drew praise from a Russian envoy and criticism from Democrats and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The waiver came two days before the law’s implementation deadline and follows a separate temporary easing of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday condemned the White House's waiver of key provisions of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine. "... The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy said in a post on X . "And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people." President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving key parts of the new U.S. sanctions on Russia. "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order. The House passed the Russia sanctions bill on Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the late Lindsey Graham , a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina. Titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 , the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continued full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas. Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders. Zelenskyy said he expects Trump to waive other sanctions on Russia, too. "Sanctions relief will continue," he posted on X. "I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately." The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran. Oil sales revenue is critical to funding Russia's war effort. The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran. High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. "The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's economy envoy, said in a post on X. "The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added. But Trump's opponents have criticized the move. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver. "Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthal said in an X post. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy had warned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives. "Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry." Earlier this week, reports emerged that Ukraine has restricted SpaceX's Starlink military application, Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.

events.title: Is FIFA scrapping its peace prize after awarding it to US President Trump?
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections FIFA committee to assess the merits of the award after several members demand its discontinuation. Remember the FIFA Peace Prize awarded to United States President Donald Trump six months before the World Cup? Well, it is now close to being scrapped, which would make the US president its first and only winner. Less than a year after FIFA President Gianni Infantino extolled Trump in the US capital while presenting the award at the World Cup 2026 draw, several members of the FIFA Council are questioning its merit and have demanded changes, including scrapping the award. list 1 of 3 India and West Indies denied a thrilling finale as rain hits final T20 list 2 of 3 Neto’s brace fires Chelsea past Everton but Martinez head injury mars win list 3 of 3 Arsenal look to end goal drought at Forest in Premier League clash The calls for scrutiny come at a time when Infantino faces ongoing criticism for his World Cup sell-off plan, which also led to calls for his removal from office. So what was the prize about, and why might it be scrapped? Here’s a look: On November 5, football’s global governing body announced a new annual award called the “FIFA Peace Prize – Football Unites the World”. FIFA said the award was created to “reward individuals who have taken exceptional and extraordinary actions for peace”. Why did Trump receive the FIFA Peace Prize? A month later, Trump became the first recipient of the award . The US leader had been heavily favoured to win the inaugural prize after failing to win the Nobel Peace Prize despite an aggressive campaign involving endorsements from other world leaders. Trump thanked FIFA and called the award “one of the great honours of my life”. He and Infantino are close allies, and the FIFA chief had made it clear that he thought Trump should have won the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts to broker a ceasefire in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. “This is your prize. This is your peace prize,” Infantino said at the glitzy, celebrity-studded ceremony at Washington, DC’s Kennedy Center. Infantino has repeatedly spoken about football as a unifier for the world, but the prize is a departure from the federation’s traditional focus on sport. Critics pointed out that the recognition came less than 24 hours after the Trump administration carried out a deadly air strike in the Caribbean. Two months later, the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, assassinating Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in Tehran and hitting nuclear and military sites around the country. The US-Israel war on Iran has gone on for months with Trump saying this week that he will not attack Iran again before the November 3 midterm elections in the US. Several FIFA member nations demanded the discontinuation of the award during Thursday’s FIFA Council meeting in Zurich, Switzerland, according to reports in British media. Others called for the prize to no longer be handed out to politicians. As a result, FIFA’s 22-member Football Social Responsibility Committee was tasked with assessing the merits of the award. It is expected to make a recommendation before the next council meeting in Doha, Qatar, on December 16. Debbie Hewitt, a FIFA vice president and president of the English Football Association, told the media at the council briefing that the committee “will consider, first of all, how the peace prize came about, whether it should have come about, whether it should have been awarded in the way that it was, who made that decision and whether or not it should be taken out or whether it should be reformed”. Al Jazeera has reached out to FIFA for comment and was referred to Infantino’s statement on it: “For the FIFA Peace Prize, it was decided that the Football Social Responsibility Committee will be tasked to analyse it, provide a proposal, and also, there, a decision will be taken at the next FIFA Council meeting.” Has the FIFA Peace Prize faced opposition? In October, the Norwegian Football Association (NFF) made parallel filings with ⁠⁠FIFA committees in relation to three recent issues, one of which was related to the awarding of the FIFA Peace Prize. “The purpose is ⁠⁠to raise these issues formally with the appropriate bodies, to have them examined, relevant evidence obtained and accountability for the conclusions reached,” the NFF said in a statement. The NFF has repeatedly raised questions about the award, and in April, its president, Lise Klaveness, said FIFA should scrap its peace prize to avoid getting drawn into ⁠⁠politics. “We want to see it abolished. We don’t think it’s part of FIFA’s mandate to give such a prize. We think we have a Nobel institute that does that job independently already,” Klaveness said.
