events.title: Anti-party, anti-politician candidates surge in midterms
events.summary: In red states and blue, unconventional candidates are downplaying — or even disowning — party labels to tap into voters' deep disdain for Washington. Why it matters: They might not all win, but the sheer number of political outsiders connecting with voters tells us something about the electorate: It's angry and willing to take risks. The candidates — whether they come from the pulpit or the NFL sidelines — are making the same bet: Voters are tired of career politicians. Zoom in: Consider three unorthodox Democrats leading in Senate contests in three red states: a Presbyterian seminarian in Texas (state Rep. James Talarico), a megachurch pastor in Kansas (Adam Hamilton), and an Alaska Native in that state (former Rep. Mary Peltola, who once skipped a week of House votes to go fishing when Chinook salmon were running). Deep-blue Minnesota's Senate race features Michele Tafoya — a former NFL sideline reporter who's endorsed by President Trump but calls herself an independent Republican. She's mounting a serious challenge to Democrat Peggy Flanagan , the lieutenant governor. In House races, on the Democratic side there's a smokejumper in Montana (Sam Forstag), a 29-year-old barista in Colorado (Melat Kiros) and a Tejano singer in Texas (Bobby Pulido). Four independent Senate candidates are courting Democratic voters without running with a (D) next to their names — and sometimes without a Democrat officially in the race. In Nebraska, Dan Osborn, a union steamfitter and former factory mechanic, is mounting a serious independent challenge to Sen. Pete Ricketts, a former two-term governor whose family owns the Chicago Cubs. In Montana, Seth Bodnar , a former Army Green Beret and University of Montana president, is running as an independent for an open Senate seat. Democrats tried to persuade their nominee to drop out, but she stayed in the race. In South Dakota, Brian Bengs, a onetime park ranger, is challenging Republican Sen. Mike Rounds as an independent. Four years ago, Bengs ran against Sen. John Thune as a Democrat. In Idaho, former Army tank commander and tech executive Todd Achilles is running as an independent against Republican Sen. Jim Risch. (Achilles previously served in the Idaho House as a Democrat. The official Democratic Senate nominee dropped out of the race in July.) For many Republicans , quasi-Democrats running as independents amount to foul play — an attempt to deceive voters by discarding an unpopular brand. Between the lines: Even candidates with more conventional backgrounds are shading their biographies to meet the populist moment. In the Maine Senate race, Democrat Troy Jackson — who spent two decades in the state House and Senate before being term-limited out in 2024 — introduces himself as a fifth-generation Maine logger. Zoom out: The populist path to Washington is at least as old as President Andrew Jackson, who first took office in 1829. It's as fresh as President Trump. In recent years, there have been unorthodox candidates on both sides. Some succeeded; others didn't. Al Franken, famous for being a writer and actor on "Saturday Night Live," won a U.S. Senate seat in Minnesota in 2008 and served more than eight years before resigning. Herschel Walker, a celebrated college and NFL running back, couldn't find the end zone in his 2022 Senate race in Georgia. Say what you want about the 45th and 47th president: The New York developer with a penchant for gold leaf has connected with disaffected working-class voters. Democrats have struggled to match Trump's appeal to non-college-educated voters, but Trump has made their task easier this cycle with an unpopular war and tariffs that voters blame for high prices. The bottom line: A version of the insurgent-vs.-establishment battle played out in Democratic primaries earlier this year, when seven House incumbents went down — tying a 21st-century high . That included Kiros, the 29-year-old Colorado barista and democratic socialist who defeated a 15-term incumbent in the primary and is on a glide path to victory next month.

events.title: The overlooked geography of American poverty
events.summary: Data: U.S. Census ; Map: Erin Davis/Axios California and Louisiana have something surprising in common: Both have among the nation's highest poverty rates when the cost of living is factored in, according to Census Bureau data. Why it matters: Southern states dominate America's traditional poverty rankings. But that familiar geographic divide starts to disappear when more of a family's financial realities are taken into account. Axios analyzed 2023-2025 state poverty estimates from the Census Bureau to see what happens when housing, taxes, medical expenses and government benefits enter the picture. What we found: Under the Census' traditional-style official measure, Louisiana had a 19.6% poverty rate and California was at 10.7%. New Hampshire was the lowest at 5.4%. The South is home to 10 of the 11 states where the traditional poverty rate significantly outpaced the national average. California's poverty rate jumped by nearly two-thirds to 17.8% under the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure , or SPM. Louisiana remained near the top at 19%. Maine posted the nation's lowest SPM rate at 6.4%, followed by Nebraska at 7.5% and Minnesota at 7.9%. How it works: The traditional measure compares pretax cash income with a family-size threshold that doesn't change by geography. The SPM adds benefits such as SNAP and housing assistance, factors in taxes and tax credits, subtracts work and medical expenses, and adjusts for geographic differences in housing costs. Zoom out: The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year to 10.2%, while child poverty reached a record-low 13.4%. Yet the SPM remained statistically unchanged at 13.1% — nearly three percentage points above the official rate . Real median household income hit a record $87,460 in 2025. Yes, but: The SPM doesn't replace the official poverty rate. Census designed it as another lens — one that captures resources and unavoidable expenses the traditional measure misses. The state figures also aren't single-year 2025 estimates. Census recommends three-year averages because state samples in the Current Population Survey are smaller. The bottom line: Income alone doesn't tell you whether a family can make ends meet.

events.title: I've never lied to my 10-year-old about death, Santa, or what's really in her dinner
events.summary: The author hasn't lied to her daughter, even about Santa. Courtesy of the author I've made it nearly 10 years into motherhood without telling my daughter a lie. I don't believe in white lies, even when telling the truth makes parenting harder. I think being honest has helped my daughter trust me and brought us closer together. From where I stand, it seems like most parents lie to their kids , at least once in a while. I am of the mindset that lying , whether to adults or to children, is wrong. Because I view it this way, I am uncomfortable with it and refuse to do it. My husband respects my stance, though he doesn't always follow suit and has told our child a handful of lies. But in the past decade since I became a mom, I have managed to avoid it. I don't think I'm better than other parents, and I don't think anyone else is bad for harmless untruths . I just knew going into this that I wanted to approach parenting differently in a lot of ways, and this is just one of them. Not lying doesn't equal to sharing every detail This doesn't mean I divulge every secret. Kids don't need to know every detail about everything, even when they ask questions. I was rather vague when she wondered why one of our relatives split up with her husband less than a year after the marriage, for example: "He did something really bad, and it hurt her a lot. She's not able to forgive him," I said, that was the end of the conversation. The author's daughter asked her if Santa was real. Courtesy of the author I believe it is OK to keep some things a mystery indefinitely, to delay certain conversations or, when choosing to reveal things, to do so in an age-appropriate way (for example, where do babies come from?). But as far as not speaking any falsehoods , I have been consistent. She asked me if Santa was real I didn't tell her that Santa existed , but of course, as a toddler, she started believing through other friends, family, and Christmas marketing. I thought it was lovely and let her believe. Why spoil her fun? But when she was a little older and asked me point blank if Santa was real, I replied in a curious tone "Hmmm, what do you think?" and instead it turned a situation where she started wondering aloud and trying to reason whether it was possible. I listened in the car, nodding along in the parent drop-off line at school. I also told her that a lot of people — including kids in her class — do believe in Santa, so it wouldn't be nice for their parents if she expressed her doubts to her peers. She agreed and went along to the classroom. Granted, I got lucky that it went in this direction. I was able to stay true to my "no direct lies" approach while not shattering a very magical childhood belief — one I remember fondly from my own youth. And other common ones — like lying about a pet fish dying, or telling the truth when asked about a dinner ingredient, knowing there'd be resistance, or whether I remembered to do everything she asked of me — I don't lie about those either. The author doesn't lie about what's in her daughter's food either. Courtesy of the author These were not always easy conversations (those situations alone resulted in her first lesson about death, her stubbornness to try some foods, and me disappointing her and admitting that "no sorry, I didn't babysit your stuffy while you were at school; I forgot this time."). Honesty has brought us closer together If she questions what I think of the makeup she did on my face, I enthusiastically compliment her creativity and say how fun it was to be in her makeover chair; I don't lie and say that the electric pink eyeshadow is the best color ever. I feel that it has built more trust between us and brought us closer. She knows that when she asks mommy something, I'm going to be straight up with her. She doesn't seem to doubt me or second-guess what I say. As a parent, I understand that we are wired to protect our children. But with lying, I think parents are often trying to protect themselves. We want things to be easier, understandably. We want to say the place is closed instead of just telling the truth that we are just too tired to take them today. We want to tell our kid, "Yeah, the spider is gone now, honey," so they'll sleep well instead of saying that I actually have no idea where it went. But avoiding discomfort is not a strong enough reason for me to lie to my daughter. It's not just that I believe lying is immoral; it's also about feeling that she deserves the truth. Plus, if honesty is one of the values that I'm trying to teach her, I want to set a good example by being honest with her. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: What help can Egypt offer Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis?
events.summary: Analysts say that any move from Egypt will remain ‘strictly defensive’, as the conflict in Yemen intensifies. Egypt’s parliament is convening on Sunday after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi requested an emergency session to approve defensive military aid to Saudi Arabia, if Riyadh asks for support in its war with Yemen’s Houthis. The request comes as the Iran-backed armed group continues attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the capital, Riyadh, and its airports and oil facilities. list 1 of 3 How far will Egypt go to help Saudi Arabia secure the Red Sea? list 2 of 3 Egypt’s el-Sisi vows to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks list 3 of 3 Saudi-led coalition intercepts drones as Egypt weighs sending help El-Sisi declared that Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia, in a speech on Saturday, but said that he “hopes” the parliament will give him authorisation to proceed. On Sunday, Egypt said it would provide “all necessary and possible support to Saudi Arabia to defend its safety and stability”. The National Defence Council, chaired by President el-Sisi, said it “stands fully with” Saudi Arabia to defend its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites. But what would Egyptian assistance look like? And what capacity does it have to “protect” Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis? What’s behind el-Sisi’s decision to offer help to Saudi Arabia? Saudi Arabia has long been a strategic and economic partner of Egypt, and el-Sisi said in a statement last month that Saudi security is “integral” to Egypt’s security. Political analyst and Gulf studies expert Thomas Bonnie James told Al Jazeera that the Houthi security threat to the kingdom is one of the “converging” pressures that have led to this decision. The other one, is economics. “Houthi pressure on [Bab] al-Mandeb threatens the Suez Canal , which Egypt’s foreign minister says has lost about $11bn since the attacks began in 2023,” he said, referring to Houthi attacks on Israeli-linked ships passing through the narrow strait, carried out in solidarity with Gaza. James suggested that the decision is also important to Cairo, because “millions of Egyptians live and work in Saudi Arabia, which is Egypt’s largest single source of remittances. An Egyptian resident was killed, and others were injured in the attacks on Riyadh’s airport.” He also said that Egypt does not want to be seen as the regional ally that “stood aside while others defended the kingdom,” as Turkiye and Pakistan have made their own pledges after activating the Mecca defence pact signed in August amid the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East. What’s the latest on the Yemen war? Hostilities in Yemen continue to escalate. Two air raids by the Saudi-led coalition hit Hodeidah in the southwest on Sunday. Saudi forces also intercepted drones near Riyadh and Eastern provinces. The capital’s King Khalid international airport has come under attack at least 20 times since fighting flared between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God. The Saudi-backed forces are fighting the Houthis on several fronts, including Taiz and Marib, and some analysts argue the Houthis are stretched thin after their summer gains. But James told Al Jazeera “that defeating them outright is a tall order”. “Ground forces backed by air power can retake the coastline; stopping missiles launched from the mountains is much harder,” he said. When will the Egyptian parliament convene? They will be convening on Sunday at 1pm local time (10am GMT). Under the Egyptian law, the President cannot declare war or send the military on foreign missions without the approval from the parliament. For the authorisation to be granted, at least two-thirds of the politicians in the House of Representatives must vote in favour of the proposal. Does Egypt have security cooperation with Saudi Arabia? Not exactly. Egypt and Saudi Arabia have not signed a formal bilateral or multilateral pact on defence cooperation. But Cairo has a long history of cooperation with Riyadh. Egypt is a founding member of the Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition, which Saudi Arabia launched in July. It aims to protect shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb – territories on Yemen’s coastline. Houthis captured towns and cities near Bab al-Mandeb last month, but the internationally recognised government has since wrested control of some of the areas from the Iran-backed group. Egypt also participated in joint military exercises with Saudi Arabia in 2024. Cairo was also part of a 2015 coalition , cobled together after the Houthi group captured large areas of north and western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa in September 2024. Egypt contributed naval and air forces to help secure maritime corridors in the Red Sea against the Houthis.

events.title: Semiconductor market to remain solid ‘at least through next year,’ South Korea finance minister says
events.summary: The semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said. Lee said semiconductor demand still far exceeds supply, even as producers expand capacity. Semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition. The semiconductor boom will last at least through 2027, South Korean finance minister Lee Hyoung-Il said on Saturday. "For now, our view is that we can sustain this growth at least through next year," Lee told CNBC on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "That's because the gap between demand and supply for semiconductors is still very wide, and supply is still being expanded." His comments come after semiconductor stocks fell sharply this week, hurt by investor concerns about interest rate hikes and rising competition from Chinese companies. South Korean chip stocks like SK Hynix and Seoul Semiconductor were part of the sell-off, along with U.S. giants like Nvidia . Chip stocks' large weighting has fueled volatility in South Korea's stock market this year, Lee said. He attributed the market's wild swings to the semiconductor industry's larger share of the economy than in other countries. Despite the market swings, South Korea's economy is "solid," Lee said. On Thursday, an opinion column in Maeil Business Newspaper , a prominent South Korean publication, urged the country's government to prepare for the coming slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom. The author said two experts expect a "flood of new supply" of semiconductors that will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" by 2029, according to a CNBC translation . events.title: Wanted: Chief small talk officers. Awkward applicants welcome
events.summary: Some people don't like to make small talk . Others — especially younger Americans — say they simply don't know how to do it. Why it matters: A communication-skills app is betting that a baptism by fire in small talk can help rebuild social confidence — and it's hiring people to approach strangers to put that theory to the test. Driving the news: RiseGuide is hiring Chief Small Talk Officers — recently rebranded from Head of Hanging Out to stress the seriousness of the assignment. The monthlong gig pays each of up to three hires $2,000, plus a budget for outings to parks, bookstores and fitness classes, where they'll strike up conversations with strangers. Officers will rate their small talk skills before and after the assignment, with regular check-ins to assess their interactions. They'll also track conversation lengths and strangers' receptiveness, Anastasia Sliusarenko, RiseGuide's brand and reputation manager, tells Axios. "I'm personally rooting for applicants who kind of feel socially awkward," she says, because their improvement could be more noticeable. She acknowledges the irony of using an app to combat screen time, but says the ultimate goal is for users to "get off the app" and practice their skills in real life. What they're saying: "We actually know from research that something like social confidence can actually be trained... it's not a personality trait," Laura Berssenbrugge, a therapist who specializes in working with Gen Z and Gen Alpha, tells Axios. Social confidence doesn't have to look like the loudest extrovert in the room, Berssenbrugge adds. "That can be social confidence for them. Ours might look a little bit different, and that is absolutely okay." The big picture: Smartphones and personalized digital feeds may be changing how Americans find common ground and navigate conversations with strangers. Earlier generations often shared cultural reference points, from limited TV channels to major sporting events, that offered easy conversation starters. Today's algorithms instead feed people niche interests, reducing opportunities for common ground. Phones also offer an easy escape from awkward interactions, potentially reducing opportunities to practice face-to-face conversation. Zoom in: Even bars, once natural gathering places for spontaneous conversations, aren't immune to the shift, D.C.-area bartender Matty Pivec tells Axios. "If you're sitting at a bar, you kind of naturally fall into place of talking to the person next to you... If you have your phone while you're waiting for the bartender, it's much easier to avoid that." "It's become more of a chore than kind of a pleasant surprise to be able to hold a conversation with a stranger," he says, adding, "I think it's kind of a dying thing to go out and meet strangers." John Lemay, a 14-year veteran bartender at D.C.-area bar Spider Kelly's, partly blames dating apps: "Why would you engage in conversation with somebody [at a bar] if you can just check those boxes and wham, your perfect date pops up," he says. Between the lines: Avoiding strangers might spare people the anxiety of appearing awkward or "cringe," but it also cuts them off from the psychological benefits of casual interactions. Psychologist Ellen Hendriksen points to a study of Chicago rush hour commuters that found those who interacted with strangers reported more positive experiences than those who kept to themselves. Many "underestimated how much they were going to enjoy that," she says. The bottom line: The goal isn't to become an extrovert. It's to get comfortable with the discomfort of striking up conversations with strangers. Go deeper: Birding, silent book club, Mahjong and more: America's meetup explosion

events.title: Gleaning group gives £1m of produce to food banks
events.summary: Gleaning Cornwall relies on volunteers to reduce food waste on farms A gleaning group has saved £1m worth of fruit and vegetables that would have been left in field and donated them to food banks. Gleaning Cornwall relies on volunteers to collect unwanted produce from harvested fields, delivering it to 160 food banks, community larders and kitchens across the South West. Despite reaching the seven-figure milestone, the group has warned more funding is needed in order to keep up with demand. Reliance on food banks is increasing and since 2015 the number of known settings providing food aid in Cornwall has risen from 20 to 180, according to Cornwall Council. The gleaning group has saved 460 tonnes of produce since the start of 2020 Gleaning Cornwall started in 2020 and said it had repurposed more than 460 tonnes of produce since then. But the charity's founder, Holly Whitelaw, warned it was now threatened by economic constraints. "There is less money around and we need to do more with it," she said. "Our infrastructure urgently needs funding if we are to keep going." The charity said it fed 11,000 people every week with the stipulation that all its produce must be completely free to recipients. However, the organisation said the cost of transport, storage and coordination was rising sharply. Listen to the latest news for Cornwall It comes at a time when food bank usage is higher than ever with statistics from Cornwall's Trussell Trust showing its food banks distributed more than 35,500 emergency food parcels between April 2024 and March 2025. A study by Cornwall Council found that 30% of children in the county are living in food poverty. Whitelaw encouraged people to play their part by reducing the amount of food they wasted at home. She said: "If we waste food, we waste the substantial energy that went into producing it. "Utilising what we already have saves money and helps the environment." events.title: Jordan-Israel border becomes new hotspot for sophisticated drug trade
events.summary: Smugglers in the Negev desert are increasingly using drones and helium balloons to transport narcotics across the border into Jordanian territory. Amman, Jordan – Jordanians fear the country’s border with Israel is turning into a major drug-smuggling route amid a surge in high-tech operations by gangs using drones and helium-filled balloons. Organised networks active in southern Israel’s Negev Desert have links to groups in Jordan and the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt, operating along one of the most heavily surveilled borders in the world, with Jordanian authorities increasingly concerned about the implications this could have for the kingdom. list 1 of 3 Three years of Israel’s mass dispossession of West Bank Palestinians list 2 of 3 King David Hotel bombing to consulate row: A timeline of UK-Israel tension list 3 of 3 If Netanyahu goes, does anything really change for Palestinians? This escalation coincides with changes in the regional drug trade, particularly after the fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in late 2024. Elements in his regime were linked to the manufacturing and distribution of Captagon, an illegal amphetamine stimulant. Syria became a hub for the distribution of Captagon to the Gulf, with Jordan a transit point and market for the drug. The Royal Jordanian Air Force carried out periodic strikes on drug manufacturing and smuggling points inside Syria, highlighting the huge security concerns Jordan had about the trade. Since the collapse of the Assad government and the establishment of a new authority that views the Captagon trade as a national security issue, there has been a decrease in the drug trade from Syria into Jordan. Although Druze militias in the Syrian province of Suwayda allegedly linked to Israel have been accused of continuing the drug trade, Jordanian security forces are increasingly focused on the Jordan-Israel border. The use of quadcopter drones and balloons is reportedly among the new tactics used by gangs in Israel to smuggle hashish, crystal meth, and amphetamines into Jordan. Jordanian security forces are said to be increasingly unhappy with the scale of the drug smuggling operations and have accused the Israeli army of not taking the issue seriously. Initial data from Jordanian forces recorded 17 interception operations linked to drones during the first half of 2026 in Jordan’s southwestern border area with Israel. They also recorded 231 smuggling and infiltration attempts and downed 56 drones across various borders during the same period. Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al Jazeera that Jordanian forces were continuing efforts to prevent drugs from being smuggled into the kingdom. But they are evidently facing more complex activities by drug dealers. “There is an increase in drug smuggling operations from Israel to Jordan using drones,” he said. “The number of seized drug cases during the current year reached 15,342 cases. Trafficking cases constituted about 28 percent of them, compared with 72 percent for usage cases.” Israeli media reports indicate that gangs active in the Negev Desert are behind some of the smuggling operations into Jordan, where drugs can fetch higher profits. There are estimates that 1kg of hashish can sell for approximately 7,500 pounds sterling (almost $10,000), according to the British newspaper The Telegraph, which recently uncovered the drug smugglers’ latest operations. Israeli security services believe that the price of hashish in Jordan is about 15 times higher than in Israel. Due to widespread disenfranchisement and poverty, elements within Palestinian communities in Israel have been linked to the drug trade, according to reports. Multiple sources have accused Israel of allowing Palestinian towns and cities to become hotbeds of crime to create divisions and prevent calls for greater rights. Ammar al-Qudah, a member of the Jordanian Senate and retired major-general in the Public Security Directorate, claimed that organised gangs in the Negev had obtained more than 1,000 drones that were originally used for agricultural and security purposes. “The smuggling networks are linked to other gangs in Jordan, Sinai and the Negev, and rely on a route starting from Sinai, passing through the Negev, and reaching Wadi Araba, in addition to other routes including the Lebanese border with Israel and the Galilee region towards Syria,” he told Al Jazeera. They are also using a range of sophisticated technology to bypass security on both sides of the border. This includes the use of helium-filled balloons equipped with GPS devices, drones capable of carrying about 50kg of narcotics, including black hashish and crystal meth, al-Qudah said. He warned that a portion of the black hashish and crystal meth being smuggled into the kingdom is being sold domestically, with the rest going to other markets in the region.

events.title: I thought working in AI would put me ahead of the curve. Two years in, I've never felt more behind and tired of the topic.
events.summary: The author works in AI and is feeling burned out. Courtesy of Santiago Barraza Lopez I'm a lawyer who decided to work in AI to try to get ahead of this technological curve. Over the last two years, I've struggled to keep up because AI is advancing faster than I expected. I feel overwhelmed and burned out by the constant conversations around AI. For most of my career, I was a lawyer. There was something reassuring about how expertise worked in law. The longer I practiced, the more I knew. But after years in a demanding profession , I burned out. It wasn't that I stopped enjoying law. I just needed a change. Around two years ago, I started shifting my career toward AI because I thought it was the future. I didn't want to wake up 10 years later and realize technology had changed my profession without me. It seemed like the smartest career move I could make. Now, I'm not so sure. Joining the AI boom early seemed like the perfect career move I made the transition while the AI boom was still gaining momentum. Ironically, I landed a job at a legal tech company thanks to a conversation with ChatGPT . It seemed like the perfect opportunity to combine my experience with my growing interest in tech. My role involved testing the most advanced models, comparing their capabilities, and exploring how they could be used in legal work. I felt like I was ahead of a major change rather than trying to catch up with it. I also became the go-to person for anything AI-related among my family and friends. People would ask me which tools to use, whether AI would replace their jobs, or what I thought about the latest developments. I enjoyed being the person who seemed to understand something that everyone was suddenly talking about. But that feeling didn't last as long as I expected. Slowly, I began to realize that this wasn't just another new technology . It was something evolving at an almost frightening pace. And being close to it didn't necessarily mean being able to keep up with it. What initially felt like an advantage was gradually becoming a source of pressure. Things that took me weeks to learn or build became obsolete almost overnight New frontier AI models and companies seemed to arrive every few weeks, each promising capabilities that the previous lacked. Just as I began understanding one model, another would appear, forcing me to reconsider everything I thought I knew about what AI could and couldn't do. There was barely enough time to breathe before "the next big thing" came. What frustrated me most was how quickly my own work could lose its value. I spent weeks developing solutions to problems that a newer model could suddenly solve within a few minutes. Things I had carefully learned a couple of months earlier became unnecessary after a single product announcement. It was strange to put so much effort into something only to discover that the technology had already overtaken me. And the constant learning didn't stop when I finished work. AI was everywhere. It was in the news, on social media , in conversations with friends, and in almost every discussion about the future of work. Sometimes, after spending an entire day testing models, the last thing I wanted to hear about was another breakthrough. Yet I still felt an obligation to read about it, afraid that missing a single development could leave me even further behind. I was getting tired. Accepting uncertainty became the only way forward For years, I had measured my professional progress by how much I knew and how confident I felt about my abilities. AI challenged that completely. I began to question whether being good at my job meant knowing the latest developments or simply knowing how to adapt as everything changed. It was uncomfortable to accept that experience and hard work might not always provide the certainty I was used to. I also started questioning how much of my personal time I was willing to sacrifice to stay relevant. I didn't want every conversation, evening, or weekend to become another opportunity to learn or talk about AI. I began making a conscious effort to disconnect after work, even if that meant missing an announcement or falling behind on the latest developments. For the first time, I was choosing not to know everything. I don't regret moving into AI, but I no longer feel as certain about the decision as I once did. The technology isn't going to slow down. All I know for sure is that we are living through one of the most important inflection points in recent history, and perhaps that's what makes it all so overwhelming. events.title: Katie Zacharia and the real problem with workers embellishing their credentials
events.summary: Samuel Corum/Pool/FTWP This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . The credibility concern When questions began swirling about new (and now former) White House press secretary Katie Zacharia's legal credentials , a colleague asked the obvious question: Why should anyone care? She was hired to be President Donald Trump's spokesperson, not his lawyer. Does it really matter if she overstated her qualifications? It does. She was let go on Friday , five days after starting the job. That's half the time Anthony Scaramucci infamously lasted as White House communications director during Trump's first term. Zacharia was widely panned for her performance during her first (and final) press briefing on Monday, as well as for misrepresenting herself as a lawyer. In workplaces, it turns out, bending the truth about one's background is not only problematic, but more common than you might think. And it can carry real consequences. BI's Sarah Needleman spoke with recruiters and found research suggesting that résumé inflation is very much a thing . A recent survey found 37% of respondents had included inaccurate information on a résumé, according to Novorésumé, an online résumé-building service. Nearly 7% said they claimed a degree, certification, or credential they didn't actually have. The trouble, of course, is that a small embellishment can raise much bigger questions. Brian Fink, a managing partner at tech recruiting firm The ReWork Group, told Sarah he rescinded an offer to someone after a background check couldn't verify certain information on the candidate's résumé and LinkedIn profile. "If you're willing to lie about your education," Fink said, "what else are you willing to lie about?" Corporate America is full of cautionary tales. Over the years, executives at Samsonite , Walmart , and Yahoo , among others , misrepresented their backgrounds and ultimately lost their jobs as a result. Credentials matter. They are a promise of basic trust. Once that trust is called into question, it's really hard to win it back. Read the original article on Business Insider

A “massive” Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg in Russia has killed at least one person and injured five others, the city’s governor said on Sunday. Alexandre Beglov said firefighters were battling blazes at the St Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchi oil depot and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district south of the city. list 1 of 3 Israel’s ties with Europe are fraying. Can its election change that? list 2 of 3 Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing list 3 of 3 Photos: Protests across France spiral into looting, blazes and clashes The governor said several residential buildings were also hit, along with two houses. City authorities said the attack disrupted flights at St Petersburg’s main airport, one of the country’s busiest, which was restricting operations “for safety reasons”, Beglov said. Russian e-commerce company Ozon said there was a fire at its logistics hub in St Petersburg, and the internet company VK said its data centre in the Leningrad region had been attacked by drones, adding that normal services were available to users. The governor of the Leningrad region surrounding St Petersburg, Alexander Drozdenko, said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity following the drone raid. Russia’s state-run news agency TASS said the attack was the largest on the region in the last four years. Moscow’s defence ministry said 1,015 Ukrainian drones were neutralised overnight. In Ukraine, Russian forces struck residential buildings overnight, killing two people and injuring 12, including two children, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Sunday. “This morning, there was a strike on an agricultural enterprise in Volyn. All necessary services are working at the site,” he said. “In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic.” The attacks came after Zelenskyy said this week that Kyiv would resume hitting Russian refineries, insisting he was standing up for his war-torn country, as support from the United States declined. Zelenskyy told the British newspaper the Financial Times this week that Kyiv was “done” with an “energy ceasefire” unilaterally declared by United States President Donald Trump and would resume strikes on Russia in retaliation for a wave of attacks. Trump announced an immediate “ energy ceasefire ” between Russia and Ukraine last week, but Zelenskyy said Moscow continued to violate the deal. “Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ago, Russia has deliberately attacked Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors 76 times,” he wrote in his X post on Sunday. “Last night alone, there were strikes on substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions,” he wrote, adding that tens of thousands of families remained without power as energy workers and repair crews worked round the clock to restore supplies. Zelenskyy also said that the main targets of Moscow’s recent strikes were energy facilities, as the Russians were trying to “cause a blackout”. “America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said. Trump is also facing criticism in both Europe and the US after he signed an executive order on Friday to waive sanctions and tariffs targeting Moscow’s energy revenues. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump’s waiver would be a pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy. “The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia. Trump said late on Saturday his decision would benefit the US. “We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said. “It’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”

events.title: For Gen Z, everything looks like an investment. But it isn’t
events.summary: Twenty years ago, the distinction seemed simple. You invested through a brokerage account. You gambled at a casino. You were entertained by watching a game, movie or TV show. For Gen Z, those distinctions are far less obvious. Gen Z is the first generation to have their sportsbook, brokerage account, crypto exchange and prediction market apps all on the same device. With a few taps, they’re buying stocks, trading options, investing in digital assets, participating in prediction markets and wagering on sporting events. While each involves risk and the potential for reward, increasingly, they’re being delivered through a remarkably similar digital experience. This convergence is influencing behavior. According to recent surveys, 61% of Gen Z investors ages 18 to 25 report gambling either online or in person [1] , and 26% consider sports betting part of their investment strategy, compared with 6% of Gen X investors and just 1% of Baby Boomers. More than half (52%) of Gen Z investors say they’ve redirected funds intended for investing into sports betting within the last year. For some young investors, that means money originally allocated to long-term strategies is being funneled to activities built around immediate outcomes. As a result, a fundamental question has become surprisingly difficult to answer: While your sportsbook and brokerage app may resemble each other on your phone, does that mean they should be treated the same? When everything looks like a bet, understanding the difference matters more than ever. The difference isn’t risk. It’s purpose Investing, speculating and gambling all involve uncertainty and the potential for loss. The key distinction is not the risk that they’re willing to take but the purpose behind their behavior. What is the goal? Build long-term wealth, express a short-term view or pay for entertainment?  It’s less about deciding whether these activities are inherently good or bad, and more about understanding their distinct purpose and whether that intention aligns with one’s financial goals. Today’s challenge is that they are becoming harder to tell apart. The Lines are blurring No generation has experienced the convergence of investing, speculation and entertainment more than Gen Z. Sports betting platforms, investing apps, crypto exchanges and prediction markets increasingly share the same characteristics: intuitive mobile experiences, instant funding, real-time updates and constant engagement. For younger consumers who have always managed much of their lives through apps, these experiences often feel like different versions of the same activity. As financial markets have become more accessible, consumers have begun trading sophisticated financial instruments, purchasing fractional shares and gaining exposure to alternative assets in minutes.   At the same time, prediction markets have blurred the distinction between investing, speculation and entertainment. Some markets are allowing individuals to express views on economic, political or business outcomes, while others hone in on sports, entertainment and pop culture events. But from the user’s experience, they look strikingly similar, regardless of whether the activity is investing, speculation or entertainment. The result is what I call an “Is It Cake?” moment. Just as viewers of the popular show must look beyond appearances to determine whether an object is actually cake, today’s investors need to look beneath the surface to understand whether they’re investing, speculating or simply being entertained. Why it matters The blurring of these categories is increasingly shaping younger investors’ financial behaviors and likewise, long-term financial planning. A UCLA study found that average credit scores declined by 0.8 points after sports betting was legalized, and by 2.75 points when online sports betting became available, in addition to increases in bankruptcy, debt collections and auto-loan delinquencies. These outcomes can be particularly influential for Gen Z investors building a lifelong financial foundation. They aren’t inherently less disciplined or financially responsible. How they’re engaging certainly reflects the environment in which they were raised, with unprecedented digital access to markets, information and financial tools. The challenge they face is that the platforms hosting their investing, speculation and entertainment activities are being packaged to create an identical engagement experience; the interfaces, language and forms of instant feedback are all intended to keep the user on the platform. These platforms aren’t necessarily focused on helping consumers build healthy financial habits to build long-term wealth; instead, they’re primarily focused on engagement and dopamine. These functions can obscure crucial differences in how these activities are designed to reward users; a relatively small parlay wager can offer the possibility of an outsized, immediate payout if multiple outcomes occur. Conversely, long-term investing can rely on smaller returns compounded over longer periods.  Risk itself is not the problem. Risk is essential to investing, entrepreneurship and innovation. Speculation also serves an important function in helping markets operate efficiently. Even gambling, when approached responsibly, can be an enjoyable recreational activity. But we should be wary of unintentionally treating entertainment as investing, and of mistaking short-term speculation for long-term wealth building. When that happens, financial decisions become disconnected from long-term financial goals.   Understanding the differences Sports betting is primarily entertainment, and it’s having a moment in media. It’s essentially become its own asset class, growing into a nearly $17 billion domestic industry, up from $400 million in 2018. [4]  Even when participants believe they have an edge, the activity is generally pursued for enjoyment rather than long-term capital appreciation. Not to mention, the growing visibility of sportsbooks, whether advertisements on stadium fields or star athletes participating in commercials and sponsorships, has quickly become a normalized component of the consumer experience.  Prediction markets, on the other hand, are more nuanced. Speculators may play an important role in markets by contributing to liquidity, but success is measured over shorter time horizons and requires sophisticated risk management. Contracts tied to sporting events, entertainment or pop culture outcomes can very much resemble similar behaviors of gambling or entertainment. Whereas contracts tied to economic indicators, policy decisions or business outcomes more can more closely resemble speculative activity, as they allow for an expression or take on future events. events.title: Data Centers Have a New PR Plan: Your Kid’s Field Trip
events.summary: Welcome back to Power Play ! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at [email protected] or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61. The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “ What is a Data Center?, ” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.” "Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks. The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying , job creation programs , tax breaks , companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies , the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried. Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools. “A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says. In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy. Besides promoting heartwarming tales about how women can shop, 7x24 Exchange is also the brains behind a holiday it calls “International Data Center Day,” which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.” The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools , it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools , it offers data center-themed coloring pages , instructions for an evaporation-themed science project , and print-out activities like “ Draw a picture of the cloud" and “ Draw a data superhero .” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “ Polly Packet's Precious Payload ,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers. 7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers. Sabey, a company that runs seven US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students. Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry.

events.title: They're spooky, sexy, slidey — and driving ticket sales at Hershey's amusement park
events.summary: The Decayed Brigade, a team of haunt sliders that appears at Hersheypark. Hersheypark Hersheypark's "haunt sliders" — scare actors who slide on knee pads — have gained a fanbase on TikTok. "The makeup stays ON" commented one thirsty fan. The attention has translated to good business for the park, who has seen growing ticket sales for its Dark Nights event. Imagine you're walking around an amusement park in October while it's Halloween themed. The air is crisp, you've got a giant pretzel, you're strolling with friends to get in line for the roller coaster. Out of the corner of your eye, you see tall man dressed in all black with skeletal face paint walking towards you. Suddenly, he leaps to the ground on all fours, and against everything you've known in your life about how human beings ambulate, he slides across the pavement on his hands and knees, coasting right up beside you at an incredible speed. Depending on who you are and your level of awareness of the "haunt sliders" of Hersheypark, this fast encounter leaves you either terrified or terrifyingly horny. @itzarcher PUMPKINN @thrillsandmagic @Hersheypark #fyp #darknights2025 #decayedbrigade #viral #itzarcher ♬ original sound - itzarcher Since 2021, Hershey's amusement park has employed a group of haunt sliders from a crew that calls itself the "Decayed Brigade" for its Dark Nights Halloween event that runs in September and October. Videos of Fryboy and his lookalike Archer, and others have racked up millions of views and created a dedicated fan base who travel from around the world just to see the creepy, sexy, slidey guys they saw on TikTok. And their online popularity is good for Hershey's bottom line. "The comment section [on TikTok] is a treasure trove of insight into their popularity. I mean, we have seen people saying, 'I am coming from Europe. I'm coming from Australia. I had no idea Hersheypark existed, but now, because this was served to me on TikTok, I'm aware,'" said Quinn Bryner, a spokesperson for Hersheypark. Archer, a haunt slider at Hersheypark Hersheypark "We have people who have bought our season passes because of it," she added. "So anecdotally, for sure, it has had a significant social commentary, which we think has also led to tickets." Bryner cautioned they can't say that the haunt sliders popularity is the sole driver of the growth of the Halloween event, but that the Dark Nights has become a success and grown year over year in attendance and ticket sales. "We can confirm that the event's popularity in the past few years has allowed us to expand operating days throughout the fall, resulting in total Halloween attendance doubling the numbers achieved prior to 2021," she said. @hersheypark We're SO back 🙌🔥 #Hersheypark #fyp #halloween #amusementpark #decayedbrigade ♬ original sound - Hersheypark For the last three years, Fryboy and some of the sliders do a meet-and-greet for the diehard fans after the performance on weekend nights. Fans wait up to an hour in line to meet them and take photos with the sliders (or purchase keychains or other photo prints from the professional photography service the park provides, which has taken over 4,000 photos for fans this fall so far). The three sliders I interviewed — who asked not to publicize their full legal names because they are concerned about overzealous fans — have breached containment from something that happens inside the park gates to a full-blown social media phenomenon. The sliders have anecdotally noticed the effects of TikTok on the crowds in the park. "This year especially, it feels like every other person's coming up saying they drove eight-plus hours to come see us or they just came for us," Fryboy said. "We see them sit in our zone the whole night and it's pretty obvious that they just want to watch us," Valkyrie noticed. Hersheypark is well aware of the Decayed Brigade's social media success, which is clear even on its own social channels. The most viewed videos on park's official TikTok channel were all of the sliders — even during the off-season. Haunt sliding dates back decades Haunt sliding has been a part of Knott's Scary Farm, the Halloween event at amusement park in southern California, for decades. A few of the performers working there figured out they could modify knee pads and gloves with metal pieces to allow them to slide up on guests as a novel way to scare them. Sliding became a staple of Knott's Scary Farm, and the trend spread out around the country to various haunted theme parks and cornfields. It evolved into something more than just a scare tactic, with increasingly athletic stunts, choreography, and showcases during the off-season. Although haunt sliding has become a haunted house mainstay, there is no group of performers who have attracted as much attention from people who never set foot in Hersheypark as the Decayed Brigade crew. This year, there are eight sliders, but Fryboy and Archer — both well over six feet tall, lanky, and with poufy dark hair — seem to have garnered the biggest online fandom. @fryboydb We didn’t check. @itzarcher @Jet ♬ original sound - chicolantern When I spoke over a video call with Fryboy, Archer, and Valkerie, the current sole female performer in this year's crew, it was the hour before the park opened on a Friday night at 6 p.m., and they were in their full faces of makeup (they have a makeup artist on staff who does it for them), but not their performance clothes. Fryboy, whose real first name is Carter, is not technically the leader or founder of Decayed Brigade, although he has become the most visible online and has been working at Hersheypark since Dark Nights started in 2021. He first saw sliders at Knott's Scary Farm when he was 13, and was inspired to start trying it out on his own at home. By 16, he got hired at a local haunted house in Florida, and eventually landed a job at Knott's in 2018. "When sliding first started, it was mainly just a scare tactic and it wasn't really anything crazy, but once people started doing it more and more, a lot of the guys that started sliding at Knott's were stunt performers, so they would do little pre-shows before their stunt show was sliding," Fryboy explained. "They'd go out there and they'd do little rolls, and then they'd start jumping bodies, and then now they're jumping two, three, four bodies. So then tricks started getting added into it, and over time, a group was formed." "I really think in this case, Carter took it upon himself to create his own iconic character in the social space and then share it amongst an audience that loves scare, but didn't have a way to maybe communicate and build on that," said Brewer Lister, managing director of immersive experiences at Hersheypark. "He's built a following, and then he and his team have added to it by becoming more of a team in a group, especially Archer, the two of them," he added. events.title: My dad's death gave me a new perspective. I value experiences over money now.
events.summary: When the author's dad died, she reevaluated her approach to work. Courtesy of Tayla Blaire I used to push myself at work, outearning myself year after year. When my dad died, and I heard how people talked about him, I reevaluated my approach. Now, I still make enough to cover what I need, but I'm living a fuller life. I'm a reformed workaholic. I'd love to say I slowly came to realize that my value isn't monetary or based on how high I can climb a ladder , but that epiphany wasn't achieved in a growth-centric way. Instead, it was a surprising side effect of losing my dad suddenly in September 2024. He was there, and just like that, he was gone. And my willingness to burn myself out died that day, too. In the flurry of administrative chaos and world-wrecking grief that follows sudden death, it took a while for me to notice the change. It was normal to work less while grieving . Except it's now almost two years later — and yes, I'm still very much grieving — but I am back in the flow of working. And it looks completely different. I had been working hard for years When I was balancing full-time teaching with a writing side hustle , I regularly pulled ridiculous hours, working from 7 am until late at night. Not only that, but I was also frequently working both weekend days and throughout school vacation. I even had an accident in May 2024 that put me out of work while my arm was in a sling to help the broken bones heal, but once I was back, I hit my highest earning month of all time. But then my dad died, and I just don't care the way I used to. There wasn't an inheritance that suddenly made working optional. And it's not all-consuming depression either — the months that followed were immensely dark, but I'm doing really well from a mental health perspective now. Instead, there's been a reshuffling of priorities. My identity fundamentally shifted in 2024. I came entirely too close to dying in an accident while riding horses , where doctors couldn't fathom how I survived without paraplegia, and then, mere months later, my dad had a heart attack at 65. The way people spoke about my dad made me want to live a fuller life The eulogies poured in for my dad, who was a beloved doctor. Hundreds of people messaged us, telling stories of my dad's generosity, his kindness, adventurous spirit, talent, sense of humor, and utter chaos. The sheer number of anecdotes was almost mythical, as it seemed impossible that someone could do so much with their time. My dad even started kitesurfing in his 50s because he thought it would be cool, and regularly drove hours out of town to reach the nearest dam to do it. His last kiting session was the week before he died. He was an astronomer, a chess player , an artist, a rugby fanatic, a dear friend, a dedicated husband, and the best dad anyone could wish for. It made me look at my own life. I was out-earning myself , year after year. But I lived in a city that gave me little joy, and my hobbies were…well, just reading. And often, I was only reading self-help books to help me earn more or be more productive. It's not that I took a step back from work. I just didn't step forward again. I have ongoing luxury travel copywriting clients. I still do a fair bit of journalism and a little bit of coaching essay writers. I ensure I earn enough to make ends meet — pay my mortgage , set aside money for my retirement, health insurance, and so on, but that's it. Once that goal is met each month, my foot comes off the accelerator, and I focus on life instead. I moved to the coast and qualified as an advanced open water scuba diver. I knock off early on Fridays to hit the beach if it's a nice day, and I'm dabbling in surfing. I've started lifting weights. I have more friends than I've ever had before. I've started painting, and my guitar has been dusted off and tuned again. I don't have it all worked out. I'm still trying to figure out what life without my dad can possibly look like. I just know how much life he crammed into the years he had, and the best way I can honor him is to try to do the same. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Presidency says Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with support to defend its security and protect its resources. Egypt says it is ready to provide “all necessary and possible support to Saudi Arabia to defend its safety and stability”, as Yemen’s Houthis continue to launch attacks on the kingdom. The National Defence Council, chaired by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, said on Sunday that Egypt “stands fully with” Saudi Arabia to defend its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites. list 1 of 3 Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means list 2 of 3 US and Iran both claim control of Strait of Hormuz amid attacks on vessels list 3 of 3 Egypt’s el-Sisi seeks authorisation for defence assistance to Saudi Arabia The president’s office added that Cairo would also intensify diplomatic efforts for de-escalation. The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God – have in recent days attacked Riyadh’s international airport and the state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting in Yemen with forces loyal to the Saudi-backed, internationally ‌‌recognised government, following the collapse of a truce. Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would ⁠⁠act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited ⁠⁠Egypt last month after fighting in Yemen ⁠⁠reignited. He also called for an emergency parliamentary session, being held on Sunday, to authorise him to approve any requests from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance. In last month’s meeting with the Saudi Crown Prince in Cairo, el-Sisi had backed Saudi calls for secure and unhindered navigation in the Red Sea. A statement from the Egyptian presidency at the time said that “the security of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”. Analysts say Riyadh is looking for help to protect the kingdom and Red Sea shipping and that Egypt, whose Suez Canal revenue depends on the same traffic, is an obvious partner . They say Egypt is eager to prevent Iran and its allies from imposing control over the region, especially maritime traffic in the Red Sea, given the impact on the Suez Canal. events.title: What is the Budget and what could be in it?
events.summary: Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget on 28 October. He has refused to rule out tax increases after acknowledging government borrowing costs are at "historic highs". But the government's room for manoeuvre on tax is limited. Before the 2024 general election, Labour promised not to increase three big revenue earners for the government: income tax, National Insurance and VAT. In his statement, delivered to MPs in the House of Commons, Healey will set out how the government plans to raise or lower taxes. Alongside the Budget, the Treasury will publish details about the measures and their costs. The independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which monitors government spending, will also publish an assessment of the health of the UK economy and a forecast of what it thinks will happen in the future. The run-up to the Budget typically generates speculation about what might be in it, which the government is trying to keep to a minimum this year. Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households and meet commitments on defence spending, while also sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules. The previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, set out two main rules, which the new leadership has vowed to follow. These are: Not to borrow to fund day-to-day public spending by the end of this parliament To get government debt falling as a share of national income by the end of this parliament In March, the OBR calculated that the first rule would be met with a gap - or headroom - of £23.6bn. However, this headroom is expected to have shrunk. Analysts are divided on how much it may have fallen by. KPMG believe it could have fallen to £12bn, mainly due to the rise in government borrowing costs this year. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) also forecasts that debt interest will significantly reduce headroom. But it also suggests higher inflation could push up tax revenues as pay rises drag people into higher tax thresholds. It estimates the buffer could still shrink but to a comparatively less severe £20bn. One option that has been floated is that Healey could decide to accept a smaller buffer, reducing the need to increase taxes in the Budget. Bank bosses have told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector . UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes. The Treasury has options: it could raise a 3% surcharge on profits which was lowered from 8% under the previous Conservative government, or it could raise the bank levy that is based on the size of their balance sheets. Further details on the "Your First Home" scheme, aimed at helping first-time buyers in England to purchase a property, are expected to be announced in the Budget. The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase. There has been speculation that Capital Gains Tax (CGT) - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value - could be changed, through either higher rates or by removing or amending exemptions. At the moment, if you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%. The FT has reported , external that Healey has rejected proposals to raise CGT to the same rates as income tax. The Times has reported , external that online retail giants such as Amazon and eBay are expected to be made responsible for collecting tax owed by traders using their platforms. The paper said the money raised is expected to be used by the government to cut business rates for High Street shops, by raising the threshold at which small companies start paying rates from £12,000 to £18,000. Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year. Healey told the BBC in late September that the "place" and "time" for dealing with rising petrol and diesel costs was the Budget, but would not give details on whether the freeze would be extended again. Household energy bills are set to see their biggest rise in four years in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276 . There has been speculation , external that Healey is planning energy bill help for households on certain benefits. The High Value Council Tax Surcharge - dubbed the Mansion Tax - was announced in last year's Budget and will apply to properties in England valued above £2m from April 2028. There had been speculation that the government was considering extending it to properties worth more than £1.5m. However, reports now suggest , external Healey has ruled this out.

events.title: UAE signs agreement to hold 2029 World Bank and IMF meetings in Abu Dhabi
events.summary: The UAE has formally signed the agreement to host the 2029 annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Abu Dhabi. The deal, signed at the conclusion of the IMF and the World Bank 2026 annual meetings in Thailand, is a mark of growing international confidence in the UAE’s economic and financial ecosystem, the UAE Ministry of Finance said in a statement on Sunday. The formal pact to host the meetings also reinforces the status of the UAE – the Arab world’s second-largest economy – as a global financial hub that is helping to shape the stability and future of the global economic system. Mohamed bin Hadi Al Hussaini, Minister of State for Financial Affairs, and Khaled Balama, governor of the Central Bank of the UAE, signed the agreement in the Thai capital, Bangkok, with the World Bank president Ajay Banga and the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva. “The signing of the agreement marks a significant milestone, reflecting … confidence in the UAE’s readiness, the efficiency of its infrastructure and financial system, and its ability to host major international events of strategic importance,” Mr Al Hussaini said. The hosting of the event in the UAE will provide global financial leaders and decision-makers with a platform to explore how to advance the financial and monetary stability agenda as well as build development finance, the minister added. The UAE’s selection to host the event builds on the country’s track record in hosting major economic events. Scheduled to be held in October 2029, the summit will return to the Emirates for the first time in more than a quarter of a century. Dubai hosted the meetings in 2003. Participation in the annual meetings has continued to grow over the years, with more than 10,000 in-person and virtual attendees welcomed at each event. Country group meetings, civil society forums and press conferences with the World Bank president and IMF managing director are also held. They are closely watched by financial experts and policymakers from around the world. The World Bank-IMF annual meetings are traditionally held at their headquarters in Washington DC, and every third year a member country is selected to host them. London was the first city outside the US to host the meetings in 1947, while the UAE and Turkey remain the only countries in the Middle East to have hosted them. “The UAE has built institutions and infrastructure with a spirit of bold ambition and partnership, cementing its role as a global hub for economic dialogue,” Mr Banga of the World Bank Group, said. “Abu Dhabi is a fitting host for the annual meetings where our focus is on development impact, and delivering jobs, growth, and financing at scale.” The meetings usually bring together finance ministers, central bank governors, policymakers and economic experts, private sector representatives, civil society, media, and academics from more than 190 countries to examine the challenges and opportunities facing the global economy. The IMF and World Bank also release their outlook for growth and financial stability, and discuss future policy direction that supports inclusive and sustainable development. “The UAE has become an important hub for ideas, finance, innovation and international co-operation,” Ms Georgieva said. The 2029 meeting in Abu Dhabi will provide an opportunity to discuss the “challenges and opportunities ahead and help shape a better future”, the IMF managing director added.

events.title: 10 million Americans are using advance loan apps to get their paychecks in advance—and it’s costing them hundreds of dollars more, report finds
events.summary: As Americans continue to face persistent affordability concerns, they’re turning to loan tools that are actually leaving them even more strapped for cash. Those tools include apps that allow individuals to receive cash in between paychecks and are costing them hundreds of dollars each year in fees, according to a recent report . An analysis by the Center for Responsible Lending’s Julian Bond Institute of bank transactions from 10,000 consumers, found 96% of direct-to-consumer versions of payday loans included fees or “tips,” which amounted to nearly $208 per year on average, or about $17 per month. As of 2024, more than 10 million Americans used some form of “earned wage access” or “on-demand pay” tools, which give workers access to a portion of their earnings prior to their payday, allowing them to bridge gaps between paychecks. These tools are primarily used by those who make less than $50,000 according to a 2022 Government Accountability Office report , with food and rent being the key reasons people use the service, one case study of food and restaurant workers found. While these apps are free to use and don’t require credit checks or charge interest, they can charge fees for money to be transferred quickly, membership fees, and have a “tip” option, driving up costs to an Annual Percentage Rate (APR) of 232% for an average loan—nearly the equivalent loan rate as what traditional payday lenders offer, according to the Julian Bond report. A 2024 Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) report found a 90% increase in transaction volume for earned wage access from 2021 to 2022, and Tom Feltner, associate director of consumer policy at Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, told Fortune the use of payday loan apps has “certainly increased” amid Americans’ ongoing affordability concerns. The rise of loans at Americans’ fingertips Short-term financing has skyrocketed in popularity since the pandemic, when the emergence of these on-demand pay tools, as well as buy-now, pay-later apps aligned with increases in inflation. Between 2018 and 2020, transaction volume for on-demand pay apps tripled from $3.2 billion to $9.5 billion , according to Datos Insights. LendingTree found that nearly one-third of Americans have used buy-now, pay-later to finance necessities like groceries, double the 14% who used the service two years ago. “There is a certain fear” among economists about the rise of financing apps, Panos Kouvelis, a professor of supply chain, operations, and technology at the Olin Business School at Washington University in St. Louis, told Fortune last month. “There are some people that are living at the edge that are really overborrowing, and nobody knows about it.” Part of the increased prevalence of these apps is simply because they are more accessible, Feltner said. “Apps are leveraging new technology to deliver an old product because we’ve seen payday loans on the market for, in many states, well over 40 years,” he said. “But never have they been as readily accessible as they are now.” The primary danger of these apps is not the fees associated with using just one, Feltner noted. Transactions, while growing in frequency, are often small. But while just a couple hundred dollars in advance payday-related fees seems small, the ubiquity of loan apps for many different purposes, including buy now, pay later, means consumers are increasingly engaging in loan stacking, or the dangerous habit of outsourcing more and more short-term financing to apps. This use not only piles on fees, but also increases the risks of missed payments and delinquency, Feltner warned. Because many of these apps do not require traditional credit checks, users have fewer guardrails and forms of accountability for how many loans they are taking out. In 2025, CFPB found more than 60% of buy now, pay later users had simultaneous loans, and most consumers receiving these loans had lower or subprime credit scores. “In many ways it is adding new debt that’s invisible to other creditors and is ultimately, I think, driving both the variety of debt that people are in, as well the total amount,” Feltner said. “I think that’s why this is so concerning.”  Efforts to crack down on earned wage access apps have recently fallen short. In 2024, the CFPB proposed a rule that would require the disclosure of tips and fees as finance charges as an APR, or the total yearly cost of borrowing money. In December 2025, the CFPB under Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought withdrew the proposal, ruling that fees and voluntary tips were not finance charges . Why financing for some may cost all Americans more The number of Americans using direct-to-consumer financial tools has economists worrying beyond individual financial impacts to broader economic ripples. A recent study led by Kouvelis designed an economic model that included consumers’ willingness and ability to use buy now pay later (BNPL), as well as retailers’ expected profits, and found that retailers increased sticker prices to offset the merchant fees these apps charged them, “which basically means that all of us are going to pay for these practices that are out there,” Kouvelis said. This problem is directly related to the types of purchases Americans are taking out short-term loans for. BNPL was designed for discretionary purchases like furniture and entertainment consoles, which usually have higher margins. Groceries and other basic goods, however, have much thinner margins, making it harder for retailers to absorb fees associated with allowing BNPL transactions. As a result, they’re pressured to either increase prices or slash inventory and give consumers fewer choices. “Why does it really make sense for the retailer?” Kouvelis asked. “Unless they are hoping that as a result you are buying a much larger basket of goods and therefore they are making money on other products.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
