events.title: Why Berkshire Hathaway is betting nearly $1 billion on Bending Spoons
events.summary: Warren Buffett is the former CEO and chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Fortune/Time Inc Berkshire Hathaway is set to invest $330 million in Bending Spoons, adding to its previous $600 million. Warren Buffett's storied conglomerate is poised to hold a 4% stake in the owner of AOL and Vimeo. Berkshire's wager is a surprise, but there's some DNA in common with Bending Spoons. Berkshire Hathaway 's latest bet isn't a no-brainer or a head-scratcher; it's somewhere in between. What's the deal? Berkshire — which has seen Warren Buffett retire as CEO and chairman since the turn of the year — has agreed to invest $330 million in Bending Spoons, on top of a $600 million injection when the Italian tech conglomerate went public in July, giving the Nebraska behemoth a 4% stake. Bending Spoons disclosed Berkshire's backing in a press release on Wednesday, catapulting its stock up nearly 50% over two days, a phenomenon known as the " Buffett effect ." The stock fell on Friday, but still ended the week more than 20% above Monday's opening price. Berkshire has agreed to buy 10 million shares for $33 each, around a 13% discount to Bending Spoons ' closing price of $38 on Tuesday, the day before the deal was announced. CEO and cofounder Luca Ferrari described Berkshire in the press release as "among the finest and most respected capital allocators in the world," and a "longstanding inspiration" for Bending Spoons. Neither company responded to requests for comment from Business Insider. What is Bending Spoons? Bending Spoons acquires digital businesses, transforms and optimizes them to increase profits, then reinvests those earnings in further acquisitions. It has been pursuing that strategy for more than a decade and has never sold a material business. Its acquisitions to date include AOL, Evernote, Vimeo, Eventbrite, and WeTransfer. Ferrari's company said in the press release that it "strives to envision the most successful version of an acquired business," then works to close the gap between that vision and reality "as quickly and completely as possible." Bending Spoons said that typically involves "deep" transformation such as "reorganizing teams, overhauling technology, redesigning user interfaces, accelerating product development, and enhancing marketing and monetization," often with a good dose of AI. Ferrari gave the example of Evernote on a recent episode of the "Joys of Compounding" podcast. He said the business had around 350 employees when Bending Spoons acquired it at the start of 2023. That shrank to roughly 60 within 12 to 18 months, and now it's being run by around 20 people. Yet Ferrari said Evernote "launched by far the biggest update to the product in maybe a decade" this spring. Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari. Marco Bertorello / AFP via Getty Images Why is Berkshire's investment a surprise? First and foremost, Bending Spoons is a tech conglomerate, and Berkshire has eschewed tech for most of its history with a few big exceptions, namely Apple and Alphabet. That's because Buffett is a bargain hunter who likes to invest with a "margin of safety" in case something goes wrong, and tries to stay within his "circle of competence," only buying into what he deeply understands. Tech companies have rarely been a good fit for his approach, as they typically have lofty valuations, unpredictable outlooks, and complex products and services. Indeed, Bending Spoons generated 32 cents in earnings per share last year. Berkshire is paying more than 100 times that per share in the coming private placement. It's true that Bending Spoons is growing fast, with revenue surging 126% year-on-year to $704 million in the second quarter and adjusted operating income jumping 150% to $381 million. Few, however, would consider the stock a bargain from a fundamental perspective. Berkshire is also famously a hands-off acquirer, offering founders the opportunity to cash out while continuing to run their businesses as they see fit. In contrast, a core aspect of Bending Spoons' strategy is revamping its acquisitions. How does the deal make sense? Berkshire and Bending Spoons have similarities as well as differences. Both are decentralized conglomerates that buy businesses not to flip them, but to own them for the long term. Berkshire is a web of largely autonomous companies, including GEICO, Duracell, Fruit of the Loom, Pilot Travel Centers, and BNSF Railway. It has long offered a permanent home to the businesses it buys. Bending Spoons has positioned itself as a forever owner, too, emulating Berkshire's approach of taking the cash generated by a subsidiary like See's Candies and using it to acquire more businesses. Ferrari said in his recent podcast interview that Bending Spoons has fostered a culture of caring deeply about the company, and doesn't centralize decision-making in part because that "deprives people of that precious sense of ownership." Buffett famously wrote " An Owner's Manual " for Berkshire shareholders. He's championed that mindset by keeping more than 99% of his net worth in Berkshire stock, and encouraging the company's other executives and directors to have skin in the game too. Ferrari also said on the podcast that he has a "pathological love of learning" across different domains. That echoes Buffett's boundless curiosity and the late Charlie Munger's insatiable appetite for knowledge . Buffett's longtime business partner studied architecture, physics, history, meteorology, psychology, law, and, of course, investing, among other subjects. Beyond their similar philosophies, it's worth noting that investing less than $1 billion into Bending Spoons isn't a huge deal for Berkshire. It has a $1.1 trillion market capitalization, had a $365 billion cash pile at the end of June , and its biggest stock position was worth about $66 billion at that time. What's the takeaway? The Bending Spoons deal could mark an evolution in Berkshire's investing style following Buffett's departure as CEO and chairman. Berkshire hasn't commented on the purchase or on whether Buffett was involved. Its relatively small size could mean his remaining investment manager, Ted Weschler, was behind it. Or it might be new CEO Greg Abel, who piled an additional $10 billion into Alphabet in a private placement this summer after consulting with Buffett. Whoever was responsible, and whatever their reasons for investing, this will be an intriguing wager to watch for Berkshire followers. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countries
events.summary: Bank’s chief knowledge officer says the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades The World Bank is urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence. While Silicon Valley big tech firms are focused on ever more sophisticated consumer products, Paschal Donohoe, the World Bank’s chief knowledge officer, said AI could also accelerate development for emerging economies – but only if it was adapted to local needs. Small AI uses specialised models that are trained using narrower datasets for a specific purpose. “We argue that economic development in the countries that we serve and partner with that could have taken centuries to make happen, the potential is there for that economic development now to happen within decades,” Donohoe said. “Small AI would be available in a local setting, with low connectivity, and in the local language of the community – and tends to be available on your mobile phone.” Donohoe, a former finance minister for Ireland, cited the example of Indian farmers engaged in the World Bank’s agricultural scheme, AgriConnect, who needed to access soil analysis in their own language. “There’s not going to be enough scientists and agricultural experts to do that for every small farm in India. And this is where what we describe as ‘small AI’ comes in. Because small AI is AI that would be available on your phone, that can help deliver against those information needs.” He suggested such products could emerge from collaboration between the World Bank, governments and the private sector. The impact of AI on jobs and growth is a central theme of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which are being held this week in Bangkok, Thailand. Speaking on a panel about the impact of the technology on Monday, Kristalina Georgieva, the IMF’s managing director, called on governments to provide the preconditions for AI to succeed. She said: “You need access to electricity. You need access to digital infrastructure. People have to be geared to adoption. And the government should be able to give some safety, protect against bad actors so that adoption can work. “If we work hard to have the basics for it, [adoption] can be very democratic. As democratic as the cellphone.” The World Bank’s annual world development report, published in August, hailed the potential benefits of AI. But it pointed out that, for example, almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity and more than two-thirds did not have a consistent internet connection. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Georgieva warned that over time 40% of jobs worldwide were likely to be either augmented or eliminated by AI, with the impact particularly acute for young people at the start of their careers. “When we look at this, what we recognise is that the people to worry about, first and foremost, are young people that are coming into the labour market,” she said. “Normally they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then go up the ranks. But if they’re gone, I don’t think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as a professional future.” Under its president, Ajay Banga, the World Bank has made attracting private-sector funding into emerging economies a focus of its work. Donohoe said the World Bank had mobilised $120bn (£90bn) of private capital in the past year using guarantees and other financial instruments, at a time when many countries, including the US and the UK, were cutting their aid budgets. “We want to highlight the link between private capital mobilisation and jobs and economic development,” he said.

events.title: Andrew Left wants his fraud conviction tossed after witness gets caught up in insider trading probe
events.summary: Andrew Left's lawyers asked the judge to toss his conviction on 13 counts of securities fraud. Dania Maxwell/Bloomberg/Getty Images A witness who testified against Andrew Left has himself become involved in an insider trading probe. Left's lawyers asked a judge to toss the jury verdict that found him guilty of securities fraud. Prosecutors said they didn't learn about the investigation until after the trial was over. A witness who testified against Andrew Left has himself become involved in an insider trading probe, bringing a new twist to the bombastic short-seller's fraud conviction. Left's lawyers this month asked the judge who oversaw his trial to toss the jury's verdict convicting him of 13 counts of securities fraud. The trial was irredeemably unfair, they said, because they never had the chance to ask the witness about the investigation and attack his credibility. "A new trial would probably produce an acquittal," Left's lawyers wrote. In June, a federal jury in Los Angeles found Left guilty of 13 counts of securities fraud. Prosecutors said he deceived investors by using social media and research reports to set target prices for stocks — including Tesla, Nvidia, and Palantir — while quietly trading them at different prices with his own money. The founder of Citron Research, Left is something of a short-seller celebrity. He placed bets against GameStop at the same time it became a meme stock, which pitted him against some retail traders on social media. For years, he was a fixture on CNBC and Bloomberg, where he shared his views on stock prices. Left hasn't been sentenced. In addition to the criminal case, he faces a parallel civil lawsuit from the Securities and Exchange Commission that remains unresolved. Left's criminal conviction shook certain corners of Wall Street , which viewed the trial as a referendum on free speech and the legality of activist short-seller tactics. Left, testifying in his own defense at the trial , said that the views he shared about public companies were sincere. One of the trial's prosecution witnesses was Daniel Bachus, the CFO of Grand Canyon Education, a publicly traded technology company that provides services to universities. Left's lawyers say that Bachus was the only witness who testified that Left used his Citron Research reports to lie about a company, not merely omit information. On August 21 — weeks after the trial ended — Grand Canyon Education placed Bachus on paid administrative leave "in connection with an ongoing governmental investigation" involving a non-employee's trades of the company's stock, the company said in an SEC disclosure. The prosecutors in Left's case referred to it in their own filings as an "insider trading investigation." No government agency has publicly accused Bachus or Grand Canyon Education of any misconduct in connection with the investigation. In the SEC disclosure, the company said it wasn't the focus of the investigation. Representatives for the SEC and for Grand Canyon Education declined to comment. Bachus didn't respond to Business Insider's requests for comment. Left's lawyers say they should have been informed about the investigation at the time of the trial so that they could cross-examine Bachus and try to convince the jury that he wasn't a credible witness. "This evidence would have destroyed the credibility of the government's only false-statements witness," they wrote in a filing. The prosecution team told Left's lawyers it didn't learn about the investigation until after the trial was over. It's not clear which government agency opened the investigation, nor when Bachus or Grand Canyon Education became aware of it. Many of the filings about the issue remained sealed or redacted on the court docket for Left's case. In court filings, Justice Department prosecutors said Left's lawyers overstated Bachus' role in the short-selling case, which alleged securities fraud involving more than a dozen different public companies. They said Left wanted to conduct "his own shadow investigation into Bachus" to try to discredit him as a witness. "The law does not permit fishing expeditions in search of a claim," prosecutors said. Left declined to comment. Left's attorney Eric S. Rosen said he could not comment because many relevant documents remained under seal. A spokesperson for the US Attorney's office in Los Angeles declined to comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I made an impulsive decision to quit a great job in Hollywood. It felt like a mistake — but here's what I learned.
events.summary: "My worst professional mistake ultimately became my biggest professional and personal break," writes Peter Csathy. DNY59/Getty Images Peter Csathy is a studio exec, startup CEO, media and tech advisor, music dealmaker, and podcaster. He calls leaving a Hollywood studio job for a startup the 'stupidest' decision of his career. In the long run, it led him to achieve higher heights of personal and professional satisfaction. The following is adapted from a book excerpt. I began my career as an entertainment lawyer in a major firm. It was a lucrative, predictable professional path that likely would have generated more money over time than my far more circuitous one —studio executive, startup CEO, media/tech advisor, music dealmaker, author, podcaster — has. But early on, I chose a different path to pursue my bigger dream of playing a part in a major Hollywood studio. And after seemingly endless rejection, and through sheer tenacity and will, I scored the lottery when I found my way "in" — jumping the industry's velvet rope and landing in the senior executive ranks at Universal Studios. And then, just a few years later, I left. I left to enter the great unknown of entrepreneurialism — into the world of internet 1.0 in the late 1990s where dreams were big, but salaries small. Never mind that; I was going to score big and fast in my inevitable IPO. Only I didn't, and my decision to leave Universal in favor of an overblown internet startup (a digital greeting card company, for God's sake!) became my stupidest decision in my professional career. My wife, Luisa, was pregnant with our first child, Hunter. It's not as if we had built a substantial nest egg up to that point. And I had been making a nice salary in Hollywood, with plenty of upward room to grow. When I announced I was leaving Universal, in fact, the big boss at the time offered me an important, prestigious new job with significantly more money. But I left anyway. And then internet 1.0 crashed and burned — and my digital greeting card company with it. All while Luisa watched and wondered, "What the hell was he thinking?" Peter Csathy. Peter Csathy 'Young, dumb, and done' She was absolutely right, of course. She always has the better judgment and pulse on things. And so, at the time, we both felt that I had cratered both my career and our financial security. Young, dumb, and done. But you know what? My worst professional mistake ultimately became my biggest professional and personal break — the best thing that ever could have happened to us (although we certainly didn't see it that way at the time, and for several years thereafter). Here's the thing. My impulsive decision to leave Hollywood led me onto a completely different, non-linear entrepreneurial path. A path that led us down to San Diego for my next gig, pioneering online music company Musicmatch (which was acquired by Yahoo!) . That's where we had our second child, Luca and settled in the beautiful hamlet of Rancho Santa Fe. I didn't play it safe, and that decision to "go for it" opened up a whole new career path for me that I couldn't see at the time, one where I could have significantly more impact and be significantly more creative. It enabled me to take more risks, pursue more dreams, and achieve higher heights of personal and professional satisfaction (even as those risks also certainly led to more heartburn). Now, we can't even imagine a life without Luca and his big sister Hunter anywhere else. Their lives — all of our lives — have been idyllic here in Rancho Santa Fe. Could I have been equally happy in a Hollywood studio and living in LA? Maybe. But we certainly wouldn't have had the wonderful life we've had in the same way. I'm grateful for that. Pursuing dreams — putting yourself out there — is a far riskier way to live. But it all led to the personal and professional life I'm living today. For me, the trade-off was worth it. Not all dreams work out — and that's okay More recently, Luisa dreamt big and leveraged her deep spirituality to build a youth empowerment and community organizing business — something she was born to do. She's a quiet force of nature; people just gravitate toward her, effortlessly. And her business was beautiful — meaningful, impactful. But ultimately it was all-consuming and didn't give her the satisfaction she was hoping for, because not all dreams do. But Luisa acted. She tried it. No regrets. Who knows where that experience leads her next? It certainly expanded her network of people she respects, and those new relationships can lead to other new opportunities. It also gives us more priceless time to explore this country's great open roads together in our Sprinter van — which has always been another dream of hers. The Sprinter is her happy place when she takes the dogs to the beach, opens the back doors, and takes in the sunsets over the ocean. Now she can do all of it with no regrets of wondering, "What would have happened if I tried?" "No regrets" is a great way to live, even if there's some heartache along the way. The author and his wife, Luisa. Courtesy of Peter Csathy Our two children Hunter (now 26) and Luca (24), not surprisingly, are pursuing their own dreams too — Hunter as a creative in the entertainment business , making it entirely on her own, and Luca as a filmmaker, with no roadmap of getting from point A to point B. Both have chosen what many would caution as being an alternative, or even impractical, path. But because we're all dreamers, Luisa and I believe they will be better and more fulfilled because of it, no matter what happens. It will add to their lore and expose them to entirely new things — all of which can add to their long-term happiness. Gretchen Rubin , bestselling author of The Happiness Project , is widely known as being a leading expert on the subject. One of her famous mantras is, "Enjoy the fun of failure." She teaches that you simply aren't aiming high enough if you're not experiencing some level of failure or intense stress . I certainly did when my digital greeting card company flopped. Rubin's research shows that true satisfaction doesn't come from static comfort and financial security. It comes more from taking action and stretching your capabilities. Meanwhile, research by renowned relationship psychologist Dr. Eli Finkel concludes that one of the single biggest predictors of marital success is when spouses support and champion each other's dreams. He calls this the "Michelangelo phenomenon" — a spouse's support sculpts away excess stone to help reveal the core essence of their partner's dreams. Those spouses who prioritize money over dreams , on the other hand, risk creating dangerous fault lines of toxic resentment and contempt. events.title: What the rich and poor have in common: They say they're living paycheck to paycheck
events.summary: Americans at the top and bottom of the income distribution are feeling stressed. Natalia Lebedinskaia/Getty Images Higher- and lower-income Americans are more likely than those in the middle to say they're living paycheck to paycheck. The top and bottom also struggled with making credit card payments and are delaying financial goals. Lifestyle creep is one reason high earners are feeling anxious. Low and high earners have at least one thing in common: they're more likely than those somewhere in the middle to say they're living paycheck to paycheck . A July survey of over Americans by Goldman Sachs Asset Management and behavioral economics firm Escalent showed about 61% of working respondents with less than $50,000 said they're primarily living paycheck to paycheck, meaning they struggle to save or make progress toward long-term goals . The share dropped to 22% for those with $100,000 to $200,000 but rose to about 37% for those with more than $500,000. "Financial security as reported does not rise in a straight line with income; it follows a u-shaped pattern," a recent report said. However, those at the top and bottom are facing different challenges. Lower earners are struggling to keep up with the basics. A Pew Research Center survey found 42% of lower-income US adults struggled to afford daily transportation costs, and 39% of lower-income adults said the same about paying their rent or mortgage. High gas prices don't help; they're rising at a faster clip than before the Iran war. Food-at-home prices, which include groceries, are rising more slowly, but they are still increasing. And the gap between what you need to earn to afford a house and the actual median household income has worsened, according to a tracker from the Atlanta Fed. Meanwhile, high earners with more than $300,000 are facing "more complex financial lives, higher lifestyle expectations, larger fixed commitments, and a wider gap between the retirement they envision and what they believe they have secured," the report said. Lifestyle creep could also be a factor, said Chris Ceder, senior retirement strategist at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. U-shapes everywhere The report also showed there were U-shapes by income level in how often financial concerns make it tough to focus at work, how many people are struggling with credit card payments, and how many said they're delaying financial goals. Those at the highest end of the income spectrum also had the highest share saying they've had to delay retirement despite being employed, at 45%. When asked about what stands most in the way of saving up for retirement, 31% of Americans overall said housing costs, 31% said day-to-day living expenses, and 27% said debt payments. "These expenses arrive every month, cannot be deferred, and they are paid first," the report said. "Retirement is often paid last." Ceder said housing costs, family care, and healthcare are top concerns for the upper end of the income spectrum, while debt management is among the top three for the lower end. Taking on more work Ceder said that the highest-income workers were the most likely to take on multiple jobs . A likely reason could be saving up for unexpected costs. "You would think again that mostly people who are at the lower-income spectrum may be working a second job or doing gig or freelance, but it's actually flipped," Ceder said. A ZipRecruiter survey from earlier this year found workers earning over $150,000 were most likely to have supplemental work — with about 45% saying so compared to 31% of those making between $25,000 and $50,000. Ceder said this hustling from the higher earners could suggest they're aware of their long-term financial goals and want to get ahead of that. "They actually are pretty confident that they're going to be able to reach retirement, but some of that supplemental work is going towards retirement," he said. Are you living paycheck to paycheck? We're looking to hear about how people are doing in today's economy and any changes they've had to make. Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com . events.title: He retired after he got notified of student-loan forgiveness. Then his payments came back.
events.summary: Donald Knierim is fighting to get his Public Service Loan Forgiveness restored. Vanessa Valadez for BI Donald Knierim planned his retirement around student-loan forgiveness. He spent most of his career designing financial data systems for major companies. At the age of 60, he took a pay cut and moved to the public sector, working for Metra, Chicago's commuter railway. His primary draw to the job was lower stress, and an added bonus was that it qualified for the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which erases student debt for government and nonprofit workers after 10 years. Knierim had a $62,000 balance remaining on the student loans he took out to send his kids to college. If all went according to plan, a decade at Metra would wipe that clean. In November 2025, the now-71-year-old logged on to his Federal Student Aid dashboard. It read "Congratulations! You've satisfied your obligation, and no additional payments are required for this loan." That tracked — Knierim said he had never missed a payment, always verifying that his payments were counting toward his forgiveness progress. So he put in his notice and retired. Knierim retired after thinking his student-loan payments were done. Vanessa Valadez for BI Months later, he received an update: 15 payments that had previously counted toward forgiveness were changed to "non-qualifying." The notice said his payments were below the amount required under his income-driven repayment plan, but did not specify the proper amount. That means he has at least another year and a half of payments — about $470 monthly — to achieve PSLF. "If I have to restore that payment, it's going to put my wife and me in a bad situation," Knierim said. "We're too tight in retirement to be shelling out money for stuff that we can't afford." Since 2023, Business Insider has heard from student-loan borrowers whose loan forgiveness was rescinded. Over the past few months, issues with PSLF have become more widespread, with borrowers reporting challenges in receiving accurate payment counts. Some had their payments toward forgiveness removed after the Department of Education said it was correcting accounts following Biden-era coding errors. An Education Department spokesperson said that the agency "remains committed to ensuring that every qualifying payment is properly credited to a borrower's account." For years, Knierim said he made sure his payments were counting toward his forgiveness progress. Vanessa Valadez for BI Knierim said that even if he could land a new public service job, he wouldn't be able to take it. Caring for his wife, who is facing serious health issues, is a full-time job. He has reached out to his servicer and filed multiple complaints with Federal Student Aid, requesting his payments to be returned to a qualifying status. Meanwhile, he has not made the new payments his servicer said were due, which has lowered his credit score by more than 200 points. He recently received a notice that his account is delinquent and at risk of default, putting him at risk of seizure of federal benefits , like the Social Security he relies on to stay afloat. Now, he's asking for the initial communication he received from his student-loan servicer to be honored. "I thought I was done, they gave me that notification that I was done, and then they clawed it back," Knierim said. "I didn't know where that came from, or what to do." This story is part of Business Insider's "Student Debt Spiral" series, which explores how rising student debt is changing the financial futures of millions. Do you have a story to share? Fill out this form , and we'll be in touch. Read more of our student-loan coverage here: ' Hijacked': The 'code errors' that blindsided some student-loan borrowers A 60-year-old took out student loans to help her kids succeed. She's facing retirement with a $156,000 balance. 'It's going to hurt': How a surging student-loan payment is reshaping a family's future An error-riddled student-loan forgiveness program There are a few reasons a borrower might get their PSLF notices rescinded. An internal Education Department memo from 2023, reviewed by Business Insider, said that servicer MOHELA erroneously discharged loans for 64 student-loan borrowers "due to inadequate staff training." The memo recommended that MOHELA send notices to affected borrowers explaining what had happened. In 2023, one borrower received a notice that his loans had been discharged under PSLF. Nine months later, he received a notice that the forgiveness was a mistake , and his payments were restarted. Between those two notices, the borrower said he had bought a home and paid for his son's preschool. The reversal required him to reconfigure his family's budget. Some student-loan borrowers have seen their PSLF payments rescinded, which the Trump administration attributed to Biden-era errors. Vanessa Valadez for BI More recently, the Trump administration removed some PSLF borrowers' qualifying payments, with the Education Department citing Biden-era code errors that "resulted in inaccurate payment counts for some borrowers." Bonnie Latrielle, an official in the Education Department's Federal Student Aid office under former President Joe Biden, said PSLF errors often arise during communication between the Education Department and servicers; servicers report qualifying PSLF payments to the department, and the department matches that information with a borrower's employment records to determine if the borrower is PSLF eligible. "Those are all things that are outside of the borrower's control," Latrielle said. Knierim said his servicer told him that some of the payments he made toward the Temporary Expanded PSLF program — a Biden-era program that allowed payments previously deemed ineligible to count toward forgiveness — did not qualify because they were below the required amount. He said he did not receive any further explanation as to why his payment amounts did not qualify, despite following his servicer's guidance on reaching forgiveness. "I have a flawless payment history," Knierim said. "I have never missed a payment, and I paid what they told me to pay." From relief to repayment The Education Department has a "stated policy of holding borrowers harmless," Latrielle said, and borrowers have the right to submit complaints to the department's ombudsman if they have been harmed by their servicer. However, amid staffing cuts in the department as part of the Trump administration's plan to dismantle the agency , it has stopped monitoring servicer performance and routine borrower complaints . Latrielle said a growing number of states have student-loan ombudsmen and a borrower bill of rights, offering resources and protections for borrowers within the state. Borrowers can also file lawsuits against their servicer if it violates state law, Latreille said. events.title: I’m the CEO of Torani, and we've never done layoffs. I believe they're a choice.
events.summary: Torani CEO Melanie Dulbecco has been in the role for 35 years. Torani Melanie Dulbecco has been CEO of the syrup company Torani for 35 years. Dulbecco said layoffs are a choice, and that Torani's decision not to do them has helped with retention. She said that the company is hiring fewer people than it would be if Torani didn't use automation. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Melanie Dulbecco, the CEO of syrup brand Torani. She's based in San Leandro, California, where the company is headquartered. This story has been edited for length and clarity. I may sound different than most CEOs. I grew up in a blue-collar neighborhood, and my parents divorced when I was really young. When I was little, I saw my mom struggle so much, and I noticed that some kids around me didn't have the same opportunities. I felt this sense of inequity, and that became a motivating and driving force for me. I tried working in politics, then nonprofits, and eventually went into business. I wanted to build an opportunity company. When I met the family from Torani, they liked that idea. I was the ninth hire at Torani in 1991 and became the first CEO in 1995. We now have over 500 employees. When I started, we made $700,000 a year in annual revenue. We've grown 20% a year on average, and this year, we plan to hit over $800 million in revenue. But to us, growth is not a financial endeavor. The trailing indicator of success may be the financials, but we think our work together creates the momentum and value in the marketplace that drives our growth. It's very easy for us to say layoffs are not our approach . I think layoffs are a choice. I get it if a company is going through bankruptcy and has to make extremely challenging choices. Otherwise, I think it's a financial exercise that doesn't consider how you're going to be resilient or regain momentum — because you do that with a team. Our workers aren't concerned about being replaced by AI Torani is currently hiring fewer people than it would be if the company didn't use automation. We use automation to deprioritize manual, rote jobs with limited career mobility. We also use AI for consumer and market research, sales forecasting, and demand planning. However, our team doesn't get worried about things like AI because they trust that we will both automate and elevate the work, that we will never do anything that squashes opportunities for people, and that we are looking out for everybody's success. We're often in hyper-growth mode, which means we need people to know how to work together. The ability to work together, to collaborate, to address challenges, to be resilient in tough times, is critical. This strategy has also helped with retention. We were faced with a choice during the pandemic We had been planning a move to our new location in San Leandro in March 2020. That happened to coincide with the stay-at-home order . It was one of those moments where, as a leader, you feel like you have to breathe into a paper bag. We had borrowed a lot of money from the bank to build our new flavor factory. The loans were going to start coming due in April, so the executive team came together to look at what we needed to do to be OK. Before we did that, though, we asked: What will make us proud when we get to the other side of this? We had a long discussion about it and decided that making it as one team — without any layoffs or furloughs — would make us proud. So we we scaled back marketing and advertising expenses and paused all company travel. All departments had to review their budgets. They got scrappy to identify and eliminate non-essential costs. During the early months of the pandemic, Torani prepared for a 50% decline in sales. Thankfully, there was only a 20% decline in April of 2020, and revenue was back up in May. We quickly pivoted to online retail and grocery to fill the gaps left by cafés and drink shops closing their doors. Torani ended 2020 with a 15% year-over-year revenue increase. We moved to our new location in six months instead of six weeks, but we got there. We couldn't have done that if we laid off our team. We needed to come together at that moment. events.title: Innovation Accounts should do for the potential AI job wipeout what Trump Accounts did for children
events.summary: The United States is home to most of the world’s leading AI companies — yet many Americans don’t feel they share in the abundance. AI is fueling unprecedented growth and wealth creation. In the first half of 2026, tech-focused hedge funds returned 27% on average; the Nasdaq-100 rose about 20%. But many citizens don’t own that innovation and so miss out on its profits. As AI scales, that gap is likely to widen, not close. There is a way for more Americans to share in the upside of AI.  How can more Americans benefit from our nation’s ingenuity? Make more Americans owners. “Innovation Accounts,” modeled on Trump Accounts for newborns, would put seed money into a technology-stock index on behalf of adults, giving each of them a stake in America’s technological engine. OpenAI has reportedly floated the idea of giving the government up to a 5% stake in the company and suggested other leading AI companies do the same. Both President Trump and progressive Democrats have floated public ownership stakes in AI companies , as Fortune has reported. However, governments make poor stock-pickers. Better to let individuals own the upside directly. The math is simple. $1,000 invested in the Nasdaq-100 a decade ago — which has returned 21% annually — would be worth $5,727 more today. Seed ‘innovation accounts’ with $5,000, and that’s $28,635 in gains.  There is a precedent — this idea is an extension of one that is already law. Trump Accounts, created under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, give American children born from 2025 through 2028 a $1,000 government-funded stake in the stock market. Alaska has run a version of this for decades: its Permanent Fund invests a share of the state’s oil wealth and pays nearly every resident, children included, an annual dividend from the earnings. A private-sector asset manager would invest the innovation accounts under government oversight, with participants able to cash out gains at specific intervals, potentially every couple of years.  Investing in individual stocks carries risk, but a diversified technology index fund would give more Americans access to the upside of AI-driven productivity growth. Just 58% of American adults own stock, Gallup found in April, much of it held in retirement accounts. That means most people are exposed to AI’s downsides — rising electricity costs, potential job disruption — without any claim on its upside. Innovation Accounts would close that gap. Giving Americans $1,000 or $5,000 invested in a technology index is a straightforward idea; The source and use of the funds will likely be of great debate. Federal or state governments could seed the accounts, but philanthropy offers a faster, deficit-neutral start. The beneficiaries of AI – founders, early employees, investors and the foundations at labs like OpenAI and Anthropic – are a natural source of capital for this idea given the meaningful liquidity around the corner.  The hardest design question is eligibility. Opening $1,000 accounts for every American over 18 years old (when Trump accounts end) would cost roughly $270 billion. Limiting it to households with wealth under $500,000 — about 70% of Americans — cuts that to $190 billion. The program could also be targeted rather than universal — triggered by sector-specific unemployment spikes, income level, or geography, so the money flows first to the workers AI disrupts most. For example, an “unemployment trigger” could target those in highly impacted sectors: if unemployment in your sector (by NAICS code) runs 1.5x of the average unemployment level in your sector for the past 10 years, you qualify. Hopefully, other economists will offer even more elegant targeting solutions.  The broader idea of “universal basic capital” for everyone, not just those affected by AI, has drawn support from figures as varied as MIT economist David Autor, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Senator Bernie Sanders. The practical question is scope. A $5 billion pilot, plus administrative costs, could seed 1 million accounts at $5,000 each. If it works, the government or philanthropists could scale it over time. An extra $6,000 or $29,000 in gains over a decade won’t replace a lost job. But it gives people capital to retrain, start a business, or navigate whatever comes next — on their own terms. A philanthropic pilot could start compounding those returns today, without waiting on Congress. Of course, the Nasdaq-100 or a similar tech-heavy index, isn’t guaranteed to deliver 21% returns each year for a decade going forward. But when it does deliver, more Americans can win. Rather than a direct cash transfer, this is investing in more Americans benefiting from our country’s innovation prowess. We are home to most of the world’s leading AI labs and attract more private AI investment than any other country. Many other countries and even continents would kill to have this level of ingenuity on their shores. It’s no accident America built the labs driving this AI revolution and their continued success is a common project. If Americans don’t feel they’re sharing in what the labs and other AI leaders create, the backlash will land on the innovators as much as anyone.  No one knows exactly what magnitude of job displacement AI will cause — we won’t know until it arrives. But uncertainty isn’t a reason to wait or do nothing. It is a reason to build a plan, fund it, and hope we never need it. As a country, we need the economic infrastructure to help Americans absorb these shocks, and Innovation Accounts would strengthen households’ balance sheets in a time of significant disruption and abundance. Ingenuity is central to the American story. So is sharing in its abundance. This proposal isn’t partisan — it’s patriotic. events.title: Move slow and make things: What Japanese craftsmanship can teach business about quality, patience, and expertise when AI makes speed cheap
events.summary: For thirty years, the dominant logic of Western business has been simple: move fast and break things. The first mover has the advantage. Scale before you’re ready. Ship before it’s perfect. Ask forgiveness later. This thinking has produced extraordinary wealth and genuine innovation. It has also created a generation of companies that mistake velocity for value, and are only belatedly discovering that the two are not the same thing. AI has effectively disrupted the disruptors. Speed is now free, which means, for the first time in history, speed is worthless. The ability for anyone to generate strategy, code, or creative work in seconds effectively filled in the moats built on blitzscaling overnight. But this is in fact the opportunity hiding inside the greatest technological acceleration of our lifetimes. AI doesn’t just automate tasks. It clarifies, perhaps for the first time, which human contributions actually matter. It also hands companies a gift few have thought hard about. When machines absorb the administrative and the routine, the defining question becomes what to do with the hours they return. Machines excel at generating the average. Closing the gap between the merely good and the truly extraordinary remains stubbornly, wonderfully human. The Japanese have a word for people who excel at their chosen craft: shokunin. It is often translated as “craftsperson,” but what it really embodies is a quiet competence borne from mastering generations of experience, joined to a sense of pride and a dash of gratitude, both to those who came before and to the materials and people that make the work possible. That combination produces something rare: the taste and skill to deliver quality, along with the humility to admit when change is necessary and the confidence to see a pivot through. There’s a reason some of the planet’s oldest companies can be found in Japan. Nintendo opened its doors in 1889; Shiseido in 1872; the construction firm Kongo Gumi, 578. No, that’s not a typo. These firms revere tradition, but not out of nostalgia. They treat inherited wisdom as something you adapt to changing times so the next generation can flourish, not something you embalm. To a shokunin, the question is not “what can we automate?” It is “what must we never automate?” Every business leader already knows the older version of this rule: never outsource your competitive advantage, never put distance between the company and what makes it special. AI tools are simply the latest way to make that age-old mistake. Firms that know exactly where the line sits hold quiet advantages their competitors cannot purchase or replicate. Shokunin thinking deepens quality, but it also paves the way for innovation. Businesses that rediscover its values will gain what their velocity-chasing competitors cannot buy, borrow, or automate. They will have the confidence to know when something is truly good, and the judgment to pivot when circumstances demand it. AI raises the floor. Shokunin thinking raises the ceiling. Principle 1: Go deep, not wide Constraints look like limitations. Often they are the source of your advantage. Abandon them and you become one of a thousand competitors rather than the only maker of what you make. Just as important, knowing what you do best is what steadies you when conditions turn. In 1921, a small Japanese company called Shimano began making bicycle freewheels in Osaka. Over the following century, as competitors diversified and conglomerates expanded into every adjacent category they could reach, Shimano did something almost perverse in its discipline. It held its ground. The entire portfolio was bicycles and fishing equipment. When opportunities arose to expand into other sporting goods, other mechanical components, other markets entirely, the answer was consistently no. Not yet. Not us. Not that. The result is one of the most quietly dominant competitive positions in modern industry. Today, the majority of the world’s high-performance bicycles ship with Shimano components as standard. The brand rarely advertises. It doesn’t need to. A century of obsessive refinement within a deliberately narrow category produced expertise so deep that competitors who have tried to enter the market found themselves outclassed not by Shimano’s scale, but by the sheer accumulated density of what it knows. That knowledge cannot be acquired in a board meeting or replicated in an accelerator program. It is the product of a hundred years of choosing depth over breadth, every single time the choice was available. Depth also brings something subtler than the courage to pivot. It brings the judgment to know when. Startups famously change course at the first sign of friction, often too quickly. Companies that know exactly what they are can tell a passing squall from a changed climate. Shimano proved it recently. A pandemic-fueled boom in bicycle sales went bust, forcing the company to temporarily shutter its main Japanese factory, while rising e-bike sales threatened its dominance in components for traditional models. But crisis provided opportunity. Shimano used the downtime to develop an AI-driven automatic shifter that analyzes and adapts to a rider’s pedaling habits, letting them climb inclines almost as easily as on an e-bike. A fusion of century-old expertise and cutting-edge technology that no competitor can replicate, because no competitor has the century. It is also a preview of the choice every company will soon face. When automation hands back the hours once consumed by routine, you can use them to produce more, or to get better. Shimano chose better. The key insight: Master one thing completely and you will never be lost when the world turns. Depth is what makes reinvention possible. Principle 2: Taste is a skill Americans invented blue jeans. But the Japanese arguably perfected them. Introduced by American occupation forces after World War II, jeans found a market among young Japanese eager to emulate Hollywood stars. Within a few decades, local makers had gone from importing American fabric to producing their own, and by the Eighties they had grown so adept that even Levi’s began experimenting with denim made in Japan. The twist was that Japanese denim-spinners weren’t mimicking the denims of the Eighties. They were intent on taking things back to the Fifties. By any objective standard, that technology was outdated, labor-intensive, imprecise, and inefficient. American makers had long since moved on. The older spinning methods produced yarn riddled with faults that surfaced as the indigo faded, as denim expert Andrew Olah explained to W. David Marx in the book Ametora: How Japan Saved American Fashion. Where American makers saw a defect, the Japanese saw the main feature of the product. They wanted to capture a vibe. “It’s easy to make jeans exactly like vintage,” explained Hidehiko Yamane, founder of Evisu Jeans. “Anyone can do that.” Rather, he wanted to offer the feeling of seeing America

events.title: 'I took a chance on the whisky industry and I haven't looked back'
events.summary: Zoey Darnbrough took a job at Annandale Distillery after finishing her studies Zoey Darnbrough is the first to admit that just a few years ago she did not even know there was a whisky distillery near her hometown in southern Scotland. But it hasn't stopped her rising rapidly from tour guide, to group tourism and events co-ordinator at the site near Annan. She went away to study heritage and tourism in Stirling after school, but unlike many of her peers, she returned to Dumfries and Galloway for work. Now she hopes to play her part in changing people's opinions of the world of whisky "one woman at a time". Annandale distillery shut in 1919 before reopening 90 years later The 26-year-old, who attended St Joseph's College in Dumfries, was recently nominated for "rising star" recognition at the South of Scotland Thistle Awards. Zoey said her journey had not been straightforward as she did not get the exam results she had hoped for at school, so she spent time working in the kitchens at Dumfries Infirmary. But when a job came up at Annandale Distillery, she jumped at the chance. She said: "My first thought was - there's a distillery in Annan? And my second thought was - whisky? "I thought I'd give it a chance and see what it was like because there's a lot of heritage when it comes to whisky. "And I've now been here three-and-a-half years and I've not looked back." Revived distillery toasts first 10-year-old malt Published 25 November 2024 Whisky wait is over after 99 years Published 15 November 2017 What does she think the area has to offer that others her age might ignore? One thing she highlighted was the relative costs of property compared with city prices. Zoey also believes the area has a lot to shout about and is happy to have returned after university. "The south of Scotland has so much heritage and it is a passion of mine," she said. "So I would naturally like to be somewhere where there's a lot of heritage and where I can kind of grow as an individual." Zoey is passionate about what the south of Scotland has to offer But she agrees that a lot more could be done to stop young people from leaving. "I would like to think we could go back to the local schools across the region and try and explain that there are other careers out there including in heritage and tourism," she said. Zoey would also like to see the area market itself better. "We've got so much to offer in terms of castles, in terms of scenery, in terms of attractions, accommodation, it's so vast," she said. "I always like to say that we've got everything that the Highlands have, but just in a much quieter area. "But we're going to use that quietness to our strength." What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland? She has certainly achieved that in her own career in the whisky industry - despite some people assuming she might lack the knowledge of older, male counterparts. "It has been tricky, I'm not going to lie," she said. "But I always think that if you prepare yourself well, those types of questions cannot faze you. "I've been so fortunate that all my experiences have been mostly pleasant and so I have not really felt it, but I do understand the struggles that other people face. "We just need to start changing people's opinions one woman at a time." Zoey is happy to do that from Dumfries and Galloway for the foreseeable future. "I'm only beginning to stick my teeth into the south of Scotland," she said. "So to leave, it would have to be a fairly big jump." events.title: The ‘golden visa’ isn’t just for the rich: UAE offers 10-year residency to $545,000 property buyers—or for nurses, teachers, and e-sports pros
events.summary: The standard golden visa bargain was simple: residency in exchange for money. Wealthy foreigners put hundreds of thousands of dollars into real estate or businesses, and governments gave them a foothold abroad. But the United Arab Emirates stretched that model further. When the Gulf state launched its golden visa in 2019, the government offered 10-year residency to people who could invest at least $545,000 into property as well as to  researchers, teachers and specialized talent. It expanded again in 2020 and 2022 to include doctors, nurses, engineers, tech workers, and e-sports gamers.  It’s part of the country’s effort to organize talent into needed industries without having to fully assimilate foreigners as citizens—expats make up 90% of the UAE’s population. And that community has grown even after Iran launched thousands of missiles and drones at the UAE during its war with the U.S. In essence, the UAE took a visa status normally associated with the rich and powerful and turned it into an umbrella program for both capital and talent, blending  labor and industrial policies, according to Kristin Surak, a professor of political sociology at the London School of Economics and author of The Golden Passport: Global Mobility for Millionaires.   Indeed, Dubai has used golden visas to build up specific sectors. It gave more than 1,400 nurses and midwives golden visas and over 223 educators from private schools, universities, and early childhood centers. The city has also made long-term residency one part of a push to build up its gaming industry by 2033 , giving e-sports professionals a chance to apply for the golden visa in an effort to create 30,000 gaming jobs and add about $1 billion to GDP, now being home to over 350 gaming companies. “It’s not a traditional golden visa,” Surak told Fortune . “Gold sounds cooler. You want a lead scientist? You call [the visa] gold.” That branding taps into the language of a wider market for second residences, with around 100 countries having golden visa programs, including Portugal, Australia, Canada, Greece and, more recently, the U.S. with Trump’s “ gold card ” in 2025.  Golden visas are not the only way to put down roots in another country. For those looking to go beyond obtaining residency, golden passports go further by granting citizenship. Both have become tools for wealthy families seeking easier travel or a fallback if political and economic conditions worsen at home.  Demand for both has climbed among Americans too, with investment migration firm Henley & Partners finding in its 2026 report that applications from U.S. nationals doubled last year and stayed elevated this year. In June, Apex Capital Partners, another citizenship-by-investment advisory firm, surveyed 1,733 Americans earning more than $200,000 and found that six in 10 would consider leaving the U.S. within five years.  Selling more than a visa The UAE adds another incentive for skilled workers and investors pondering a move: the country doesn’t levy income taxes, though some business activity is subject to a corporate tax.  Vladlena Baranova, head of legal at Immigrant Invest, a consulting firm that advises on citizenship-by-investment and golden visa programs, told Fortune that clients who choose the UAE over competing programs often do so for safety, lifestyle, and business reasons. “So many of them just want to live there,” Baranova said, noting that her firm’s clients from the Gulf region value Dubai’s safety—it scored highly on perceptions of public safety and quality of life last year—while its European ones seek out its tax environment and real estate opportunities. But since the Iran war, Dubai and the rest of the Gulf region are seen as less safe. Iranian missiles and drones struck several Gulf states repeatedly including the UAE , hitting five star hotels and Dubai’s airport . Official figures cited by The National show Dubai lost 61,000 residents in March, a 1.3% drop that brought the population to 4.65 million, though it rebounded to 4.74 million by the end of June and has added 157,000 residents in the year to date. That’s despite the UAE revoking visas or residency permits for some Iranian expats during the conflict. “We have certainly seen a slowdown in enquiries and applications for UAE residence in recent months, with geopolitical uncertainty influencing sentiment,” Dominic Volek, who advises wealthy families on residence and citizenship planning at Henley & Partners, told Fortune . “We see this as a moderation in demand rather than a fundamental shift in the UAE’s appeal.” The UAE has not publicly changed the golden visa’s eligibility rules since the Iran war, but it did take steps to return foreign residents who were affected by the war to the country. On March 15, authorities said they helped 500 golden visa holders and residents return after airspace closures and flight disruptions stranded them abroad. Immigration officials also let stranded residents whose permits expired while overseas return without applying for a new entry visa and waived overstay fines. At the end of March, Dubai approved a roughly $272 million relief package that included faster issuance and renewal of residency permits, which the government said would make it “easier for talent to live and work in Dubai.” Surak said before the golden visa program, foreigners relied on two-year, employment-linked visas. For a government overseeing a population dominated by mobile expats, that created a lot of uncertainty in terms of establishing an economic base that can support a welfare system and basic state infrastructure. But the 10-year residency system made it possible for foreigners to stay without tying their status to one job by issuing it directly to the person instead of the employer. Dubai’s media and residency authorities and the UAE’s federal immigration authority did not respond to Fortune ’s multiple requests for comment. A visa that doesn’t belong to your boss For Swanand Pagnis, co-founder of enterprise AI engineering firm Superlinear Insights, this independence was the golden visa’s biggest attraction.  Pagnis moved to the UAE in 2022 on an employer-sponsored visa before securing a golden visa in 2023. He has a wife and daughter, and the possibility that losing his job could also jeopardize their ability to stay in the country weighed on him. “When you’re in a foreign country, one of the levers a company has on you is the visa, and there’s always a little bit of this tension where if you lose your job, you have to leave the country, leave everything behind,” Pagnis told Fortune . “The golden visa allows me to sponsor my family on my own.” Iran’s attacks on the UAE made his daughter’s school announce an early term break, and so his family temporarily relocated to India, then came back when flights to the UAE resumed and were declared safe, he said. events.title: Trump's Russia diesel deal may offer Putin more than money — and spell trouble for Ukraine
events.summary: A series of moves by U.S. President Donald Trump has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner. The U.S.-Russia diesel deal offers Moscow limited financial gains but could encourage Putin to seek further Western concessions, experts told CNBC. According to Serhiy Derkach, Ukraine's first deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport, Starlink restrictions emboldened Russia to intensify attacks on Ukraine. Ukraine is facing increasing uncertainty over its ability to sustain the war against Russia as a series of moves by U.S. President Donald Trump has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner. Trump's agreement with Putin to ease sanctions for Russia to provide global markets with diesel, as well as restrictions on U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukrainian forces, has put President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a difficult position as winter looms. On Saturday, Zelenskyy condemned the White House's waiver of key provisions of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine. ″... The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy said in a post on X . "And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people." Higher diesel prices – essential to transporting goods and agricultural production – tend to drive up costs across the wider economy and fuel inflation. With November's U.S. midterm elections approaching, Trump is under pressure to bring fuel costs down. But experts told CNBC that the diesel deal would deliver only a marginal financial benefit to Russia, and not move the needle much on global energy prices. Its wider political implications may be more significant, potentially reinforcing the Kremlin's belief that it can secure concessions from Washington without making compromises over Ukraine. "Russia's main gain is political: Trump's decision eases sanctions pressure and undermines Western unity," Sergey Aleksashenko, senior research fellow and head of economics at the NEST Centre, told CNBC. Trump's agreement with Putin was for Russia to supply the global market with 4.8 million metric tons of diesel, the equivalent of about ten days of U.S. domestic demand , or about a single day of global demand. Experts say it will do little to affect prices. "It does not even touch the sides – it is very, very small," Neil Atkinson, former head of the IEA's oil industry and markets division, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday. Aleksashenko estimated that the initial part of the phased agreement that covers 1.8 million metric tons of diesel could generate up to $1.25 billion in additional export revenue over three months, equivalent to around 1% of Russia's commodity export revenues during that period. However, the benefit to Russia's federal budget would be substantially smaller, at less than $30 million per month, or under 0.07% of monthly federal revenues. The deal was therefore unlikely to meaningfully strengthen Russia's war finances, Aleksashenko said. Instead, its main benefit to Moscow is political, because it eased sanctions pressure and undermined Western unity without requiring Putin to make concessions over Ukraine, he told CNBC. The research fellow also argued that the additional Russian diesel entering global markets is not sufficient to produce a noticeable reduction in consumer fuel prices in the short term. "Funding the war is currently Putin's priority, and he is prepared to increase that funding even if it means cutting all other expenditures," Aleksashenko added, pointing to Russia's draft budget for 2027. "Rather than encouraging compromise, the [diesel] deal likely boosts Moscow's belief that continued pressure will eventually yield further Western concessions," Maria Snegovaya, senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy also warned that the diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives. "Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry." Earlier this week, reports emerged that SpaceX's Starlink military application Starshield has been restricted in Ukraine. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network. The order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, according to a Reuters report citing three officials familiar with the matter. CNBC has contacted the White House for comment. The consequences were felt sharply in Ukraine.

events.title: Fuel prices dominate midterm election discussions, but spiking utility bills may be the difference maker
events.summary: Record-breaking fuel prices triggered by the Iran war and global refinery outages have dominated the discourse leading up to the November midterm elections, but skyrocketing utility bill and the data center boom are squarely on the ballot too—and could tip the balance of power in many states and in Congress. Prior to the beginning of the Iran war, electricity and natural gas utility bills led the nation in inflation and helped trigger the AI and data center backlash, even though data centers are only partly responsible for rising utility bills in some parts of the country. But the uproar hasn’t dissipated—despite fuel prices winning more headlines of late—and many positions from public utility commissioners to U.S. senators to governors hang in the balance, said Charles Hua, executive director of the PowerLines nonprofit, which seeks to modernize the utility regulatory system. “This is no longer a boring, sleepy energy story,” Hua said. “I cannot think of another election cycle prior to this 2026 midterm cycle where electricity and utility bills were on the ballot. “Energy has always been an issue that’s animated voters, but primarily on the oil and gas and fuel cost side in terms of what people pay at the pump. What is new and distinctive about this moment is the way in which electricity is now an issue and the way in which utility bills are one of the predominant sources of frustration for energy consumers across the country,” he added. Over the last five years, U.S. electricity prices have risen by roughly 40% on average. Through the first three quarters of 2026, utilities have requested another $23.1 billion in rate increases, on track to match the record-smashing high of nearly $31 billion in 2025. The record set last year was nearly double the previous high. And utility rate hikes are typically associated with increased spending. Investor-owned utility companies increased their capital expenditure plans by more than 27% to at least $1.4 trillion through 2030, up from $1.1 trillion a year ago, and that’s not even counting privately held companies, according to PowerLines. While most of the rate hikes from previous years are attributed to an aging grid in need of upgrades, increasingly extreme weather events, and volatile fuel prices, much of the future spending is also for new power generation, in part to power the AI data center boom. Data center developers can build their own power behind the meter or cover the costs to help reduce the impacts on ratepayers, but it varies by project and region. Some states have data center moratoriums while others have rejected or reduced rate hikes. The White House pushed for a non-binding “Ratepayer Protection Pledge” with hyperscalers to keep costs down on consumers. “Data centers are putting significant pressure on the grid and whether or not, in any given electricity market or state, data centers are actually driving up electricity rates is a very nuanced conversation,” Hua said. “Regardless of the reality, there certainly is a perception in most, if not all states at this point, that data centers could be driving up utility bills.” All forms of energy rising Retail gasoline and diesel prices have spiked to new highs this year, but they’re not expected to go up substantially higher from now. The same may not prove true of utility costs where many rate hikes remain pending and a tough winter could cause further spikes. The latest consumer price index showed heating oil in September was up 74% from a year ago, nearly double the jump in gasoline, just as residents start filling their tanks for winter. “This winter’s spike in heating oil prices is going to hit families hard as heating season starts now,” said Jamie Van Nostrand, policy director of the Future of Heat Initiative, which advocates for heat pumps. “A typical oil-heated home burns 500 to 700 gallons a year. At today’s prices, that’s $3,000 to $4,000, or 50% to 75% more than this time last year, landing on households already stretched by higher costs everywhere else.” In terms of motor fuel, as of Friday, the average price of a gallon of regular unleaded gasoline was $4.33, up 42% from 12 months prior. This is the first time gasoline has ever exceeded $4 a gallon in October. Likewise, the average diesel cost was $6.33 a gallon, up 73% in a year. Diesel had never exceeded $6 a gallon on average until this year. Fuel and utility costs are being compounded by many consumers, Hua said. “People do notice when their gasoline prices are high. There’s just a general feeling of malaise and frustration that bills are going up, that they can’t afford it, and part of what’s new is just the degree to which energy costs are now the greatest in magnitude drivers upwards of prices.” There is little people can do to combat fuel prices, but they can push back against utility rates, especially with their elected officials, including their public utility commissions that typically approve rates hike requests. Nearly half of the $4.5 billion in rate hike requests from the third quarter were in southern U.S. states, according to PowerLines. But the single-biggest quarterly rate request came from Jersey Central Power & Light, which asked regulators for a $700 million increase. Many states and commissions are looking harder at ways to better utilize existing grid resources—a lot of generated power is never used—such as incorporating more utility-scale batteries and virtual power plants (automatically reducing power usage at times of peak demand, including from data centers ). These are essentially ways of turning a dumb grid smart. “Electricity politics are ratcheting up in terms of the pressure point. What was once a boring, sleepy issue where the PUC made decisions more or less in a vacuum is no longer the case. This is now a political issue,” Hua said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Condé Nast’s UK profits drop by more than a third as sale of Vogue publisher ruled out
events.summary: Magazine group points to restructuring bill but says it ‘remains profitable in the UK for another year’ Profits at Condé Nast’s UK arm slumped by more than a third last year, according to figures published shortly after the billionaire family that owns the luxury magazine group and titles from Vogue to GQ ruled out a sale. The publisher, which enjoyed a bumper 2024 after booking £64m in proceeds from the sale of its UK headquarters Vogue House in London, saw pre-tax profits excluding exceptional items tumble 36% from £28m that year to nearly £18m last year. Revenues generated in the UK fell 7% from £75.9m to £70.6m, newly filed accounts showed. However, an 18% increase in international revenues, to £29.7m, helped keep the company’s total revenues almost flat, at £100m. “Condé Nast remains profitable in the UK for another year,” a spokesperson for the publisher said. “The change in the exact level of profit reflects a period of planned investment in customised client solutions.” Restructuring costs at the company, which publishes glossy titles and brands including Vanity Fair, House & Garden and Tatler, more than doubled year on year, from £1.9m to £4.3m. Condé Nast said the latest restructuring charge was “primarily due to severance costs”. Despite the hefty restructuring bill, staff numbers remained almost flat, dipping from 466 to 461 between 2024 and last year. “There were no large restructures in the UK business in 2025. There were isolated instances of redundancy, but headcount remained flat as hiring continued across the business,” the spokesperson said. “In addition, there have been changes to the pension scheme projections and wage inflation, which also impacted profit for this year.” Last week, Steven Newhouse, the chair of the Newhouse family holding company Advance that controls Condé Nast, ruled out a sale of the publishing giant. There had been speculation that the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, who owns the Washington Post, could buy the business. Newhouse made the comment after the abrupt departure of the chief executive Roger Lynch, hired in 2019 to turn around the business, to become the boss of the toymaker Mattel. “Maybe for a certain class of non-media owner, there’s a prestige to owning media properties,” he told the Financial Times . “But we’ve been a media owner for 100 years. So we’re not in it for the glamour.” Earlier this year, Lynch described the introduction of Google’s AI Summaries – which often negate the need to click through to source material – as “another sort of death blow” to the way consumers have traditionally searched online and reached media outlets. He said Google searches were “no longer a meaningful driver” of Condé Nast’s business, accounting for only about a quarter of visits to its websites last year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Globally, seven of Condé Nast’s largest brands – Vogue, GQ, the New Yorker, Wired, Vanity Fair, Architectural Digest and Condé Nast Traveler – account for 85% of the company’s revenues. Newsstand sales and other subscriptions account for about 14% of total revenues, with advertising and “other services” accounting for about 86%. The publisher’s accounts filed at Companies House show that the highest-paid director - Natalia Gamero del Castillo Calleja, the company’s most senior executive outside the US who resigned last August - took home more than £1.3m. Earlier this year, Condé Nast announced plans to shutter Self , its women’s health magazine, after 47 years.

events.title: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely
events.summary: Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden said hedge funds’ growing presence in bond markets heightens the risk of financial shocks spreading across markets. The IMF this week warned that hedge funds' use of leverage and crowded trading strategies could amplify market stress. The warnings follow a sharp sell-off in global government bonds in recent weeks. Hedge funds' increased presence in global bond markets makes the likelihood of a broader market shock "greater than what it was," Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden told CNBC Thursday. Breeden — the central bank's deputy governor for financial stability, and a member of its rates-setting Monetary Policy Committee — said the changing mix of bond market investors, and their increased use of leverage, raises the risk of localized market turbulence turning into broader financial stress. "One of the things that has become increasingly apparent over the last several years is that the investors in our core government bond markets globally have changed," Breeden told CNBC's Sri Jegarajah in an interview Thursday. "It's not the real money investors, the insurance companies and pension funds, in the way it used to be. It's increasingly hedge funds, and those hedge funds are price-sensitive, leveraged, international. That, of course, means that the likelihood of a shock in one market transmitting to another is greater than what it was." Breeden was speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. With gross assets now standing at about $13 trillion, hedge funds have become an increasingly important part of the global investor landscape, the IMF said on Tuesday. In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, published Tuesday, the IMF acknowledged hedge funds' role in supporting market liquidity and efficiency. But it also warned that the hedge fund industry's use of leverage to boost returns, and its tendency to pursue crowded trades, could turbo-charge market stress in times of turmoil. That, in turn, could spill over into broader financial markets, and areas such as banks' prime brokerage businesses, according to the IMF. "The source of the shocks are bond markets, and the likelihood of a spillover is higher than it was," Breeden said. Hedge funds' presence in the global government bond market — particularly their use of so-called "basis trades" — has come under sharper scrutiny this year, following the sharp sell-off in sovereign debt. Hedge funds held a record 7% of the $30 trillion Treasury market at the end of 2025, according to U.S. Office of Financial Research data published on Aug. 19. Basis trades are an arbitrage bet in which hedge funds are positioned long in cash Treasurys while shorting their corresponding futures contracts, with the aim of profiting from the price gap. While the price differential between the two is relatively small, hedge funds often employ large amounts of leverage to further inflate returns. Earlier this month, 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest levels since 2002. Across the Atlantic, yields on 10-year U.K. government bonds , known as gilts, also touched multi-decade highs. Yields on France's government bonds, known as OATs, have moved sharply higher in recent weeks amid rising concerns about the country's fiscal outlook — fueling fears of a fresh sovereign debt crisis impacting the euro zone.
