events.title: Heating oil customers face tough winter
events.summary: Nicola Sharpe said she would normally have stocked up by now but was holding off in the hope the price would fall Some people say they are finding it hard to heat their homes after increases in heating oil costs fuelled by the US-Israeli war with Iran. Residents in the South West told the BBC they have held off buying fuel for the winter in the hope prices could come down and feared some people might go without. It comes as the government announced new measures aimed at regulating the market and reviewing the minimum amounts some people have to buy. Heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the conflict, according to the Minster for Energy Consumers Polly Billington. Billington told the BBC: "We need to make sure the market is working as fairly as possible." She said it was "striking" how rural communities with "so many people off grid" were "some of the most exposed" to the price increases. Nicola Sharpe, from Dunsford, Devon, said this time last year she was paying about £340 for 500 litres, but the price was currently just over £600 for the same amount. "I'm looking at ways to spread the cost when I have to bite the bullet and get it," she said. Earlier in October, the government promised better regulation of the sector . Ministers said they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things went wrong. Minimum order levels, set for some customers, would also be reviewed. Pauline Trubody said she usually had the heat on during the day in the winter Sharpe said she was not hopeful the government measures would help. "I can't see how regulating it is going to bring costs down." Pauline Trubody, from Porkellis, Cornwall, said she had already spent more on two deliveries of 500 litres this year compared to previous years. The 76-year-old said: "I probably won't put it [the heating] on as much as I would have. "There is going to be a lot of people who can't afford it and folk who are going to go cold." Lee Fossey, from St Agnes, Cornwall, pays £30 a month into a savings scheme to spread the cost of heating oil throughout the year. She said: "I have done everything I reasonably can to budget and prepare for winter, yet despite this, the dramatic increase in prices means I can no longer afford to fill my tank." She said she faced the prospect of having no heating this winter or using the money for an alternative heating source. Prices have soared since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran. In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil. Follow BBC Cornwall on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: Heat pumps and insulation would cut UK living costs more than new oilfields, study suggests
events.summary: Warm homes plan would create 50,000 jobs, compared with about 1,100 for Rosebank oilfield, thinktank finds Insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps would do more to cut the cost of living, create jobs and boost the UK’s economy than drilling for new oil, research suggests. The government’s £15bn warm homes plan, currently under threat of cuts as ministers seek budget savings , would slash £1bn a year from household energy bills across the UK, concentrated on those on low incomes, according to research by the thinktank E3G. It would also provide a £1.6bn yearly boost to the economy, and about 50,000 new jobs spread across thousands of small businesses. The Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, would create about 1,100 direct and indirect jobs, the analysis found. The jobs would be concentrated in the North Sea and in two companies, one of them – Equinor – an overseas investor. A decision on whether to give the green light to the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea was “imminent”, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said on Wednesday. A decision on Rosebank would take a little longer, she said. Labour promised in its 2024 election manifesto to halt new licensing for oil and gas, but Jackdaw and Rosebank could be exceptions because they were already in the licensing system. Equinor previously estimated 3,500 jobs would be created at peak for Jackdaw and Rosebank combined. Experts have repeatedly pointed out that new North Sea oil and gas would not bring down fuel prices or ease any supply constraints on the UK arising from the Iran war, because oil and gas are sold on international markets. Some proponents of drilling argue that the economic boost to the UK and tax revenues for the government are reasons to grant licences. But related research by WWF and the campaigning group Uplift shows that tax revenues are likely to be limited, given the concessions that drillers can expect . While the total profits from Rosebank for its backers, Equinor, Shell and Ithaca Energy, could be £1.5bn over its 25-year lifespan, the UK government faces a potential loss of £258m through tax breaks and incentives. Tax revenues from the North Sea were about £4bn in 2025-26, but upstream tax relief and support measures amounted to an estimated £3.26bn. As the North Sea is a basin in steep decline, tax revenues from drilling are projected to fall to about £100m by 2030. Decommissioning costs for drilling platforms are also a major factor: taxpayers are likely to be asked for £12bn as the North Sea’s infrastructure is dismantled. The warm homes plan , under which up to 5m homes would be insulated, would draw in a further £15bn in private investment, according to E3G, which would be spread across the country rather than concentrated in one area, in line with Andy Burnham’s pledge for economic growth “in every postcode”. E3G also estimates that delivering the warm homes plan in full would boost GDP by 0.08%, while AI modelling suggests Rosebank would add about 0.025% on average through its lifetime, assuming the average oil price returning to $70 a barrel from recent highs. If the UK taxpayer paid for decommissioning, this would outweigh any positive impact. James Huw Dyson, a senior researcher at E3G, said: “When the first cold snap rolls in, the public aren’t going to thank the government for cutting home insulation while giving big oil tax breaks to drill for polluting energy that keeps our bills high. If the government is serious about tackling the cost of living, and investing across the country, it should focus its attention on insulating homes and rolling out clean energy, which will cut bills and create good jobs across Britain at the same time.” Ten major unions wrote to the government on Thursday to oppose granting a licence to the Rosebank oilfield. Scores of Labour MPs also oppose the move , and 600 scientists wrote to ministers over the summer urging a rethink. Dhara Vyas, the chief executive of Energy UK, which represents the energy industry, said: “We need government to stick to its ambitions on electrification. Watering down the warm homes plan or making further changes to the zero emissions vehicle mandate sends mixed signals to a market that has been in a state of flux for far too long – these businesses cannot easily ramp up production again, and sadly for too many have already had to close.” The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero declined to comment on E3G’s findings or the future of the warm homes plan. A spokesperson for Adura, the joint venture between Equinor and Shell that owns Jackdaw and Rosebank, said: “Analysis has shown that approving Rosebank and other planned North Sea oil developments would support £35.3bn in UK economic value between 2026 and 2035. Rosebank alone represents private sector investment of £8.7bn, three quarters of which will be spent in the UK, and together with Jackdaw will contribute £4.1bn in additional tax revenue over the next decade.

events.title: £3,500 and no work done: the offer to help that’s really a roofing scam
events.summary: Citizens Advice warns of its No 1 scam as growing number of people are targeted by criminals posing as roofers The builder who calls at your door says they are doing some work in the area and has spotted a loose tile on your roof. They offer to fix it for a good price that you agree to. But when they go up on their ladder to inspect the problem, they see another problem. Rain has been splashing out of the gutters and the wood around them is getting damaged. The only solution, the builder says, is to have rigid PVC trays installed to divert the water. More rain is forecast and you are worried about what damage could be done so you pay the builder via bank transfer to get the job done there and then. They are gone within an hour, having apparently completed the work. But nothing was done because there was no problem with your guttering. Instead you were one of a growing number of people who have been targeted by criminals posing as roofers, only to make off with payment after doing unnecessary or no work. The charity Citizens Advice says suspected roofing frauds were the top scam it heard from consumers about in the last year. It received more than 2,200 complaints of suspected roofing scams in the year to August in England and Wales, about 10% more than the previous year. “The vast majority of cases is … somebody just knocking on your door saying that they’ve noticed that there’s something wrong with your roof and they’re in a position to help you,” says Ruwani Purcell, the director of external affairs at Citizens Advice. “The difficulty is [that] your roof is out of sight and out of reach. You can’t fully see what’s going on.” Purcell says the fraudsters use really persuasive tactics to offer you confidence and reassurance that they know what they’re talking about. “And you might not be familiar with [the] terms,” she says. “In the worst case scenarios, they’ve been quite intimidating to compel people to hand over money there and then.” While more than three-quarters of the roofing scams reported to Citizens Advice start with someone knocking at the door, some criminals look online for potential victims. In one case dealt with by Citizens Advice, a 65-year-old woman posted on an online platform that she needed someone to fix a dripping sound in her gutters. A builder phoned her to say that it would cost £250 but when he and another man came and examined her roof they said they had discovered more problems and the price quickly grew. At one point they showed her a bucket of cement and said it was crumbling from under the tiles. The woman said the man and his accomplice said the work needed to be done immediately and once they claimed to have finished they wanted the payment straightaway. “I was afraid, two men in front of me in the dark, demanding money and making it clear they weren’t moving,” the victim told Citizens Advice. “They knew I was alone, I didn’t feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500.” She paid it using bank transfer. “The next day there was no trace that any work was done,” she said. “I felt stupid, and tried to contact them, but couldn’t get through.” Be wary of anyone offering unsolicited work by cold calling and demanding confirmation of a job and payment there and then. No reputable builder will do that, says Purcell. To check the roofer’s authenticity, ask for references and for all proposed work to be confirmed in writing. Treat it as a red flag if they refuse this or if they insist on being paid in cash. To see if a trader is reputable, you can check your local council’s website as it often lists trusted traders. The government runs the TrustMark scheme which lists approved tradespeople. Citizens Advice says that if a trader has done a poor job without reasonable care and skill, the victim is entitled to ask for the problem to be fixed or get a refund under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Keep any paperwork and receipts, take photos and document what happened to make your case.

events.title: For investors, there are now just 2 kinds of offices: the best and the rest
events.summary: The global office market has become deeply divided, with rents in prime buildings rising while others sit empty despite cutting rates From Hong Kong to New York, a deep divide is opening up in office markets around the world, as tenants compete for space in prime buildings while other properties face falling rents, low occupancy and financing pressures. The divergence reflects a global flight to quality, but also a disconnect between improving leasing fundamentals and a recovery in property values, according to analysts at Morgan Stanley and JLL. The divide is being reinforced by limited new supply in prime locations, differences in how cities remove obsolete offices, and companies’ efforts to attract talent through better workplaces.

events.title: Two people in custody after protest at offshore Woodside gas platform
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australian Border Force responds to Greenpeace protest at Woodside's Scarborough gas platform Greenpeace say activists spent the night on the platform. ( Supplied: Greenpeace ) Two people are in police custody after occupying an offshore Woodside gas platform about 200 kilometres off Western Australia's coast to protest against the company's gas operations. An Australian Border Force (ABF) spokesperson said they were working with federal and state agencies to respond to the situation after activists occupied the rig overnight and disrupted the gas giant's operations. Images shared by environmental advocacy group Greenpeace Australia Pacific show its activists scaling a Woodside gas platform and hanging a banner in protest of the company's planned gas project at Scott Reef. Greenpeace said four protesters travelled to the platform early Saturday morning, and two of them set up "temporary hanging tents" to occupy the platform for "as long as possible". On Sunday afternoon Greenpeace said two of its activists had been taken into police custody. Protesters scaled a gas platform operated by Woodside. ( Supplied: Greenpeace ) "Special police forces landed a helicopter on the [platform] at around 11:30am AWST," Greenpeace said. "The activists safely removed themselves from their equipment before being taken into police custody around 1pm." Woodside confirmed the protest had disrupted operations at the rig, which forms part of the company's $12.5 billion Scarborough natural gas project. "Pre-commissioning activities at Scarborough have been paused as part of routine procedures following the unauthorised access," a spokesperson said. Scott Reef is Australia's largest standalone oceanic reef and a refuge for thousands of aquatic creatures and shorebirds — Woodside's plans have been heavily contested by environmental groups opposed to gas developments in the area. Woodside's Browse gas project plans to tap into Australia's largest undeveloped offshore gas reserve, and is estimated to cost about $48.7 billion according to a Deloitte analysis. A banner unfurled by protesters at a Woodside gas platform. ( Supplied: Greenpeace ) Woodside said Greenpeace's activists had "deliberately and unlawfully" accessed the floating production unit and had "not only endangered their own safety, but that of Woodside staff". "Greenpeace's actions have triggered a significant, potentially costly and entirely avoidable response, requiring Western Australian resources to be mobilised to manage the safety, security and operational consequences of their actions," a Woodside spokesperson said. Greenpeace Australia Pacific CEO David Ritter said the activists involved in the latest demonstration were "highly trained and experienced", and said care was "always taken in the health, safety and welfare of all involved". He said environmental groups had been scaling up their activism in response to Woodside's planned Browse project. "Greenpeace and other community organisations have been building up their activities matching that rise in community concern," Mr Ritter told the ABC. "There is no question that our activities are increasing to match this reckless threat of Woodside." Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King said the activists had broken several laws, and described the protest as "reckless behaviour in the extreme". Madeleine King says the behaviour of the protesters was "reckless". ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) "Putting so many lives at risk all for a 20-second TikTok ... we expect the authorities once they've done their proper processes to throw the book at them," Ms King said. WA Greens fossil fuels and climate change spokesperson Sophie McNeill rejected Ms King's comments. "The real selfish ones putting lives at risk is Woodside — not these Greenpeace activists — as the fossil fuel giant recklessly opens massive new gas projects in the middle of a worsening and increasingly deadly climate crisis," she said.

events.title: Dubai's economy reaches Dh473 billion in first half of 2026 as key sectors expand
events.summary: Dubai's economy reached Dh473 billion in the first half of 2026, down 2.3 per cent from a year earlier, as growth in financial services, healthcare and construction helped offset weakness in other sectors. The emirate's real gross domestic product declined from Dh484 billion in the same period last year, according to figures released on Sunday by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment at Digital Dubai. The slowdown came as the Iran war, which began on February 28, disrupted regional travel and trade, weighing on Dubai's tourism and transport sectors and dampening economic activity during the first half of the year. GDP at current prices, however, increased by 0.2 per cent to Dh505 billion, reflecting growth across several key sectors. Helal Almarri, director general of the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, said the figures demonstrated the emirate's ability to navigate global uncertainty. "Dubai’s H1 2026 GDP performance reflects the strength and adaptability of an economy built to navigate periods of significant global uncertainty," he said. The first-half numbers, however, mark a reversal from the 2.4 per cent annual growth recorded in the first quarter , when Dubai's economy reached Dh232 billion despite regional economic challenges. Financial and insurance activities were among the strongest performers in the first half, expanding 8.8 per cent in real terms to Dh65.9 billion, compared with Dh60.6 billion a year earlier. The sector's contribution to GDP increased to 14 per cent from 12.5 per cent, highlighting its growing importance to the emirate's economy. The expansion comes as the Dubai International Financial Centre continues to attract international financial institutions , with the number of companies operating at the financial hub exceeding 10,000 in the first half of the year. Healthcare and social work activities recorded the fastest growth, expanding 14.3 per cent, while information and communication activities increased 2.7 per cent. Construction grew 2.4 per cent in real terms, generating Dh33.2 billion in value added, while government services expanded 2.9 per cent. However, several major sectors contracted during the period. Dubai's GDP reaches AED473 billion in H1 2026 #WamNews https://t.co/x6Y1agL9wD https://t.co/G8rxQVRfZ9 — WAM English (@WAMNEWS_ENG) October 17, 2026 Wholesale and retail trade, Dubai's largest economic activity, declined 6 per cent in real terms, although it continued to account for 20.5 per cent of GDP. Transport and storage fell 7.4 per cent, while real estate activity contracted 2.5 per cent in constant prices, despite growing 5.4 per cent at current prices. Manufacturing also declined 0.9 per cent in real terms. The slowdown reflects wider economic challenges across the region, with the UAE's economy expanding just 0.4 per cent in the first half amid disruption caused by the Iran war. Free zone boost However, despite the geopolitical headwinds, trade in the first six months of this year through Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (Diez) free zones achieved another record. The total value of trade across its three economic zones climbed 17 per cent annually to Dh246 billion, Dubai Media Office said on Sunday. The results marked Diez's sixth consecutive year of record first-half trade performance, reflecting the confidence of investors and international trade stakeholders in Dubai's and the UAE's position at the heart of global trade. The value of imports during the first half rose to Dh134.8 billion, a 14 per cent increase compared to the same period last year. Re-exports grew by 22 per cent to about Dh109 billion. Trade volumes reached approximately 270,000 tonnes during the first half of the year, compared to approximately 298,000 tonnes during the same period in 2025, the media office said. Projects continue Dubai is moving ahead with Dh2.1 trillion in projects covering housing, aviation and transport, including the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport, as part of efforts to support long-term economic growth. Meanwhile, Dubai CommerCity announced a Dh1.8 billion expansion this month to boost its digital commerce sector and attract more technology investment. Mr Almarri said that continued growth across strategic sectors highlighted the strength of Dubai's economic fundamentals and its focus on long-term development. Dubai is pressing ahead with its D33 economic agenda, which aims to strengthen its position as a global business and investment centre. The emirate has also introduced measures to support businesses, including a Dh1.5 billion economic relief package announced in May to help sectors affected by regional uncertainty.

events.title: 7-Eleven adds hot-food counters at 16 Singapore stores as DFI Retail sharpens growth focus
events.summary: The section for ready-to-eat meals at the 7-Eleven outlet in East Coast Parkway. SINGAPORE – Convenience store chain 7-Eleven is introducing hot-food counters at 16 outlets in Singapore, offering options from customisable bowls to pizza and waffles as it expands its meal offerings to meet the rising demand for more ready-to-eat food. The Foodbar roll-out, unveiled on Oct 16, is part of DFI Retail Group’s push to draw more customers to its stores through new products and experiences. Having sold its Singapore supermarket business, the group is expanding food offerings at 7-Eleven and Starbucks in the Republic, while strengthening Guardian’s health and wellness range. At larger Foodbars, customers can build their own bowls from $4.50, choosing a base such as rice, penne pasta or noodles, as well as sauces, toppings and garnishes. Options include roast chicken, hash browns and chicken cutlets. Other outlets will offer hot snacks such as pizza, croissants, pancakes and waffles for dine-in or takeaway. The format will vary depending on each store’s location, customer profile and available space. The new 7-Eleven concept comes as a survey commissioned by the retailer found that busy schedules and unpredictable routines are shaping meal choices among convenience-store customers, while perceptions towards convenience food have become more positive over the past three years. The online study, conducted in August, surveyed 1,020 convenience-store shoppers in Singapore who had purchased ready-to-eat meals in the preceding month. In the Republic, ready-to-eat products already account for a double-digit percentage of sales and are recording double-digit sales growth, 7-Eleven Singapore managing director Anushree Khosla told The Straits Times. She added that customers here are increasingly seeking new food experiences, including products and concepts they had come across at convenience stores while travelling in Japan, Taiwan and Thailand. Khosla said 7-Eleven is refitting its Singapore stores and broadening its product range to become a destination for food and shopping discoveries. The changes include creating more space for browsing and dining, as well as expanding its range of ready-to-eat meals, drinks, snacks and exclusive collectables. She added that 7-Eleven launches more than 1,000 new exclusive products a year, including trending items such as kunafa chocolate. It also carries more than 100 protein-focused products, ranging from shakes, milk and bars to chicken breast. Its ready-to-eat range now comprises 130 products across breakfast, meals, desserts and snacks, inspired by convenience-store food in Japan, Taiwan and Thailand. Recent additions include halal-certified Korean-inspired kimbap and onigiri, desserts and Thailand-inspired toasties. Since 2021, the chain has also collaborated with local brands, including Andes by Astons, Lau Wang Claypot Delights, Playmade, Chocolate Origin and Nasty Cookie. The retailer noted that these brands are more popular with customers than healthier or budget-friendly meals. 7-Eleven, which has 450 stores in Singapore, is operated by DFI Retail Group, which has been reshaping its portfolio in recent years to concentrate on businesses where it sees stronger growth prospects or greater operational control. In 2025, it sold its Singapore food retail business, comprising Cold Storage, CS Fresh, Giant and Jason’s Deli, to Malaysian retailer Macrovalue for $125 million. Earlier in October, the Singapore-listed group also took full control of Starbucks’ licensed operations in Asia, including in the Republic, where the coffee chain has 138 outlets. In response to queries from ST, group chief executive Scott Price said DFI sees room to grow coffee and tea consumption in Singapore given the country’s strong cafe culture. He added that the group plans to introduce more food and drinks tailored to local tastes at Starbucks and to expand the coffee chain’s lunch and evening offerings. DFI has also been expanding Guardian’s health and wellness offerings in Singapore, where the chain operates more than 120 outlets, through partnerships with supplement brands and healthcare providers. In August, DFI announced an expanded partnership with supplement company GNC, becoming the brand’s exclusive wholesaler, distributor and franchisee in Singapore, Hong Kong and Macau. This followed a multi-year agreement with British wellness retailer Holland & Barrett, whose products became available at selected Guardian Singapore stores and on its app in June.

events.title: Palm oil stocks tumble as S’pore looks for firms responsible for haze: Markets this week
events.summary: In this column, ST’s business correspondents unpack the latest developments in Singapore and global markets during the week – and explain what they mean for investors. Palm oil stocks fell as Singapore and Indonesia investigate companies that may be responsible for haze-causing fires. Singapore is investigating firms linked to haze fires under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. Palm oil shares fell as Wilmar, Golden Agri, Bumitama and First Resources denied or limited links. Deluge began trading on the SGX mainboard after a 3.86 times subscribed IPO. It plans to use about $20.1 million net proceeds for growth, partnerships and fire-detection services. Tech stocks recovered after a sharp global sell-off, while SGX reported stronger turnover and new ETFs and SDRs. Next week, Singapore will release CPI data and the US will enter a major earnings week. SINGAPORE – The worsening haze across Singapore in recent weeks has cast a pall over the skies and certain stocks. Palm oil shares took a tumble when some Singapore-listed companies were linked to plantation areas in Indonesia where fires and smoke were detected. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also said on Facebook on Oct 15 that Singapore is looking into which companies may be responsible for haze-causing fires. He added that Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act and explore joint action with other countries, where warranted. The law, which was enacted in 2014, targets those responsible for causing or condoning fires if the haze causes the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) to stay in the unhealthy range in any part of Singapore for 24 hours or more. Air quality is considered unhealthy when PSI levels are 101 and above. The PSI levels have been over 200 in some areas over the last few days. Agribusiness group Wilmar International and palm oil company Golden Agri-Resources were among the Singapore-listed firms that have addressed their involvement in the ongoing forest fires in Indonesia. In response to queries on Oct 16 from the Singapore Exchange Regulation, both said that they have no-burning policies in place. Golden Agri said that it “is not aware of information indicating that its operations or activities have caused or contributed to the recent transboundary haze”. Wilmar said that it has not undertaken any new oil palm planting in its plantations in Indonesia since 2013. Since then, the firm’s field activities in Indonesia “have been limited to the replanting of existing planted areas, which is carried out mechanically and without the use of fire”. Meanwhile, palm oil company Bumitama Agri said that some of its operations in Indonesia were affected by fires spread from surrounding land. In a Singapore Exchange (SGX) filing on the evening of Oct 16 , it said that based on internal observations and preliminary investigations, “no evidence has been established linking the group’s operations with initiation of the fires under investigations and to the haze in question”. The firm, which had earlier called for a trading halt, was named in an investigation by environmental group Greenpeace, along with Singapore-listed palm oil company First Resources. First Resources said on Oct 15 that the fires detected within its Indonesian oil palm concessions were largely caused by external blazes spreading across its boundaries. Privately held company First Borneo Plantations, which has ownership links to Singapore-incorporated companies, was also named in the Oct 5 report. The report identified plantation concessions associated with the three companies where fires and smoke were detected between August and September. A concession grants a company the right to use or develop an area of land. Wilmar’s shares closed 1.2% down on Oct 16, while Golden Agri-Resources saw shares tumble 3.5%. First Resources saw shares fall by nearly 7%. Bumitama Agri’s prices fell by 4.8% before the company requested a trading halt before the afternoon session. In a quirk of timing, fire-protection specialist Deluge started trading on the SGX mainboard on Oct 16. Its initial public offering was 3.86 times subscribed. The offering comprised 15.6 million shares at 60 cents apiece. Of these, 14.8 million were placement shares, and 800,000 were for the public offer. The gross proceeds from the offering and cornerstone tranche are about $23.4 million. After deducting listing expenses, net proceeds are expected to be about $20.1 million. Deluge said it plans to use the proceeds to invest in infrastructure, facilities and operational capabilities, pursue strategic partnerships through installations and lifecycle services, and strengthen its integrated fire-detection platform. Deluge opened at 63 cents and closed 6.7% higher on its first trading day at 64 cents . Tech stocks started to show signs of recovery on Oct 16 after a six-day rout that wiped some US$1.6 trillion (S$2.05 trillion) off global semiconductor stocks.

events.title: UAE Property: 'Can I stay in my company-rented apartment after resigning?'
events.summary: Question: I recently relocated to Dubai for work and my employer has rented an apartment for me as part of my package. The tenancy contract is in the company's name and the company pays the rent directly to the landlord, although I'm the person living there with my family. I'm considering leaving the company for another job. The HR department has told me that if I resign, I may have to leave the apartment almost immediately because the company is technically the tenant. I assumed that because this is our family home and there is still plenty of time remaining on the tenancy contract, we'd be entitled to stay until it expires. Who actually has the rights in this situation – me or my employer? Michael, Dubai Answer: This is one of those situations where the person living in a property and the legal tenant aren't necessarily the same person. If your employer is named as the tenant on both the tenancy agreement and Ejari, then the contractual relationship with the landlord is primarily with the company, not you personally. Your right to occupy the apartment may therefore come from your employment package rather than from having an independent tenancy relationship with the landlord. I'd check three things before making any assumptions: the tenancy agreement, the Ejari registration and your employment contract or company housing policy. There may be specific provisions explaining what happens to company-provided accommodation when employment ends. I wouldn't assume that the remaining term of the tenancy automatically gives your family the right to remain. Equally, however, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll have to move. If you like the apartment, approach the landlord early. They may be happy to replace the corporate tenancy with a new agreement in your name once the company's obligations have been dealt with. You're already living in the property and presumably you've looked after it. From the landlord's perspective, retaining a known occupant may be preferable to remarketing the apartment and accepting the risk of a vacancy period. Just make sure any new arrangement is formally documented. Don't rely on an informal understanding that you can simply “take over” the company's tenancy. Q: I'm considering buying an off-plan apartment in Dubai and the developer is advertising a “guaranteed 10 per cent return for three years after handover”. On paper, it looks fantastic. The projected return is considerably higher than I could achieve from a normal long-term rental, and the broker says I don't need to worry about finding tenants because everything will be managed for me. What I'm struggling to understand is where the 10 per cent actually comes from. If the apartment doesn't generate enough rental income, is the developer legally required to make up the difference? And should I be suspicious when a guaranteed return looks much higher than normal market rent? Daniel, Manchester A: Whenever somebody uses the word “guaranteed” in an investment proposition, my next question is always: guaranteed by whom, and where exactly is that guarantee written down? Don't assess the investment on the headline percentage alone. Ask for the actual rental guarantee agreement and establish which legal entity is responsible for paying you. Is it the developer, management company or another company entirely? A guarantee is ultimately only as strong as the entity standing behind it. Then establish exactly how the 10 per cent is calculated. Is it based on the original purchase price, the amount you've paid, or another figure? Are service charges, furnishing costs, management fees and maintenance deducted before or after your guaranteed payment? I'd also want to know whether you're free to occupy or sell the apartment during the guarantee period and what happens to the arrangement if you do. There may be restrictions that aren't obvious from the headline advertisement. Most importantly, compare the promised income with the property's realistic open-market rental value. If a Dh2 million apartment would ordinarily rent for Dh120,000 a year, that's a 6 per cent gross yield. Someone promising Dh200,000 every year isn't creating the additional Dh80,000 through magic. There is an economic reason for it somewhere, and you need to understand where the money is coming from. Sometimes, these schemes are perfectly legitimate and genuinely useful to an investor. In other cases, part of the promised return may effectively have been incorporated into a higher purchase price. So I'd judge the property first and the guarantee second. Look at comparable prices, realistic rent, location, developer track record and likely resale demand without including the incentive. Then, ask yourself one simple question: if the guarantee disappeared tomorrow, would I still be happy owning this apartment at the price I'm paying? If the answer is no, I'd think very carefully before signing anything. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. events.title: Bill Lark is the godfather of Australian whisky but he has never seen times like these
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts The worldwide whisky downturn is putting Tasmania's top shelf industry on edge Whisky was legally distilled in Tasmania two years before it was in Scotland, yet the home-grown industry lay dormant for more than 150 years. Then known as Van Diemen's Land, the distilling of spirits was declared illegal in 1839 by Governor John Franklin, whose wife, Lady Jane, reportedly declared that she would "prefer barley be fed to pigs than it used to turn men into swine". The ban only eased in 1901 when national distilling laws passed, but it would take nearly 91 years before smaller producers were legally allowed to manufacture the liquor, thanks to the efforts of a man who became Tasmania's whisky godfather. It ushered in the dawn of the state's booming whisky economy, thriving on the world stage even when it was shocked by jaw-dropping scandals. Now a global whisky downturn is hitting distillers from Kentucky to Kilkenny and industry giants are bearing the brunt of it, pausing production and laying off staff as customers leave bottles on the shelves. While the old-fashioned boom-and-bust cycle is familiar for most distillers, the downturn represents the biggest challenge for Tasmania's whisky businesses since the state was governed by colonial law. Tasmania is home to a third of Australia's whisky distilleries. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) 'Let's give it a go': The birth of an industry Until 1992, small-scale spirit operations were not permitted in Australia, with the country's distillation act requiring people to have built a commercial-sized distillery before applying for a licence. But that requirement was scrapped after a campaign from Hobart-based land surveyor and pub owner Bill Lark. Bill Lark and his wife Lynn during the early days of Lark Distilling. ( Supplied: Bill Lark ) "The idea to make whisky came … from a realisation that Tasmania must have had good barley because our local beers were being exported all over the world at the time and we knew our water was probably some of the best water in the world," Mr Lark told 7.30. "And I just made a comment to my father-in-law and my wife, 'why isn't somebody making whisky in Tasmania?' and Lynn said to me, 'I don't know, Bill, but let's give it a go'. "When I look back, that was the start of the modern-day spirits industry in Australia, opening up the door for ... people to start with a small still and help us to produce good spirits here in Australia." The Larks sold their first bottles of whisky in 1998. ( Supplied: Bill Lark ) With a licence in hand, Bill and his wife Lynn went on to found Lark Distillery, and thanks to some advice from Scottish whisky giant John Grant, released their first batch of Tasmanian whisky in December 1998. "We had 150 bottles we could take to the market. We weren't sure whether people would like it, let alone buy it, but that sold out almost straight away," Mr Lark said. Bill Lark spearheaded a campaign that led to Tasmania's booming whisky industry. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) In 2014, a seismic shift occurred in the whisky world when Hobart-based distillery Sullivans Cove was awarded best single malt whisky at the World Whisky Awards. Sullivans Cove chief executive Andy Gaunt said the victory "changed everything" for the global whisky industry, and for the distillery, which until then had only been producing small amounts of the spirit. "It was really a moment that the whisky industry almost literally fell off their chair and realised that whiskies from the non-traditional countries were as good as, if not better in terms of quality, than whiskies from places like Scotland and Ireland and Japan and North America," he said. Andy Gaunt is the boss of Sullivans Cove distillery based in Hobart. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) Despite its rapid growth and award victories, Australian whisky hasn't been immune from controversy. The collapse of Tasmanian whisky producer Nant in 2017 left investors thousands of dollars out of pocket, after they had purchased barrels with the promise of them being bought back by the distillery when the whisky matured. Nant founder Keith Batt last year pleaded not guilty to 736 criminal offences. His case returns to court next February . In 2022, Lark chief executive Geoff Bainbridge resigned from his role after The Australian published footage of him intoxicated while allegedly smoking amphetamine. And earlier this year, a Hobart magistrate dismissed charges against the Salamanca Whisky Bar, after allegations it had sold fake versions of the award-winning Sullivans Cove whisky . Tasmanian whisky is globally renown.

events.title: Timor-Leste president says first gas agreements to be signed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Timor-Leste president says country to sign Greater Sunrise gas agreements within months Jose Ramos-Horta says the Greater Sunrise gas project is "finally happening" after years of "deadlock". ( ABC News: Warwick Ford ) Timor-Leste President José Ramos-Horta has declared that his country will sign the first agreements for the long-stalled Greater Sunrise gas project early next year, as the South-East Asian country pushes on with the hugely ambitious and contentious development. But there is still widespread scepticism in the sector about the commercial viability of Timor-Leste's plan to pipe gas from the Greater Sunrise fields to the country's south coast, where the government hopes to develop a multi-billion-dollar liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant and domestic gas facility. Timor-Leste says that will generate badly needed jobs and economic activity in the country, but the project has been beset with delays, disagreements and doubts. In November last year the Australian energy giant Woodside Energy, which holds a stake in the venture along with Timor-Leste's state-owned oil and gas company, struck an agreement to "mature and progress" the plan. The Greater Sunrise gas project was meant to transform Timor-Leste and bring billions in revenue, but locals are still waiting for the jobs and opportunities that were promised. And Mr Ramos-Horta told the ABC in Sydney that Greater Sunrise was now "finally happening" after "years and years of procrastination [and] deadlock". "I was told by Prime Minister Xanana [Gusmao] that he's confident that within the next few months they will sign the agreement, [that] we will finalise the three main documents," he said. Those three documents will help Australia, Timor-Leste and Woodside establish the regulatory and fiscal settings needed for the exploration and development of resources in Greater Sunrise. Mr Ramos-Horta's government previously said the parties reached technical agreement in Canberra on three documents: the Petroleum Mining Code, Production Sharing Contract and fiscal regime. But analysts, as well as government and industry sources, all caution that there is still no guarantee that Timor-Leste and Woodside will strike a commercial agreement on a development plan, and that any final investment decision is likely years away. Woodside and Timor-Leste's government said last year that the first LNG from Greater Sunrise may be produced "as early as 2032-2035, subject to concept selection and investment decisions". One-third of the Greater Sunrise project is owned by Australia's Woodside. ( ABC News: Margaret Burin ) Last month, Timor's petroleum minister pushed the production start date back to 2034-2035, saying the country hoped for a final investment decision by 2029. Mr Ramos-Horta said the regulatory agreements should be signed early next year after being checked and approved by both governments and Woodside. He struck a bullish tone, suggesting it was a significant moment for the project. "We cannot wait much longer. We have to do it now," he said. "Now is the time, is the opportunity." An airport built in anticipation of the gas project opened almost a decade ago, but it has hardly been used. ( ABC News: Nick Sas ) The issue is urgent for Timor-Leste because it remains heavily reliant on past oil and natural gas revenues invested in its Petroleum Fund. The lucrative Bayu-Undan gas field, which pumped billions of dollars into the fund over the last two decades, permanently ceased production last year. And while the fund now contains $26 billion, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned last year that it could be depleted by 2038 if Timor-Leste continues to rely on it to finance fiscal deficits without replenishing it. Mr Ramos-Horta warned back in 2022 that Timor-Leste would run off a "financial cliff" if it could not get Greater Sunrise up and running within a decade. Timor-Leste has also warned the Australian government that it would turn to Chinese investors to make the project a reality if it cannot secure agreement from Woodside, although analysts have previously questioned whether they would have the appetite. In the meantime, the airport built in anticipation of the project lies idle , while roads and other infrastructure constructed for the processing hub are beginning to crumble. But Mr Ramos-Horta said he was confident that Woodside was "determined to follow through" with the project to pipe gas to Timor-Leste. "It's beneficial to Woodside, beneficial to Australia, beneficial to Timor-Leste," he said.

events.title: AI trade reversal pierces Asia’s star picks-and-shovels stocks
events.summary: Investors have turned their attention to the trillions of dollars being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. Asia’s AI hardware stocks fell as US tech shares sold off and oil rose, raising fears that higher borrowing costs could slow AI infrastructure spending. Big winners such as Nan Ya Plastics, Unimicron Technology and Samsung Electro-Mechanics dropped sharply, while CoreWeave’s bond slump highlighted funding stress in the AI boom. Analysts warn that delayed investment could hit earnings for TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix, though some investors still expect AI demand to stay strong. A deepening sell-off in US technology stocks is exposing a new vulnerability in Asia’s artificial intelligence trade: mounting financing costs could choke off the spending needed to sustain the boom, threatening earnings across a supply chain that has powered the region’s stock-market rally. The pressure intensified last week as oil surged to US$110 a barrel for the first time since May, stoking inflation concerns, and investors turned their attention to the trillions of dollars being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. An eight-session rout in US semiconductor shares – the longest since 2008 – wiped roughly 16% off the sector’s benchmark, while the Nasdaq 100 suffered its worst week since April 2025. For Asia, where chipmakers and hardware suppliers that make printed circuit boards, precision components and manufacturing equipment have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI frenzy, the implications could be significant heading into the Oct 19 open. A Goldman Sachs Group basket of regional AI hardware stocks tumbled 11% last week, its steepest decline since mid-July. The sell-off showed little sign of abating despite an upbeat revenue outlook from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), underscoring how concerns over AI spending are spreading across the hardware supply chain. Some of Asia’s standout performers were hit particularly hard in the maelstrom. Nan Ya Plastics , a maker of printed circuit board materials and the best-performing stock on the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index in 2026 , tumbled 12% from a record high. Rival Unimicron Technology , the index’s second-best performer, fell 14% in a week, while Samsung Electro- Mechanics , which makes an array of electronic components, plunged 23%. “Financing costs are like gravity for the AI boom,” said Jian Shi Cortesi, a fund manager at GAM Investment Management in Zurich. “Rising borrowing costs could make infrastructure projects harder to finance and delay spending. Even a delay could trigger a reset in Asian suppliers’ earnings expectations and valuations.” The concern is no longer just whether demand for AI chips will hold up. It is whether hyperscalers and neocloud operators can keep financing the infrastructure needed to deploy them – and whether the expected returns will justify the scale of investment. Bonds of neocloud provider CoreWeave sank to levels signalling distress last week as investors questioned whether AI demand and revenue could support the borrowing behind its expansion. Its shares slumped 12% on Oct 16 , resulting in the stock’s worst week since November, with a 25% drop. The episode brought the financing risks of the boom into sharper focus, with surging oil prices adding to worries that inflation could keep borrowing costs elevated. While TSMC, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics supply the chips and memory needed for AI computing, their earnings ultimately depend on continued investment in the infrastructure that uses those products. Component makers and equipment suppliers face the same underlying risk, potentially with less visibility into the timing of individual projects. “AI funding stress is a bigger challenge for downstream beneficiaries than for the core compute ecosystem,” said Kevin Net, portfolio manager at Financiere de l’Echiquier in Paris. “Basically, the further away you get from the actual chip, the greater the risk you might see timing delays.” Warnings about funding risks have come from industry executives, including Broadcom c hief executive Hock Tan, who said that capital, rather than shortages of memory chips or manufacturing capacity, would become the biggest constraint on AI growth. Gartner has warned that more than US$3.5 trillion (S$4.48 trillion) of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as investment threatens to outpace the revenue needed to justify it. “If hyperscalers and neoclouds cannot fund their data centre investments, that would translate into lower orders for Asia enablers like TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix,” said Vey-Sern Ling, managing director at Union Bancaire Privee. “Given how jittery the market is, the read-through would be very negative for the semi picks and shovels.” The stakes are particularly high for Asian equities, where the AI buildout has become a dominant investment theme.

events.title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control?
events.summary: Published 18 October 2026, 01:11 BST "Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than £20m on new players. The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of £8.5m. That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when £100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business. All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than £300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time. It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate. But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis. This year's Champions League final - won by Paris Saint-Germain - sparked an argument about TV viewing rights And this summer saw signs of a clampdown. In August, a man in Lancashire was jailed for six and a half years for running an illegal streaming service that police said had generated almost £1m in illicit profits. In June, a postman from Pembrokeshire was jailed for over three years for selling illegal subscriptions and supplying pirate software to nearly 2,000 people. A third man, from Merseyside, received a suspended 32-month sentence in August for similar offences. Several pubs have been fined thousands of pounds for screening matches illegally. TV companies that have paid huge sums for exclusive rights to high-profile sports are having to work harder than ever to protect their investments. To some extent, broadcasters used to see copyright theft as a cost of doing business: irritating and expensive, but not an existential threat. But now, as advertising revenues fall, and viewers move away from long-term subscription services like Sky or TNT Sports, the industry is getting seriously worried. There is a great deal at stake. The Premier League alone is a sporting monster. In its most recent deal, it sold its viewing rights to domestic audiences for £6.7bn over four years, with almost as much coming from foreign rights. Armed with bundles of TV cash, clubs have been able to attract the finest players in the world. That in turn has given the league a major international profile. Although football has been the main beneficiary of paid-for TV in the UK, other competitions such as Formula One, Six Nations rugby and the Wimbledon tennis championships have also commanded very high fees for selling exclusive rights. Live sport on free-to-air television has become increasingly rare. Yet that wealth could be threatened by a surge in piracy and illegal viewing. The practice is most common among younger, digital-native audiences, who each year become a larger and larger share of sports fans. But many older viewers also seem comfortable with it. Rupert Murdoch (left) launched Sky TV with the broadcaster Andrew Neil in 1989. It went on to transform Britain's sports-watching landscape "For 18 to 34-year-olds, it's over 70% who admit to doing this regularly," says Daniel Monaghan, a researcher at Ampere Analysis. "Over half of 35 to 44s admit to doing it, and about a third of those aged 45 to 64." This year's Champions League final went behind a paywall in the UK for the first time in more than 30 years. Viewers were asked to pay at least £4.99 to watch it, prompting a backlash, including from the then-prime minister, Arsenal fan Sir Keir Starmer. "Hardworking people shouldn't have to fork out for a subscription to watch this match," he wrote on X. Many simply refused to pay: 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match in the UK, according to research carried out by the Gaming Compliance International consultancy, on behalf of the Guardian newspaper. That compared to around seven million people who watched it legally in the UK. One prolific user of pirate streams is "Kiran", a tech sector worker in his 30s, who prefers not to give his real name. A keen Arsenal fan, he likes to watch Premier League and Champions League games, as well as big matches in Spain's La Liga. He has a paid subscription to TNT Sports, but uses streaming websites to see games that are not available there. Many fans watched this year's Champions League final legally at pubs - but at home, 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match, according to one analysis "What it comes down to is the financial side - that's the big one - and ease of access as well," he says.

events.title: Gas company called 'rude' for not sharing decommissioning news earlier
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Secret meetings over Albany gas network held months before decommissioning announced Canadian firm ATCO owns assets around Australia but it no longer wants Albany's gas network. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) Redacted emails show ATCO Australia and the WA state government discussed the future of the Albany gas network months before customers were told it would be scrapped. ATCO will transition customers off the network over the next three years, forcing customers onto alternative energy sources. The government has ruled out taking over the network. When Hayden Jones and his wife bought an Albany laundromat three and a half years ago, it seemed a sensible investment decision. The City of Albany, 400km south of Perth, is one of Western Australia's largest regional cities, fuelled by relatively cheap and available liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Hayden Jones wants the Albany LPG network retained. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) But news earlier this year that Albany will lose its reticulated LPG gas network has put the Jones's business in jeopardy. In January, energy provider ATCO Australia announced it would decommission the Albany network over the next three years, citing aging infrastructure and high maintenance costs. Redacted emails between ATCO and the state government. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) However, emails obtained by the ABC under Freedom of Information show the Canadian-owned company and the state government had been discussing the network's future eight months before affected customers were informed. The redacted emails include a confidential briefing note sent to the Department of Energy and Economic Diversification (DEED) on May 28, 2025, under the subject line "In Strictest Confidence: Albany Gas network". They also show a meeting was held between the utility and Energy Minister Amber Jade Sanderson a week later to discuss the network's future. Amber Jade Sanderson said the government tried to persuade ATCO to remain in Albany. ( ABC News: Armin Azad ) Ms Sanderson said she did not receive a copy of the briefing note, but confirmed she attended the meeting. "ATCO put the view that the network was no longer commercially viable … and that they were considering making that commercial decision to walk away. "I put the government's view that we would prefer they did not walk away." Greg Stocks said ATCO should have told the city of its plans sooner. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) News of the 2025 meeting was criticised by City of Albany Mayor Greg Stocks, who said residents had been blindsided by the abrupt announcement, and should have been told earlier to assist the city in retaining the network. "I think it was particularly rude that ATCO had not informed us and all businesses that they were connecting," he said. In a statement, ATCO said any change to its licence conditions required approval by the WA's Economic Regulation Authority, prompting its meeting with the state government. "When ATCO began considering the future of Albany gas network, it was therefore appropriate to consult first with the state government," a spokesperson said. Hayden Jones's business relies heavily on LPG gas. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) But business owners, including Jones, say the consultation did not go far enough , and want to see an alternative put on the table. In August, a petition signed by more than 2,500 people was tabled in parliament calling for the state government to intercede. "Either a local supplier or the government take the network back, which is what the Albany community really wants," Mr Jones said. "They want the government to stand up, right the wrongs of the past, and take this network back into government hands." ATCO customers will have to transition to bottled gas or switch to electricity. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) Energy Minister Amber Jade Sanderson said the government was not considering that option . "I understand that Albany residents are frustrated and angry that ATCO has made the decision to walk away. I absolutely understand, and I share that frustration and anger," she said. "The reality is this gas network is at the end of its technical life and would need to be entirely rebuilt. "The least-cost result is to allow customers to transition either to bottled gas or to electrification.

events.title: Assistant treasurer knew about ATO's credit card ban plans months ago
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino concedes he knew of ATO's credit card ban plans in July Daniel Mulino says the ATO was told to negotiate with credit card companies. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) The assistant treasurer says the government knew in July the tax office was considering a credit card ban following the Reserve Bank's surcharge changes. Outrage about the change from the business community forced the prime minister to step in. The issue has exposed tensions between the prime minister and the treasurer. Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has conceded the government knew the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) was considering banning credit card payments in July, months before the decision was made public. The ATO's decision in late September to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1 sparked backlash from the business community. That outrage eventually forced an intervention from the prime minister and the treasurer to underwrite the costs and allow credit cards to be accepted by the tax office until mid-2027. Mr Mulino today said he and Treasurer Jim Chalmers were first made aware of the ATO's intentions months ago. "In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options and that at that point their preference was to not accept credit cards," Mr Mulino told ABC's Insiders. "The indication we gave to the ATO was that they should continue to engage with the credit card companies, and that there should be a transition period." The admission comes after the Australian Financial Review yesterday revealed the ATO had privately informed the government about its credit card ban and presented the government with options. The ATO's decision followed changes from the Reserve Bank of Australia to scrap card surcharges from October 1, which the bank has said was "in the public interest" and was costing consumers about $1.6 billion a year. Mr Mulino was asked why the government did not push for the ATO to continue accepting credit card payments from small businesses back in July. Small businesses were informed of the ATO's decision on September 30, a day before it was made public, and given a two-month grace period. "But the transition period, as it turned out, from stakeholder feedback, wasn't enough. And so that's where the government stepped in," Mr Mulino said. He was asked if he had any regrets about not stepping in earlier. "We've changed our position. So I've listened to stakeholder feedback, as has the PM and the treasurer," he said. "So, obviously we've changed tack and we've listened to feedback. And that's a sign of a government that is putting in place important big reforms." Earlier this month, Mr Chalmers said he was informed by the ATO ahead of their decision, but did not give a specific timeline. "The ATO made this decision late in September, not to accept credit card payments. Obviously, we were aware before then that they were grappling with this issue," he said. Mr Mulino denied the government had a "hands-off approach", saying they "didn't get into all of the details" but insisted that the ATO should continue to negotiate with credit card companies. Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson slammed the government, saying they "had three months to fix this" and "only stepped in when the backlash got too loud to ignore". Tim Wilson has criticised the government's approach. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) "At every point the Albanese government has failed to understand the implementation consequences of their higher taxes," he said. He questioned Mr Mulino's assertion that the ATO made the call as an independent agency, only for the government to then fund the transition period for credit card payments. "You can't claim it's somebody else's decision while you're the one paying for it," he said. Government backs down on ATO credit card ban The federal government will temporarily cover credit card surcharges after businesses warn that losing the payment option will put them under pressure. Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said it was concerning these discussions were happening in July when businesses were only informed the day before it became public. "Business wasn't made aware until just hours before the surcharge ban took effect in October," he said. "This looks like a completely deficient policymaking process that took small business for granted." The ATO initially defended its decision, saying it was not tenable for the agency to absorb the $200 million cost and that it would result in less revenue being collected and therefore less funding for government services.

events.title: Mark Carney makes closing argument to Alberta against path to independence from Canada: outsiders ‘are working to break us so they can own us. Never’
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path  toward independence  in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty. With U.S. President Donald Trump waging a  trade war  and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted. “Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up. “This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he said. Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier Friday, the Liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence. Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies. “I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta. Smith noted that Carney grew up in Alberta and remains an Edmonton Oilers fan. “He can’t be all bad, right?” she joked. Trump’s threats raise the stakes “Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us. Never. Never,” Carney warned Friday in Edmonton, repeating a warning he made a day earlier in Calgary. At  Thursday’s Calgary rally  and Friday’s Edmonton rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the United States. Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies. “Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said. But he also emphasized his deep ties to the province. “Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said. Some Albertans say the vote shouldn’t have been called Outside the Edmonton rally venue Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading “Say no to Carney’s new world order.” Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22% of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high. Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism. But some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote. “I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada. Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline. Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions. Political leaders unite against separation Carney’s chief political rival, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, also urged Albertans Friday to remain in Canada. “Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said. Despite their agreement on keeping Alberta in Canada, Carney and Smith remain divided over nine other questions on Monday’s ballot involving immigration and provincial powers. Smith wants voters to approve them, while Carney has urged their rejection. “For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said. events.title: ‘France, truly, is on the brink’ and just days away from a make-or-break moment in its debt crisis, analyst warns, as protests turn into riots
events.summary: Nationwide protests over the high cost of living roiled France on Saturday, adding to turmoil over public spending and debt ahead of a critical vote in the National Assembly. Rioting broke out in some cities as luxury boutiques and supermarkets were looted while public buildings were defaced and even set on fire. That followed mass demonstrations earlier this month, with students decrying run-down classrooms, missing teachers, and buildings that aren’t equipped for rising temperatures. Protestors blamed years of underinvestment in public education. At the same time, France’s looming debt has sent bond yields to the highest levels in 24 years, flashing warning signs not seen since the eurozone debt crisis in 2011. With far-right and far-left candidates in the lead to become France’s next president in the spring, markets are losing confidence that either side will take the painful steps necessary to rein in the deficit. For Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, France is suffering from a crisis of liberal democracy, a crisis of fiscal mismanagement, and a crisis of youth disaffection. “But the fiscal crisis is the most dangerous, underlying many of the country’s woes and threatening to bring it to ruin,” he wrote in a New York Times op-ed on Thursday. “France, truly, is on the brink.” The crises are also related to each other. For instance, Rahman pointed out that while France’s education spending tops the European Union average, more than a quarter of the money pays for pensions of retired teachers. Nobel laureate Paul Krugman similarly drew a straight line from France’s retirement largesse to the student unrest. Due to its very generous government pension plan, education spending has suffered, meaning France is effectively subsidizing older French at the expense of everyone else, he wrote in a  Substack post last week. France’s public debt is now a record $4 trillion, or 119% of GDP—the highest ratio since the immediate aftermath of World War II. While the pandemic as well as the Ukraine and Iran wars worsened France’s fiscal picture, President Emmanuel Macron has also pulled back from reforms meant to rein in the debt. Sébastien Lecornu, the latest in a revolving door of prime ministers, has proposed a 2027 budget that would modestly bring the deficit down to 5% of GDP from 5.4%, and faces a first critical vote in the National Assembly on Tuesday.  “If his government fails to pass the budget, the cost of servicing French debt may explode,” Rahman predicted. “France could be forced to seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund and to pray for it from the European Central Bank — a humiliation for the world’s seventh-biggest economy.” The market’s distrust of France is more political than economic, fearing it has become ungovernable with the extreme left and right unlikely to make necessary changes, he added. Indeed, far-right leader Marine Le Pen has vowed to roll back the official retirement age to 62 and even previously suggested dropping it to as low as 60. Meanwhile, far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is campaigning on a plan to have the central bank simply  cancel its holdings of French debt . Such positions help explain why bond investors have sent France’s borrowing costs to sky-high levels, Rahman said. “The country, they fear, is becoming socially volatile and institutionally paralyzed.” In fact, the presidential election in May will not even be that decisive for financial markets, as a legislative election in June might fail to produce a parliamentary majority for the new president, setting up further political gridlock, he said.  France could avoid imminent catastrophe this coming week if Le Pen orders her allies in the Assembly to abstain on the budget, allowing it to pass. “That may avert, for now, the kind of meltdown suffered by Greece after the financial crash. But France is no longer in control of its destiny,” Rahman warned. An explosion in borrowing costs would signal that France is at the mercy of the bond market, which has started pricing in growing odds of a debt default . That’s similar to how the United Kingdom is effectively in thrall to so-called bond vigilantes . Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group, argued in a note Tuesday that a series of convulsions would have to occur for France to get its act together and appease the bond market. That could include a no-confidence vote that leaves France with no governance from the Assembly, a Moody’s credit downgrade, a widening of street protests and violence, a sharper and contagious spike in France’s bond yield spread, and the election of Le Pen as president. The European Central Bank also wouldn’t come to the rescue quickly for fear of encouraging “moral hazard,” and other bailout mechanisms lack the firepower for an economy as large as France’s, Wizman argued. “Either way, it would seem that one would have to go through the valley before getting to the other side of the fiscal responsibility gap,” he added. “And only  after  all that transformational pain of the next few months may France find its spine and commit to austerity.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
