events.title: Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system still restricted in Ukraine
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine's use of the Elon Musk -owned SpaceX satellite system remains partially restricted, despite earlier signs this week that it had been fully restored. Why it matters: The current restrictions limit the Ukrainian military from using drones to intercept Russian attack drones and from using its drones to send supplies to soldiers on the front lines, Zelensky said. The intrigue: Ukrainian officials say they are still scrambling to determine whether the restrictions result from a political decision by the Trump administration or Musk. Ukrainian officials have heard different versions of what happened, with the Trump administration and SpaceX executives accusing each other. "SpaceX as a company tells us it is a technical problem. But our contacts in the company say it is coming from the White House. When we ask the White House, they say it is Elon," a Ukrainian official told Axios. Musk said in a Wednesday X post that the U.S. government was involved in disrupting Starshield. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. President Trump said on Friday that the White House was not involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the system. Behind the scenes: The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk proposed to Trump throttling the Starlink and Starshield satellite networks used by the Ukrainian military. A source familiar with the discussion told Axios that Trump didn't push back on Elon's idea. A White House official denied the Telegraph's account. "This is totally false. As President Trump said, we didn't slow down Starlink at all, and the service is currently operational," the official said. State of play: But the service is not fully operational. Before the restrictions, the Starlink and Starshield network operated even on drones that reached 400 kilometers per hour. Now it is restricted to 161 kilometers per hour, Ukrainian officials say. Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that the Ukrainian military tested the system on Friday in cars in European Union countries. The cars drove 180 kilometers per hour, and the satellite systems continued working. But once the cars crossed into Ukraine, the system disconnected at 161 kilometers per hour. "The conclusion is that the restrictions apply inside Ukraine but do not apply in European Union countries. In other words, this is a planned operation," Zelensky said. Zelensky also expressed skepticism about SpaceX's claim that the speed limit results from technical problems. Catch up quick: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems: One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Ukraine said both systems were restricted. What to watch: On Friday, Ukraine's chief negotiator, Rustem Umerov, spoke with Trump's adviser and envoy, Jared Kushner, to discuss the Starlink issue, Zelensky said. They also spoke about holding a meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian teams next week to continue the discussions on the latest Trump administration proposal for a deal with Russia on ending the war.

events.title: ‘I can do stuff that is unbelievable.’ Trump boasts about his self-proclaimed power and tells voters DOD will revive a Kentucky drug plant if GOP wins
events.summary: President Donald Trump touted  his power in his second go around  in the White House Saturday while rallying in Kentucky to bolster Republican turnout as his party struggles in the midterms, saying, “I can do stuff that is unbelievable.” Trump, who spoke in the city of Highland Heights to boost Republican candidates including Ed Gallrein for the U.S. House, was riffing on his decision to change how the U.S. government refers to the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. “I don’t think I could have done this in my first term. This is a much more powerful term,” Trump said. “Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first. Now, they kiss my ass.” “Well, I also changed the name of a lake in Canada to the Lake America,” he continued, referring to Lake Ontario. Trump’s self-proclaimed power is set against voter  frustration with how he’s wielded it , with tariffs and the Iran war driving up prices and more Americans seeing the president  looking out for his own interests  and not those of the country. With control of both chambers of Congress on the line, and with it the prospects of Democratic-led investigations of his administration should they win, Trump has put himself at the fore for voters, asking them to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” But Republicans privately worry that growing disapproval of his administration is a liability. Trump nominated one of his personal lawyers to serve as attorney general, ordered  military strikes  on accused drug smuggling boats, is trying to put his name on the Kennedy Center, and has  enriched himself and his family while he’s been in office. While meandering through topics onstage in Kentucky, Trump touched on gas prices, saying that the war with Iran was going to end soon — an assertion he’s made many times over the course of the nearly eight-month conflict — and that gas prices will drop to lower than previously. The crowd cheered. Facing the electoral headwinds, Trump is working to paint a portentous picture of Democrats in the final weeks before the midterms. That includes the claim that if his opposing party wins, the U.S. will “have a depression,” and that the Democratic platform includes abolishing the U.S. Senate and U.S. Supreme Court. Those are not on the Democratic Party’s platform. But Trump is trying to lump them in with the Democratic Socialists of America, which have had a few candidates win in this year’s primary elections. Trump also rehashed his  dubious promise  that if Republicans win the House and the Senate then every adult American would get $5,000. That would most likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, while exacerbating the country’s nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit. Trump added a new, seemingly conditional promise for Kentucky. That if Republicans win, he said, the Department of Defense would invest in revitalizing a drug manufacturing facility in the state. The president pulled Gallrein on stage, the Republican candidate for the U.S. House district who beat Rep. Thomas Massie in the GOP primary. Massie had aggravated Trump by pushing for the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and opposing the Iran war, and the president responded by successfully backing Gallrein in the party’s primary. Massie, however, still has a following for standing on his staunchly conservative principles, even when it meant voting against his own party. When Trump lashed out at Massie as a “jerk” and “loser” and trumpeted Gallrein as a more loyal replacement, the crowd’s response was tepid, with about half the arena clapping at Trump’s barbs and other half silent. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Like facial recognition for lobsters, AI technology tracing from pot to plate Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Scientists have developed artificial intelligence technology capable of recognising individual lobsters. The innovation allows traceability from pot to plate and has the potential to strengthen consumer trust — and even break into new markets. The scientists want to further develop the technology for both the processing sector and the fishery. After nearly three weeks at sea, Joe Sayers docks a boat filled to the brim with treasure — it's red, thorny and alive. "There is one in here, I know there's 220 millimetres just in the carapace … there's a couple of fish in here that are probably going to be three, four kilos, I'd say, somewhere there," he said. Tasmania's southern rock lobster industry is bouncing back after some unsteady years. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Every year, Tasmania's commercial fishers catch just over 1,000 tonnes of southern rock lobster, valued at about $90 million. While things are now on the up, it's been a tough few years for the industry, brought on by trade restrictions and a domestic market flooded with cheap lobsters. Fisher Joe Sayers says the overheads of lobster fishing are only growing. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) "Now we're up to getting a few dollars in the bank from better prices, but our costs are going up … all the time, like fuel and baits," Mr Sayers said. But for Mr Sayers, it's a way of life, and after more than 30 years at sea, he wants to hand over an industry in good shape to the next generation. Southern rock lobsters are caught measured, photographed and recorded as part of a new Lobster AI program, 01 September 2026 ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Scientists from the University of Tasmania's Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS), in partnership with Fiordland Lobster Company and the South Australian Lobster Company, are trying to ensure just that, through newly developed artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Scientists Dean Giosio and Quinn Fitzgibbon photograph a lobster to see if it's in the database. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) "It's just like a fingerprint or facial recognition technology," associate professor at IMAS Quinn Fitzgibbon said. "We've used AI machine learning to look at the features on the shell of the lobster, and amazingly, we've been able to show that this technology can pick up those features and they're individual. The AI technology has been developed by Dean Giosio, Quinn Fitzgibbon and Tara Kelly from the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. ( Supplied: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies ) It's as simple as a quick snap on an smartphone. If the lobster has been photographed before, the AI recognises it, and if it hasn't, into the database it goes, joining thousands of others from across Australia and New Zealand. This lobster has been scanned before. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) The team has tested the AI under various scenarios, finding it recognises a lobster three years on, dressed up in barnacles and algae, or with a fresh exoskeleton. In time, the idea is consumers themselves will be able to photograph their dinner and know exactly where it came from. Southern rock lobsters are caught, measured, photographed and recorded. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Tackling distrust around product misplacement The technology could be transformative for exporters like Michael Blake, who processes up to 300,000 lobsters per year at his Bicheno facility. "It's the most premium-priced lobster in the world," he said. Exporter Michael Blake hopes the technology will help Tasmanian southern rock lobster reach new markets. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Scientists physically tag lobsters during population surveys, but that's not viable for the industry because tags can be removed or forged. That means once fish leave the state, there's no way of proving where they came from, and money to be made from branding a foreign lobster as prized southern rock lobster. Once lobsters are exported, they can end up in tanks with lobsters from Australia and other parts of the world. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) "The lobsters are taken out of the boxes and placed in tanks with other lobsters from other countries, as well as from Australia," Mr Blake said. He is hopeful AI could help break into new markets, like the European Union, and strengthen trust in existing ones. "Giving some of those restaurateurs overseas the confidence that this is guaranteed to come from here, will put the lobster on plates that it's currently not on," Mr Blake said.

events.title: From the navy to bullion trading: Start-up founder builds wealth through precious metals, discipline
events.summary: Ian Chan invested a significant portion of his personal savings and profits from previous investments to start precious metals trading company Big Bullion in December 2025, along with financial support from his family. SINGAPORE – Former naval officer Ian Chan enjoyed his time at sea, although he sometimes struggled with seasickness. “I eventually decided not to continue along that path, which was a difficult decision because serving the nation was something I genuinely wanted to do,” he said. The 25-year-old subsequently invested a significant portion of his personal savings and profits from previous investments to start precious metals trading company Big Bullion in December 2025, along with financial support from his family. The company has generated about $1.5 million in revenue thus far, comprising $1.2 million from investment-grade gold and silver bullion and the remainder from buying back precious metals jewellery for refining. Big Bullion is expected to become profitable by December 2026. However, getting the business off the ground came with its own challenges, from establishing relationships with reliable suppliers, to sourcing gold and silver inventory, to developing hedging strategies to manage fluctuations in bullion prices. “The experience has taught me the importance of managing business finances carefully, particularly cash flow and working capital,” said Chan. The final-year student at NUS Business School added that he hopes to make investing in precious metals more accessible to younger Singaporeans through social media and educational content that explains how gold and silver pricing, premiums and buyback values work. “Ultimately, our goal is not just to sell precious metals, but also to help customers better understand what they are buying, how pricing works and how physical gold and silver may fit into their broader financial plans,” he said. Chan is engaged to his 25-year-old fiancee, who also helps him with his business. Q: Do you invest? If so, what do you invest in and why? Apart from precious metals, I also invest in a broad range of stocks, including exposure to the US market through indexes such as the S&P 500. Equities give me exposure to businesses around the world and the potential for long-term capital growth. I also believe liquidity is important. Cash gives me the flexibility to meet short-term needs, manage unexpected expenses and take advantage of opportunities without having to sell investments at an unfavourable time. Q: What is your biggest or most valuable asset right now? My business is one of my most valuable assets, alongside my gold and silver holdings. Building a business has also taught me that an asset’s value is not always immediately reflected in a bank balance. It can lie in the relationships, systems, knowledge and opportunities built over time. Q: What is your approach to growing your money? I believe younger investors with longer time horizons can generally consider taking more investment risk, provided they understand what they are investing in and can withstand potential losses. At the same time, taking risk does not mean concentrating everything in one asset. Diversification is important because different assets behave differently under different market conditions. Above all, I believe consistency matters. It is tempting to keep searching for the next big opportunity, but building wealth often comes down to investing regularly, controlling costs and allowing time for compounding to work. Q: What was your first exposure to investing, and what was your first investment? My first investment was at the end of national service, when I put about $200 into the S&P 500. It was a small amount, but it gave me a starting point. Q: What has been your biggest financial mistake? One area I could have managed better was my use of Singapore’s tax-advantaged savings schemes, particularly the Central Provident Fund and Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS), where additional contributions may have been appropriate for my circumstances. The right CPF or SRS contribution depends on factors such as eligibility, tax bracket, liquidity needs and long-term plans, so it is not simply a matter of contributing as much as possible. Q: What has been your best financial decision? One of my best financial decisions has been consistently spending below my means and investing at least 20% of my income, even when it was tempting to spend more or pause investing. I have dollar-cost averaged into investments over approximately seven years, including diversified US equities and precious metals. This has helped me develop discipline rather than trying to predict the perfect time to enter the market. I have also been grateful that I learnt the importance of insurance planning early. Arranging appropriate coverage while younger helped me secure protection before potentially facing higher premiums or changes in insurability later on. Q: Moneywise, what were your growing-up years like?

events.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday. Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates. Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%. Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.” One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.” In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized. Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining. The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Trump's Russia waiver draws instant bipartisan backlash
events.summary: Top Republicans and Democrats alike lined up Saturday to condemn President Trump 's decision to waive recent sanctions on Russia , calling it "irresponsible" and "a deal with the devil." Why it matters : Trump already faces a bipartisan effort to overturn his Russian diesel deal when Congress returns after the election. Now he may have to deal with even broader outrage over sanctions Congress approved just a month ago. Driving the news: Late Friday night, Trump issued an executive order waiving implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which he signed in September. The act would have imposed broad sanctions not only on Russia, but on other countries buying its oil. What they're saying: Democrats forcefully criticized Trump's decision. "By giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote . "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X. "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X. Republicans were equally unsparing. "We should be increasing economic pressure on Russia, not easing up. We need to use every tool at our disposal, including fully implementing the Graham sanctions and my REPO Act, to squeeze Putin until he ends his illegal and barbaric war in Ukraine," Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.) wrote . "I have requested a classified briefing on the rationale for this decision." "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day." Sen. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) posted simply: "Lindsey would be appalled." One soon-to-depart congressman , Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), hinted at the trouble Trump may face when Congress returns. "Congress has a lame-duck session. The President has an agenda: supplemental, reconciliation, Ballroom, etc… I think the agenda is dead. Many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus," Bacon wrote . For the record: The White House defended Trump's decision. "President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests." What to watch: The question now is just how hard Congress will push back when it returns in a few weeks.

events.title: Hiding in plane sight: the invisible turbulence that can strike out of a clear blue sky
events.summary: As the planet warms, airlines are grappling with what this means for air travel – and for the passengers who simply refuse to keep their seatbelts fastened It was a swelteringly hot afternoon in south-west Myanmar on 21 May 2024. Tropical thunderstorms, showers and highs of 36C were forecast for the area around the Irrawaddy Basin. High above, monsoonal heat and humidity were building into a vast convective column of water vapour, a towering cumulonimbus cloud soaring up to 35,000ft (more than 10,500 metres) into the air. From the ground, it would have looked like something from a children’s picture book – a soft, fluffy white mass. But for Singapore Airlines flight SQ321 passing just above, it was anything but benign. In the cabin of the Boeing 777, passengers were being woken up for breakfast with three hours to go on the journey from London to Singapore. For the 210 travellers on board, the past 10 hours had been uneventful. The seatbelt signs were off. Some were milling around, others were using the toilets, and cabin staff were preparing trolleys for service. At 2.19pm and 23 seconds local time, moderate turbulence shook the plane for 17 seconds and the seatbelt sign was switched on. Then, as one passenger described it, it was “like a grenade had gone off”. In just 4.6 seconds, any passenger not strapped in hit the roof with 1.5 times the force of gravity and was thrown back on the floor in an instant. Passengers reported hearing people screaming in agony, blood streaming down faces, with overhead panels broken by the force of bodies hitting them. One person was left dead and 79 were seriously injured. The turbulence had lasted just over 21 seconds. While SQ321 was an extreme case that made global headlines , turbulence is the leading cause of injuries to passengers and crew in non-fatal accidents, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA). Figures from the Federal Aviation Administration record about a dozen serious injuries a year from turbulence across the US alone. It can be caused by a multitude of factors, including geographic features such as mountains – the top 10 most turbulent routes are all over either the Andes or the Himalayas. Some forms, such as the type caused by mountains and wake turbulence, which is caused by other aircraft, are fairly well understood and avoided. Pilots have always had to contend with the sky’s speed bumps as part of the job. But the threat of turbulence across the world is increasing due to the climate crisis. Not only will pilots need to contend with the frequency and severity of these episodes rising, they’re facing a future that includes a large surge in clear-air turbulence – an invisible, largely undetectable turbulence that comes, quite literally, out of the blue. Richard Woodward is a former Royal Australian Air Force test pilot and Qantas A380 captain who served the airline for 32 years. He has flown routes all around the world and has seen more than his fair share of difficult conditions, including flying over a cyclone (it was surprisingly smooth and the radar “painted it beautifully”). But Woodward says airlines and the aviation industry are increasingly aware of the threat posed by global heating. “There’ll be an increase in the severity of thunderstorms and storms in general because, as the planet warms, the amount of energy inputting into these events will become massively greater,” he says. Thunderstorm or convective turbulence – the cause of the SQ321 incident – creates strong updrafts, then strong downdrafts as the air and water vapour cool. It may be encountered several thousand feet above clouds and as far as 20 miles (more than 30km) on either side. This can be particularly dangerous, Woodward says, given that “there’s more energy in a typical thunderstorm than there is in a nuclear weapon”. That massive amount of energy can be seen in lightning – which sometimes even reaches into space, Woodward says – but it also manifests in turbulence. More heat, and greater differences between hot and cold areas, will supercharge already powerful thunderstorms. It’s a problem that pilots and passengers have encountered in Australia. In the same month as the SQ321 episode, a Qantas Boeing 737 encountered severe turbulence while on approach to Brisbane airport after entering a storm cloud at 11,400ft. Three cabin crew, who were not seated at the time, were injured; one was left with a broken ankle. Another crew member with an undiagnosed concussion returned to work on several subsequent flights without medical attention. The Australian Transport Safety Board report was highly critical of the airline’s response, saying the crew member “returning to work with an undiagnosed concussion likely compromised [their] ability to perform safety-critical tasks”. Qantas has since overhauled its safety protocols for crew injuries.

events.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. Its title has been updated, as well. events.title: The tactics used by companies to push pregnant women out of work
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts How pregnancy discrimination is pushing Australian women out of the workforce When Abby McCawley found out she was having a girl, she sent a message to her coworkers to share the exciting news. "Everyone around me was so happy, including the people I worked for and the people I worked with," she said. Abby was five months into her role as a rental property manager at Ray White Brunswick in Melbourne's inner north. After taking two days off work to manage morning sickness, Abby returned to her desk in the office and discovered something odd. She couldn't log onto her computer. Moments later, Abby's boss called her into his office and terminated her employment. Abby McCawley believes she experienced pregnancy discrimination. ( Four Corners: Ron Foley ) "I was shocked, I was upset … I thought about the baby. "I just thought, 'I haven't done anything wrong, why am I being let go?'" Abby said she had never received warnings she wasn't performing. More than 100 women have told Four Corners they lost work after becoming pregnant or having a child. Some were employed at Australia's biggest companies, and nearly a quarter worked in the public sector. Together, the cases reveal the problem is far bigger than a few bad bosses. After analysing dozens of cases, Four Corners has established a collection of tactics used to push mothers out of the workforce, revealing an unwritten playbook used by employers. Fired after being publicly praised by the company on social media In the weeks before Abby was let go, she had no idea her job was at risk. Then, in her first trimester, she asked to work remotely for a few hours to manage morning sickness. Her request was denied by the office manager. Instead, Abby was told a new policy required employees to give a day's notice to work from home. "It [was] quite disappointing, because it's obviously not something that you can predict," she said. Still, Abby felt secure in her job and wasn't worried. A week before Ray White Brunswick terminated Abby's employment, the real estate agency publicly praised her on Instagram. Ray White Brunswick endorsed Abby McCawley on its Instagram page. When she was fired, Abby said she was told it was partly due to a company restructure. She took her employer to the Fair Work Commission seeking compensation, but mediation failed, so she is now suing Ray White Brunswick in the Federal Court. Her lawyer, Laura Blandthorn from Solidarity Solicitors, alleged Abby had experienced "very clear, direct discrimination based on her pregnancy". She said Abby was initially told her employment was terminated due to an "office restructure", then was later advised it was due to "performance reasons". Laura Blandthorn represents Abby McCawley. ( Four Corners: Ron Foley ) Ray White Brunswick's director Jamil Allouche declined an interview with Four Corners. In a statement, he said: "Abby's employment was terminated for the reasons that we discussed with her at the time her employment ended. "Those reasons related to her behaviour in the workplace, reported to me by other employees and observed by me as the decision-maker. "As the matter is currently before the court, I am not able to comment further, and I will allow the process to take its course." Mr Allouche did not respond to further questions about what that behaviour was. Lawyer Susan Price, from the Working Women's Centre NSW, has represented women facing pregnancy discrimination for decades and said in other cases, criticism of a new or expectant mother's performance in the workplace was common. Susan Price says some mothers are still treated differently at work in Australia. ( Four Corners: Ron Foley ) "You do see what I describe as a real shift in attitude towards a worker once they've come into the workplace and announced they're pregnant," she said. "It's almost like that worker has now been identified as a problem and things that were absolutely fine before, start to get criticised, their performance gets managed." Twenty-one women told Four Corners they had been let go after becoming pregnant, only to find someone else had taken their job, and in some cases under a different title. It's a practice lawyers call a "sham restructure". Zana Bytheway, executive director of employment rights legal centre JobWatch said it could sometimes happen to women on maternity leave. "They may find their job has been made redundant, but it's often a construct," she said. "Often they found that their actual position … is still there.

events.title: Trump waives new Russia sanctions in the "national interests"
events.summary: President Trump waived new sanctions on Russia late Friday night, saying it was in the "national interests" to hold off on the sweeping levies under the Graham Act that he signed just last month. Why it matters : Trump is easing American pressure on Russia despite a bipartisan chorus calling for him to do the exact opposite. It comes a week after his surprise deal to let Russia sell diesel internationally, which Republicans have condemned as loudly as Democrats. It also puts Republican candidates making their final midterm sprint in the position of having to defend the president's warmer relationship with a country voters overwhelmingly see as an American enemy . The latest: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky lamented Trump's decision in a post to X Saturday morning. "This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters," he wrote, amid fresh Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Driving the news: The White House released the text of an executive order late Friday night detailing the implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The bill, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), imposed broad new sanctions on Russia and countries that do business with it, including buyers of its oil. The order notes that the law allows the president to "waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person, any restriction with respect to a person, and any duty." "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order. What they're saying: Republicans and Democrats alike blasted the waiver. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X. "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X. "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) posted on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day." Sen. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) posted simply: "Lindsey would be appalled." The big picture: The waiver caps a historic week in recent U.S.-Russia relations, where Trump abruptly eased pressure on multiple fronts. Whether it was the diesel deal, or a fight over Ukraine's ability to use Starlink to defend itself against Russian munitions, or a public denial of Russian involvement in the Iran war, Trump has spent the last few days shifting America's position on an old foe. By waiving the Graham Act's so-called secondary sanctions, Trump will also avoid putting fresh pressure on China and India, major buyers of Russian oil. The bottom line : The louder the bipartisan anti-Russia chorus gets, the more Trump doubles down on pulling back the pressure. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional reactions. Ben Geman contributed.

events.title: Investors are buying up vast tracts of timberland across U.S. in one of market's longest-term bets
events.summary: Institutions have been buying timberland at the rate of one million acres a year, according to Bank of America. But lumber prices have been on the decline and profiting from timber can take many years, current owners warn. It isn’t as passive of an investment as it seems, either: hunting, illegal logging, wildfires, pests, disease, and land values all need to be monitored. When the economy and the market look shaky, gold and government bonds are the traditional places to park money. Lately, some investors have also been looking at something more rooted: timber. The pitch is easy to like: a back-to-basics, natural asset that grows on its own, matures into a harvest and can be cashed in all while you use it to hunt, pitch a tent, or forage. Institutions have been buying timberland at a rate of one million acres per year, according to Bank of America, and some financial advisors say individual investors, including younger Americans priced out of the housing market, are also taking a look at the asset class. But it is far from a rush, and investors who already own timberland caution that it may not be very profitable in the short term. "Timber is a very low return investment. I have curtailed my investments," said Pat Dorn, founder of Anchor Investment Management, a fee-only advisory firm in Columbia, South Carolina, and a former chairman of the South Carolina Forestry Association. Dorn owns 2,500 acres of timberland in South Carolina's booming upstate region. Dorn said the problem is that right now more timber is being grown than is needed in a sluggish housing economy. "Supply beats demand, and that causes flat prices. Timber is not an investment I would make currently," Dorn said. Nationally, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' producer price index for logs, bolts, timber, pulpwood and wood chips ticked up in September, but prices have been mostly on the decline since summer 2022. This measures prices received by producers for those products, rather than timberland values or investment returns. Over the very long-term, prices have climbed substantially. Financial institutions point to the asset class as one of interest specifically for the long-term investor. Ken Shepard, head of specialty asset management at Bank of America Private Bank said that timberland is not a tactical asset class that can be easily entered or exited in response to short-term market conditions. "We view it as a strategic, long-term investment supported by several favorable secular trends, including the continued expansion of the timber industry in the U.S. South and growing demand for wood products beyond traditional construction uses," Shepard said. For example, he said, demand for wood pellets used in bioenergy, while controversial , has increased significantly. In addition, timberland values are benefiting from strong demand from recreational and lifestyle buyers , providing support for land prices beyond the income generated from timber harvesting. The National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries' Timberland Property Index, which tracks privately held U.S. timber properties owned at least partly on behalf of institutional investors, posted a total return of 0.95% in the second quarter of 2026, comprising 0.34% income and 0.61% appreciation. Timberland managers dominate acquisitions Bank of America's 2026 outlook reported that the one-million-acre annual pace of buying is a three-year streak of dealmaking it expects to continue. According to Bank of America, timber managers acquired 55% of all acres that changed hands in 2025 against just 15% sold. Institutions are playing the long game. Large timberland managers buy for pension funds and endowments that can wait decades, and that can make bets on a longer-term recovery in a currently slumping U.S. housing market that will be good for lumber pricing. But a private owner living through today's market sees things differently. Dorn pointed out that timber companies buy less mature trees for pulpwood, which goes into paper towels or notebook paper, and those trees can take 12-14 years to mature. The chip-and-saw variety of trees take a little bit longer, while the big prize, timber cut for houses, can take 25 years. "That is where the top value is," he said. According to Dorn, what landowners are paid for standing timber varies depending on what the trees are used for. Pine pulpwood consists of trees ground into paper and packaging, while pine sawtimber is made up of larger trees cut into lumber for homebuilding. Meanwhile, hardwood sawtimber, consists of oak and other big trees used in flooring, furniture and pallets. Each product feeds a different set of buyers, so one can climb while others fall. South Carolina Forestry Commission data show statewide average pine pulpwood stumpage prices, what buyers pay landowners for standing timber, fell from $5.67 a ton in the third quarter of 2025 to $3.79 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of about 33%.

events.title: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3 , the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip. Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades. The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click. Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate. It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app. That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach. If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings. The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.) The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149. The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green. Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2 , which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out. events.title: Software’s new consolidator gets big vote of confidence from Berkshire
events.summary: Italy's Bending Spoons has emerged as a major player in tech M&A, and is now moving aggressively to snap up out-of-favor software names. The holding company's stock price shot up this week after Berkshire Hathaway bolstered its investment, putting in more than $300 million. "This is what private equity firms were planning to do but they got their nose bloodied," said Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight. At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote. Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway . Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion. "Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement. The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio. For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the " SaaSpocalypse ." "You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore." Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus . Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo , AOL and Eventbrite in 2025. The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07. Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price. Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions. Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied." "They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020. Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years." As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar.

events.title: Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and scary – Chinese AI
events.summary: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge. Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence. In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by. The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They are cheaper than other EVs sold in the UK and, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries. Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level. It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again. Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last century in Tiananmen Square . A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule. Then came AI and the state discovered complete control. Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to. Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished. For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world. Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigorated belt and road initiative creates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology. Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions. Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights. Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents. There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need. Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, as many AI experts have documented . But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option. As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation. He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.

events.title: 'Dead money’ for a decade: Why this hedge fund approach may deliver an advantage over bonds
events.summary: Investors may want to rethink their bond allocation and opt for managed futures exposure. DBi's Andrew Beer suggests the popular hedge fund strategy could deliver a modern twist to traditional 60/40 portfolios . "[Bonds have] been dead money for the entire decade," the firm's co-founder and managing member told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "I fell in love with a strategy called managed futures because tactical is really good. Be nimble when other people's [portfolios] aren't." Beer contends the managed futures strategy, historically only available to hedge funds, could counterbalance stocks better than bonds during periods of volatility , which has been moving higher due to recent worries surrounding debt and the artificial intelligence trade . His reason: Managed futures exchange-traded funds can go long and short across global markets to position early against turbulent market events. "You want something that has low correlation to both stocks and bonds, and something that will do well in crises," Beer said. "It's very, very hard to find a better hedge fund strategy than managed futures to accomplish that." He helps manage the iMGP DBi Managed Futures Strategy ETF (DBMF) . The fund replicates the performance of leading managed futures hedge funds inside a low-cost, liquid ETF, according to the firm's website. "There's an existential crisis right now in strategic asset allocation and the model portfolio world," Beer said about the 60/40 approach. "I love my bonds … [but] I'm not making it a 40% allocation for something that is not adding to the rest of my portfolio." As of Thursday's close, Beer's ETF is up almost 19% so far this year, according to FactSet data. However, managed futures may not be a replacement for bonds . According to NovaDius Wealth Management's Nate Geraci, bonds still have a place for diversifying a portfolio. "I call fixed income the most challenging area in investing right now," the firm's president said in the same interview. "[Alternatives] fit in the sleeve of a well-diversified portfolio that includes stocks and bonds. But I don't think you just give up on the bond side of the equation." Geraci added that investors should understand how alternative investment strategies like managed futures ETFs could interact with the rest of a portfolio. These funds can outperform during volatile markets, but they may also have periods of underperformance. "You have to let that work out over the long-term," said Geraci, who is also an ETF Institute co-founder. "To me it's just a balance. It's all about diversification."

events.title: Low-cost clinic helps pet owners with vet bills
events.summary: Christine Gardner described support from the clinic as "amazing" A reduced-cost veterinary clinic has treated 160 pets in its first 11 days, according to the RSPCA. The animal charity's Medway West branch has launched to offer cut-price care for the pets of people on low incomes or receiving benefits. "Your pet would come first. You'd have a bit of toast yourself and pay out for your pet," said Chatham cat owner Christine Gardner. "Having somewhere like this is amazing." She told the BBC it was "just really good to have something nearby that I can get to" with her six cats. Angela Adams said her pets were her "babies", adding: "I would rather starve than they starve." She said she had eight cats, two rabbits, four guinea pigs, two African land snails and a tortoise, and that she did not know what she would do without the animals, as she was unable to work for health reasons. "It's very expensive. Seven of my cats were due for vaccine this month and you can imagine the cost of that," she told the BBC. "That's a lot of money." "I've had friends messaging me struggling, so this place is brilliant for people." The RSPCA's Imara Ó Niocail says some people can longer afford to care for their much-loved pets RSPCA branch account manager Imara Ó Niocail said that "a lot of people who were more than capable of affording to have these animals" were no longer able to care for them due to the cost of living or a change in circumstances. "We would like to keep the animals at home with the owners and treat them there," Ó Niocail told the BBC. The low cost clinic meant that pet owners in Medway could "seek the treatment that they need and then take the animals home", without having to pay the full vet costs , she added. Medway West branch manager Kevin Morton said the charity's centres were "full-to-bursting" with animals and some people "give their animals up because they can't afford to look after them". "Some people might think that if you can't afford to feed it, then don't have it, but if it's your only companion you have, they can keep people going," he said. The branch has supplied 18,909 food items, 1,294 treats and 919kg of biscuits so far in 2026 through its pet food bank. events.title: A welcome recovery milestone for Pope Leo after cancer surgery
events.summary: Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after having surgery to remove a cancerous nodule in his lungs. Why it matters: His discharge clears the way for his rigorous upcoming travel schedule and may alleviate fears of a leadership vacuum at the Vatican. What they're saying: " In light of the blood tests and chest X-ray performed this morning, and following an assessment of his clinical condition, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge ," The Holy See Press Office said in a Saturday statement attributed to Leo's doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora. Catch up quick: The Vatican announced Leo would be having surgery to remove a nodule from his lung on Oct. 11, and later said the surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung. The Vatican confirmed the surgery was successful on Tuesday, and later said that Leo was walking around, eating normally, and that his blood tests and chest X-rays were normal. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center, and if caught early, survival rates are very high. Zoom out: His hospitalization and subsequent cancer diagnosis struck fear into Catholics across the world, who offered him prayers and well-wishes as he recovered. For example, a group in Chicago, the first American Pontiff's hometown, created a care package for Leo featuring get-well cards and a Chicago White Sox blanket. The Vatican has not yet said if any additional treatment is needed. Go deeper: Chicago Catholics pray for Pope Leo XIV after lung cancer diagnosis

events.title: Trump's student loan overhaul could lead to more bankruptcy filings, former judge says
events.summary: After nearly three decades as a bankruptcy judge, Sarah Sharer Curley details what she calls the unfairness of the legal process in her new book, "The Price of Forgiveness: Debt, Bankruptcy, and the Future of Fairness in America." "We allow the financial markets to take innumerable risks, yet we refuse to allow an individual to be forgiven for choosing to pursue an advanced degree," Curley wrote. In 2025, more than half a million personal bankruptcy cases were filed — an almost 50% rise from three years prior, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. In Judge Sarah Sharer Curley's nearly three decades presiding over bankruptcy cases, some were especially painful to witness, she said — such as the 73-year-old woman who stood before her in 2012 with a student loan balance of more than $584,000. The debt dated back to the 1970s and had grown throughout the woman's public sector career, Curley writes in her new book, " The Price of Forgiveness: Debt, Bankruptcy, and the Future of Fairness in America ." She had "never made a lot of money," Curley said, and by the time she sought debt relief, the woman was living in poverty, with Social Security as her only income. Even so, strict bankruptcy laws can make it nearly impossible to discharge student loans . Curley, the first woman appointed to the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Arizona, said it was a familiar story. CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Thousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher payments Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 Curley retired in 2014. CNBC spoke with her this month about her new book, in which she describes a legal system that often fails to give indebted Americans the second chance it promises. In 2025, more than half a million personal bankruptcy cases were filed — an almost 50% rise from three years prior, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. 'People are subject to many unexpected events' Annie Nova: What do people get most wrong about those who file for bankruptcy? Sarah Sharer Curley: People assume that individuals who file for bankruptcy are committing fraud, trying to hide assets and cheating creditors. Nothing could be further from the truth. AN: And so why did people end up in your court? SSC: People are subject to many unexpected events. People can't always plan adequately for the next earthquake, hurricane or natural disaster. But usually, it's someone losing a job. It could also be an illness that becomes chronic with medical costs that increase dramatically over a short period. Student loans is another area of concern. Universities are charging more for basic degrees, as well as graduate programs. The cost of medical school over four years can be more than $400,000. AN: You write that many people who file for bankruptcy are not unemployed; they're just living paycheck to paycheck. What does this tell us about our economy and labor market? SSC: Despite the increase in wages that most economists tout, many people are working as independent contractors. They receive few benefits and have few rights. The company is not responsible to them. Other individuals may be working for a company but find the wages or benefits are insufficient. Many people are forced to work for several employers to meet their needs on a weekly basis. Although unemployment may be low, the quality of the employment is also low. AN: The story in your book about the woman in her 70s with the six-figure federal student loan balance really stood out to me. What happened in her case? SSC: The federal government would not agree to any settlement. I was the one who would have to decide whether her debt would be discharged or not. But the case law I had to follow was not in favor of discharging student loan debts. So, I didn't have a lot of flexibility in granting her relief. However, I gave her credit for seven years of public service helping out troubled teens in San Diego County, since people who are in certain types of public service only have a 10-year repayment period. That meant that she'd need to repay the debt for just three more years. AN: Wow. Why wouldn't the federal government agree to any settlement with her? SSC: The federal government retains law firms to represent it in bankruptcy court, allowing the law firms to have a certain amount of discretion as to how to proceed. As a result, some law firms are aggressive in the positions that they take. In the case of the woman in her 70s, the law firm attorneys didn't believe her when she said she had no assets and was on Social Security.

events.title: Move over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogroping
events.summary: Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women Y ou may be familiar with rule 34 of the internet, which states that if something exists or can be imagined, there will almost certainly be online porn of it. Now let me introduce my rule 35: whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women. See, for example, Meta’s “ pervert glasses ”. As anyone could have foreseen, putting a tiny camera and microphone into smartglasses would immediately lead to people using them to record and harass women. Lo and behold, that is exactly what happened. So-called manfluencers have filmed themselves trying to flirt with women in public spaces and then uploaded the footage to TikTok. The women in these videos are often not aware they’ve been recorded until their identities are shared online and they are harassed by strangers. And what’s Meta doing about this? It’s instituted a few bans and made some privacy updates, but doesn’t seem to have an appetite to properly solve the problem. Indeed, at the Meta Connect 2026 keynote, Mark Zuckerberg did not feel the need to apologize to the women whose lives have been upended by his technology. Then there is the Flock license plate tracking system, which has been abused by an extraordinary number of law enforcement officers to track the locations of their exes or other women they are sexually interested in. And, of course, there are the AI image generators, which have been used to create deepfake pornography of women and girls. According to a 2023 report , “deepfake pornography made up 98 per cent of all deepfake videos online, and 99 per cent depicted women”. Now, there’s a new toxic tech trend to worry about: livestreamed robogroping. Police in Cologne, Germany, are currently investigating an incident in which a humanoid robot controlled by two teenage males touched a 16-year-old girl’s buttocks and made sexually suggestive gestures toward her. Footage of the groping robot, which was wearing human clothes and a fake mustache, was reportedly livestreamed by the two males online. The robot in question has now been confiscated by the local police, who seem a little befuddled by the whole thing. “We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far,” a police spokesperson told the Associated Press, adding it was “new territory for us”. It may be new territory but I can guarantee you that this won’t be the last time we hear about an incident like this. Getting your hands on an AI-powered humanoid robot is still a lot more expensive than buying a pair of smartglasses, but the technology is rapidly becoming a lot more accessible. Earlier this year, a school in New York made headlines after announcing its new teaching assistant would be a humanoid robot called Sally, made by a company that makes realistic sex dolls. Outrage over the announcement forced the school district to halt its plans , but it’s only a matter of time before we see humanoid robots in schools. Indeed, in a report published last year, Bank of America predicted that, as costs go down, we will see mass adoption of humanoid robots from 2035 onwards. By 2060, they expect there to be 3bn humanoid robots, which will replace 20% of the workforce in the industrial sector and 50% of the workforce in the service sector. As the industry develops, expect corporations to ensure that their profit-maximizing robots have more legal protections than the humans they may harm. This week in Philadelphia, for example, a woman was arrested after allegedly blocking the path of one of the annoying Uber delivery robots that are now ubiquitous in the city. (The fact the police intervened is absolutely wild to me as a Philadelphia resident, considering they rarely seem interested in doing their jobs.) A growing body of case law has found that police officers are not under any legal obligation to protect citizens who are not in their custody. Yet they seem surprisingly keen on protecting robots. Our brave new world, everyone! I’m afraid pervert glasses are just a small glimpse of what’s to come. By 2060, robogroping may be as commonplace as catcalling is today. You can pay $7,500 to take dating lessons from a man accused of rape Braden Eric Peters, who goes by the nom-de-influencer Clavicular, shot to fame for smashing his face with a hammer in order to beautify himself. Bonesmashing, as it’s called, is part of a toxic trend called looksmaxxing , which involves people (largely young men) going to extremes to increase their “sexual market value”. When not bonesmashing, Peters gets into regular trouble with the law. Most lately, he was charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts last month; his attorneys have denied the allegations. Nevertheless, it seems that there are people out there willing to pay $7,500 for a week at Camp Looksmax, a new venture in which Peters coaches attendees on confidence and dating.
