events.title: Up in the air: Tesla's 'flying' Roadster raises more questions than answers
events.summary: Elon Musk 's Tesla Motors has flaunted a new flying car – well, sort of. Mr Musk touted it as “something that you haven’t seen in any movie” but it's not exactly Back to the Future stuff. However, the stunt seems to offer a glimpse of the future of transport. It's a great idea, but several points need clarity before road-and-air-legal cars become a reality. What happened Late on Thursday, Texas-based Tesla introduced the redesigned Roadster, the electric vehicle maker's original model. It was a long-awaited unveiling for the new version of the car after production ceased in 2012. The Roadster was “launched” off a curved ramp, flipped over in mid-air and landed with the help of built-in thrusters designed by Mr Musk's other major venture, SpaceX. The car was also made to fly and barrel-roll over a line of Tesla vehicles, including its electric cars, Semi Truck and Cybertruck, although it seemed to take off vertically as it neared the first vehicle rather than launching well before. The latest Roadster, which is set to go into production in 2028, is billed as going from zero to 100kph in a second – significantly faster than the first-generation model, which achieved that speed in under four seconds. What's inside At the event at SpaceX's hub in McGregor, Texas, Mr Musk said the new Roadster used an “advanced ultra-high pressure air tank”, with 10 nozzles that carry about 250kg of air, which can recharge by itself without the use of any propellant. Air tanks are critical in vehicle systems, as they are key components for brakes, suspension, tyres and thrusters. In the space race – one of Mr Musk's closely-watched endeavours – they are very high pressure to support propulsion. The Roadster's air tank will “literally puff itself up and be able to do these manoeuvres whenever you'd like”, Mr Musk said. However, the thruster-powered Roadsters will only come in limited-edition models and there will not be any street-legal versions. Legal questions That means not everyone can, at least not yet, “fly a car”, let alone perform barrel-rolls and kick-flips with the upcoming Roadster – especially as laws on the vehicle are both very tight and vague. In the mid-2010s, US regulations had stated that flying cars would need two licences – one for the road and one for the air. The very niche nature of flying cars – whose technologies are still very much in their infancy – makes it difficult to assess rules by region. Whoever drives the flying car is another issue. A notable example of this was the AirCar, which was granted an airworthiness certification by Slovakian authorities in 2022. Its maker, Klein Vision, subsequently said its operator would need a pilot's licence – not just a driver's licence – to operate it. Mr Musk acknowledged this, saying, “I'm not sure if it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.” However, he emphasises that with the new Roadster, “we can go further … this will be an actual car on the roads”. Insurance and air space Then there's the thought of having to load a car with compressed gas, which can cause explosions and raise alarm bells for owners and insurers. “[It's] a tremendous feat of engineering. It’s hard to argue otherwise,” said David Thomas, director of content marketing at US software developer CDK Global. “I’m not sure where you fill up a car with that. And it’s unlikely anyone will insure it either.” And after ensuring any flying car is safe and legal, commercialisation is also a big question, said George Agathangelou, general manager and executive director of Cyprus-based financial services firm Teroxx. “Would drivers need aviation certification or a pilot’s licence? What happens to liability, insurance and airspace restrictions,” he said. “Imagine explaining to your insurer that you didn’t rear-end another vehicle, you attempted to fly over it.” Yes, it's real Tesla isn't the first to unveil such a vehicle: in 2021, Britain's McMurtry introduced the Speirling, an electric hypercar using powerful fans to generate downforce. Tesla's approach is different as it combines suction with thrusters. Mr Musk made sure that there was an audience to witness the Roadster stunts in Texas and ensure people would not claim it was AI. Analysts at Chinese logistics company Raman Technology noted that it was “not antigravity magic, [as] it integrates aerospace technology inside an electric vehicle”.

events.title: Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But he says the gym he’s opening in December has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness. Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing. It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago with a casual sportswear line. The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg freely volunteered “was not a good idea,” given that clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt. It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.” By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.” Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges . But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.” Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly building a waitlist for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership. Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.” When we asked whether the gyms will double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand , for example), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.” He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out). Wahlberg’s last big bet on a gym chain might have scared off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “ Wahl Street ,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience. “I think the biggest takeaway was just making sure that I’m involved with people that share the same approach that I do.” He also said he always thought big box was the better model. F45’s classes suit people who are short on time, but he wants members to hang around Municipal for hours. Plenty of gyms run on a “join up but don’t show up” model, he said, adding, “I can’t understand that philosophy.

events.title: The humble chickpea has just boomed in value
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chickpea prices hit $1,000 per tonne as importers rush to lock in supply Aussie chickpea prices are on the up. ( ABC Everyday: Heidi Sze ) Chickpea prices have skyrocketed to $1,000 per tonne. Several countries are rushing to lock in supply ahead of Ramadan. Australia's chickpea production is forecast to be down more than 50 per cent this season. Australian chickpeas are in hot demand, with delivered prices surging this month towards $1,000 per tonne in some regions. It is a significant jump from earlier in the year, when the market was trading closer to $600 per tonne. Grains Australia Pulse Council chair Peter Wilson said it was a great result for growers. "We haven't seen $1,000 per tonne since 2024 , so it's significant. It's a great price," he said. Chickpea prices have gone up considerably this month. ( ABC Landline ) So what is driving the sudden price surge for Australian chickpeas? Mr Wilson said it was due to a combination of factors. "There's a lot of volatility globally right now, which is creating enormous turbulence in logistics and supply chains, which is keeping buyers on edge," he said. "We're also seeing the impacts of El Niño, which looks to have left parts of India with lower-than-average rainfall from the monsoon, which has caused their local chickpea prices to rise, which is pushing everything along." The season's first delivery of chickpeas to the Mt McLaren receival site in Queensland. ( Supplied: Marc Johnston/GrainCorp ) Mr Wilson said there were several nations wanting to lock in supply ahead of Ramadan, which starts in early February. "Ramadan creates peak demand for a lot of our pulse crops [like chickpeas], and we see buyers wanting to have product pre-positioned at least one month ahead of Ramadan," he said. "So we're seeing some urgency from buyers trying to get product onboard vessels for key destination markets such as Pakistan, Bangladesh and the UAE, so it's in the market and ready for that Ramadan demand." In its most recent crop forecast, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES) predicted Australian chickpea production would fall by 52 per cent "to just over 1 million tonnes in 2026–27" due to significant cuts to area planted and expected lower yields in the major growing regions of northern New South Wales and Queensland. ABC Landline has been told that forecast may be "optimistic" and the overall crop might be even lower, which is another reason why there is some buyer urgency at the moment. Prices are expected to ease as harvest supply increases. New season chickpeas arrive at the receival site at Yamala, Queensland. ( Supplied: Fred Smith/GrainCorp ) North West Queensland chickpea grower Lucas Findley said he was pleased with his harvest, yielding about 1.2 tonnes per hectare. Although he had already forward-sold most of his chickpeas at a lower price, he said it was still exciting to see the market rally. "High prices are always good for any commodity and I'm happy for anyone who can take full advantage of these prices," Mr Findley said. "We'd sold around 75 per cent of our chickpea crop prior to this recent price rise at a good price that we were happy with. "But we still have around 25 per cent of the crop available to take advantage of the stronger prices, which will be a very nice finish to the season." Hummus is made from cooked, mashed chickpeas. ( ABC News: Wesley Mitton ) Mr Findley grows about 1,300 hectares of chickpeas as part of his grain and cotton rotation in Julia Creek. His chickpeas will be exported out of the Townsville Port, which is gearing up for its second-ever dry bulk shipment of the pulse. Last October, more than 38,000 tonnes of chickpeas were sent to India and Pakistan in a first-of-its-kind shipment from north Queensland, sourced from growing regions including Richmond, Julia Creek, Maxwelton and Marathon. This year, the port will also export sorghum for the first time, which Mr Findley said was "fantastic". "It just shows that people are supporting the expansion of North West Queensland farming more and more," he said. Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or on ABC iview . events.title: Faisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bosses
events.summary: When it comes to the future direction of the global economy there is a bit of a tug of war going on. There are starkly opposing forces. On the one hand holding back growth are the familiar, recurring crises from the energy shock, trade conflict and actual war. This is reflected most clearly in the sharply rising interest rate costs for the world's advanced economies. Pulling in the other direction is the boost from massive spending on AI, and the frankly astonishing resilience shown especially by smaller economies, as new routes for trade, including for oil and gas, have been established out of necessity. At the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week these themes came up again and again, including among those at the very top table. But not even they know which way things are going to go. In the meantime it's a sportsman's bet where the roving eye of the bond markets will focus next. Currently they seem to be looking at the US and France. However, the French finance minister, Roland Lescure, has been telling the world he has had no problem selling debt, though it was more expensive, and that his Budget would be fine. He also suggested he had helped save the G7 group of advanced nations, which was at risk of collapsing a year ago amid Donald Trump-inspired tensions. In some ways it is a miracle there has not been a global recession, or a debt crisis in a major emerging economy. Indeed the Thai finance minister was boasting to me of how little his borrowing costs had gone up, especially in relation to the US. Another surprise is the UK being taken off the bond markets' naughty step, and instead being named model pupil by the IMF. The IMF has taken the government's Budget plans at face value and on trust. The reality is that the rest of the G7 lack even this. And beauty is relative, especially when it comes to borrowing. And this moment gave Chancellor John Healey the chance of a hearing, to highlight that the UK's actual growth data has continued to outperform expectations and so far in 2026 can now be described as strong. Healey told me that he saw the figures as the first sign that AI and tech investment was starting to increase UK economic growth. The bond financiers milling around the IMF meetings seem to be taking another look at the UK after years of crisis. Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget Published 4 days ago 'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK Published 8 October Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF Published 5 days ago But there is a third big challenge to wrestle with, on top of geopolitical instability and bond market uncertainty, one that's apparent even on the streets of Bangkok, as the chauffeurs dropped off the bankers and finance ministers for this week's gathering. Like other nations Thailand has experienced first hand the astonishing boom in sales of Chinese electric vehicles. Thailand is sometimes dubbed the "Detroit of Asia" for its own strong car making heritage. Now nearly a third of all car sales are Chinese EVs. It is the clearest example of what is known as the China Shock Two. The sheer speed of China's dominance in advanced manufacturing. The first China shock came in the 2000s in basic manufacturing. This second wave of dramatic change has led in just the last few months to a reappraisal of how world trade is functioning and how it is going to be managed. This is especially the case in the EU, which is scrambling to reassess what currently feels like a one-way street when it comes to China-Europe trade. The extra "Made in Europe" protections that the bloc is drawing up will have a profound impact on the UK too. If the UK is outside the new rules, China could divert its excess car production to the UK, where, like Thailand, there are currently lower tariffs and even subsidies. Or the EU could invite Britain in, but ask it to follow its suit by raising tariffs to match its own. Then there is the sub-plot of the UK's relationship with the European Union. This was a theme that cut through more than might have been expected in Bangkok this week and even seemed to provide a little entertainment. The managing director of the IMF Kristalina Georgieva rolled with laughter, suggesting the Brexit "divorcees are now dating again". The Finnish finance minister told me the UK was "flirting" with the EU. Major banks were issuing reports about the prospect of "Breturn". It is, however, the AI boom that is being relied on to provide the trampoline that is required to bounce the world economy out of its current era of multiple simultaneous crises, so many of which are linked to the decisions of President Trump. But even that is not clear cut. In one room the transformative economic effect of AI is lionised by finance ministers. In the next, central bankers fret about its power to break the cybersecurity of most of the banking system. The financial boom around it can't last.

events.title: Travel booking platform Klook Technology files to withdraw US listing
events.summary: Klook joins a growing list of companies that have deferred IPO plans in 2026, including smart-ring maker Oura and nuclear services company Holtec. Klook Technology has filed to withdraw its US IPO plans on Oct 16, saying “this is not the right time to proceed with an IPO” because of market conditions. Reuters said US IPO activity has slowed as higher bond yields, a restrictive policy outlook and geopolitical uncertainty have made investors cautious. The Hong Kong-based travel platform, founded in 2014, said revenue rose 24% to US$417.1 million in 2024 and bookings are on track to exceed 80 million in 2026. Travel booking platform Klook Technology on Oct 16 filed to withdraw its US initial public offering (IPO) plans amid market volatility. “Given current market conditions, Klook has decided this is not the right time to proceed with an IPO,” a company spokesperson told Reuters. “We will continue to evaluate the right time for a listing.” IPO activity in the US market has softened in recent weeks as higher bond yields, a prolonged restrictive policy outlook and geopolitical uncertainty have made investors more cautious. Klook joins smart-ring maker Oura and nuclear services company Holtec among a growing list of companies that have deferred IPO plans in 2026 as volatile markets continue to curb investor appetite for new listings. The Hong Kong-based company had filed for a US IPO in November 2025 , and at the time disclosed a 24% jump in 2024 revenue to US$417.1 million (S$534 million). Founded in 2014, Klook offers bookings for tours, attractions, transport and other travel experiences across a wide range of locations globally. It competes with global platforms such as Booking.com, TripAdvisor, China’s Trip.com and South Korea’s Yanolja. “Our business continues to grow, with total experiences booked on track to exceed 80 million this year,” the spokesperson said. Klook was aiming to list its shares on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol “KLK”. REUTERS

events.title: Katie Zacharia ousted as White House press secretary
events.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted Friday after just five days on the job, according to two senior Trump administration officials. Why it matters: Zacharia will be the shortest-tenured press secretary in modern history, with her first and only week in the White House marked by speculation about her legal credentials and criticism of her first press briefing. Trump told reporters Friday that he had urged Zacharia to "reconsider" the job, saying: "The news has been so nasty to her. I've never seen anything like it actually. And I said to her, 'honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider." "POTUS is a big fan of Katie's, and what POTUS said to the reporters is exactly what he said in private," a senior White House official said. "President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and the most hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him," Zacharia said in a post to X on Friday evening. "No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to," she said. It was an honor to work for him." Driving the news: Zacharia was seen as a surprise pick when Trump announced her hiring on Oct. 9. She started work the following Monday, Oct. 12, and gave her first — and likely only — press briefing the following day. In that press conference, she was visibly shaky and nervous and left the president unimpressed, a White House official told Axios. Trump was also "blindsided" when he learned she wasn't an "attorney" as he had posted on Truth Social when he announced her hire. Zacharia tried to do damage control after a Wall Street Journal report that she wasn't licensed to practice law in any U.S. state. She told Fox News that she failed the exam and never retook it, since she was moving to China But her interview explanations weren't seen as up to snuff by Trump, the source said. Background: Zacharia's hiring was solely a Trump decision, one furthered along with the strong input of his personal assistant Natalie Harp. Zacharia flew out Thursday to Washington, slipped quietly into the White House without seeing any friends in the media or administration and had a good meeting with Trump. On Friday, Trump offered her the job on the spot. Contrary to other reports, Trump told Chief of Staff Susie Wiles his decision. Wiles, who did not know Zacharia before, raised no objections because she knew the press secretary job is a personal one for the president, another administration source said. Before hiring Zacharia , Trump wanted to hire former Fox News host Maria Bartiromo, two administration sources said, but she signaled she was not going to take the job. Conservative commentator Scott Jennings was in contention but wasn't offered the job. Behind the scenes: Zacharia's arrival concerned some staffers who feared she wanted to replace them. Zacharia denied this and tried to put their minds at ease. A White House official told Axios that Zacharia and her family are having dinner tonight with Vice President Vance and Vance's family at the VP's residence at the Naval Observatory. "The warmth for Katie goes well beyond the president," the official said. What we're watching: Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy said he spoke with Trump on Friday and that the president is in "no rush" to name a replacement for the press secretary. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout. Go deeper: Trump press secretary explains failed bar exam Barak Ravid contributed to this story.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Regional Development and Planning The 4.5-star hotel will offer almost 100 rooms. ( Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council ) Work has started on Bundaberg's first hotel development in 20 years. A recent report into the region's accommodation needs showed it was 800 beds short every night. Construction on the new hotel on Airport Drive is due to finish by the middle of next year. It has taken two decades, but Bundaberg's next hotel development is underway. Four hours north of Brisbane, the city is a key tourism destination for the southern Great Barrier Reef but has not attracted significant short-term accommodation development in 20 years, according to Bundaberg Regional Council. The 4.5-star, three-storey hotel, situated across the road from the Bundaberg Airport, will offer 97 rooms. Mayor Helen Blackburn said the demand for accommodation was constantly growing. "The hotel demand study showed us that we were 800 beds short every night in our region," she said. "This is just one step towards bridging that gap." Cr Blackburn said it had been difficult to attract hotel developers to the region due to the current stock of aging motels. "Those older motels sell their rooms at a cheaper rate, which then doesn't give investors the confidence to think that if they build a new hotel, they can get the price for the rooms that they need," she said. Developer MVP said the new hotel would refresh the hospitality offering in Bundaberg. "We hope that it will be a destination of choice for travellers to the region and will bring more travellers to the region," a spokesperson said. Construction is due to finish by the middle of next year. ( Supplied: Bundaberg Regional Council ) The hotel has been funded by investor MyState Limited, with chief executive Brett Morgan saying the demand was clear. "Every time you go down the street in Bundaberg, there's no-vacancy signs everywhere," he said. Mr Morgan said the hotel would also create about 50 ongoing jobs. Bundaberg Tourism chief executive Duncan Littler said the development would cater to leisure and business travellers. "Already, there's more than 750,000 people that choose to visit the beautiful Bundaberg region each year and they stay for more than 2 million nights," he said. "We hope that investments like this will also encourage other [tourism] operators, potentially even airlines, to consider investing in the region." Brett Morgan, Helen Blackburn and Duncan Littler have welcomed the project. ( ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside ) Cr Blackburn said other accommodation applications were in the pipeline but did not elaborate. "We have definitely been encouraging accommodation providers in terms of hotels, student accommodation and even aged care accommodation to set up in our region because we know that we need that here," she said. Construction on the Airport Drive hotel is due to finish by mid-2027, with the first guests expected later next year. events.title: Darwin accountant trades tax for cane toad taxidermy
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'More to life': Darwin accountant trades numbers for cane toad taxidermy Mithram Selvaratnam transforms cane toads into souvenirs sold at Darwin's Mindil Markets. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) There are 531 dead cane toads in Mithram Selvaratnam's Darwin backyard freezers. By Christmas, some will be wearing Santa hats. The former accountant runs an unusual souvenir business, which sees him doing everything from sandblasting and whitening crocodile skulls to gutting and stuffing dead toads. Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam now sells taxidermy cane toads and crocodile products at Darwin's markets. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) It's a far cry from the life he envisioned for himself when he left Malaysia to study accounting in Australia 16 years ago. "When I grew up it was all about the rat race," he said. The decision to leave it all behind came to Mr Selvaratnam after working full time as an accountant in Melbourne. "I was doing that corporate life, 9 to 5, stuck in the office, and I just felt like there was more to life," he said. Christmas-themed cane toads are being prepared for the festive season. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Word of Mr Selvaratnam's dilemma got out to his Darwin-based aunt, who offered an unexpected solution. For decades she had been selling curries at the iconic Mindil Markets and a neighbouring stall had put his Territory souvenir business up for sale. That was in 2017 and the transition from spreadsheets to stuffed toads hasn't always been smooth sailing. Mr Selvaratnam was initially purchasing the toads from a taxidermist in Queensland, but when the supplier decided to retire, he was left with two choices — give up the business or take matters into his own hands. Grace Ray works on a taxidermy cane toad at Mithram's Leanyer work space. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) "Before I started doing this, I could barely pick a toad up," he said. "But I thought, we have plenty of toads in the Territory, an abundance of supply, so I'll just make them myself. "I went [to Townsville] and put myself through a two-day bootcamp of learning how to do it." It was through gritted teeth and pinched nostrils that Mr Selvaratnam learnt to gut, tan, stuff and dry the warty pests before painting them with varnish to make them "look pretty". Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam couldn't even touch cane toads until he underwent 'taxidermy bootcamp'. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Armed with his new-found knowledge, a head torch and gloves, Mr Selvaratnam began scouring golf courses and gardens hunting the pests. Community 'toad busts', like the one held recently at the Territory Wildlife Park , can provide hundreds of dead toads to Mr Selvaratnam in a single night without him having to lift a finger. Territory Wildlife Park ranger Luke Hare says toad busts aim to reduce the numbers of the pests while also educating the community of their dangers. "Cane toads produce significant risk to a lot of our native species," he said. "A lot of our natives can't tolerate the toxins cane toads have, so when they eat the cane toad, or try to eat them, often it will kill them." Mr Hare estimates that there could be hundreds of thousands of cane toads running rampant in the wildlife park on Darwin's outskirts. For Mr Selvaratnam, the park's latest haul of 531 toads has come just in time for his end-of-year Christmas orders. Soon, newly minted santa hat-clad critters will join their rum-drinking, ukulele-playing and occasionally X-rated counterparts. The recent toad bust has filled the freezers at his Leanyer workshop. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) But cane toads aren't the only unwanted creatures finding a second life in Mr Selvaratnam's backyard. Among the tanning equipment and taxidermy tools are chest freezers full of crocodile heads. "I started with the toads and the skulls came about a year after that," he said. Crocodile teeth and skulls are also turned into souvenirs. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Mr Selvaratnam had initially been buying the skulls from a supplier, but in a case of deja vu, retirement once again threatened his supply chain. "This time I didn't go down to Queensland to learn, I just got him on the phone and he ran me through it, and from then, on experimentation, really," he said. The skulls are a by-product from crocodile farms in the Territory, and along with croc teeth, buffalo heads and other leather goods, they make up the rest of Mr Selvaratnam's unlikely livelihood. He's also recently been experimenting with other forms of taxidermy including the Territory's iconic barramundi.

events.title: U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year
events.summary: The Treasury Department said the U.S. budget deficit came in at nearly $2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year. The U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with a budget deficit of nearly $2 trillion, the latest measurement to underscore the extent of the country's financial stress. The $1.992 trillion figure was about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in the prior fiscal year, the Treasury Department reported Friday. It's the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the federal government was doling out trillions of dollars in financial stimulus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2026 fiscal year saw record sums for both receipts and outlays, according to a Treasury Department official. With Friday's release, the U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The government last recorded a surplus — meaning its revenues were larger than debts — in 2001. Friday's report offers fresh evidence of how the U.S.'s fast-growing debt pile has dragged on the nation's overall financial health. The rising debt bill has helped exacerbate angst among bond traders, who sent the 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week. Social Security amounted to the biggest slice of government spending at nearly $1.7 trillion for the full fiscal year, up modestly from the roughly $1.6 trillion spent in 2025. Medicare was the second biggest contributor, costing almost $1.1 trillion for the fiscal year. By comparison, the government-run healthcare program required slightly under $1 trillion in fiscal 2025. Net interest – a calculation of the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives – also topped $1 trillion for the fiscal year. In the 2025 fiscal year, net interest totaled $970 billion. Individual incomes taxes helped lessen the total deficit by bringing in more than $2.8 trillion, an increase of about 7% year over year. Corporate income tax provided $381 billion in receipts during the 2026 fiscal year. That was a decrease of about $70 billion from fiscal 2025 stemming from the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill act passed by Congress last year. In the 2026 fiscal year, the U.S. shelled out more than $1.3 trillion in interest on the national public debt. The total owed exceeded $40 trillion earlier this year and has more than doubled over the last decade. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in August that the U.S. can "grow our way out of" its increasing debt pile. "Our message to our allies, our trading partners, is that global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt," Bessent said in August. President Donald Trump pitched his plans for broad and steep tariffs as a way to drive up revenue and shrink the government's debt. The White House has pushed forward with its strategy of increasing levies on trading partners despite the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that many of those instituted by Trump were unconstitutional. The Treasury saw a record high for gross customs duties in the 2026 fiscal year, according to a department official. But the total revenue from customs took a hit due to refunds required following the Supreme Court ruling, which sent billions of dollars back to retailers. The Treasury also reported Friday that September's monthly deficit came in at $27 billion, a reversal from the prior year, when the department saw a surplus of $198 billion in the month.

events.title: Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
events.summary: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange before the closing bell in New York City on Oct 16. Wall Street tumbled on Oct 16, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend. The Nasdaq was on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise. Nvidia-backed CoreWeave slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data centre operator’s bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%. Broadcom fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index sank 2.5%, on track for its eighth straight day of declines. Investors on Oct 16 were also watching oil prices jump more than 3% due to Middle East supply worries. “There is some fear in the market,” said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at US Bank Wealth Management in ​Seattle. “High oil prices, in particular, tend to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk.” Adding to concerns around AI financing, some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors are weighing a lower valuation for the company in its upcoming IPO, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The S&P 500 was down 1.22% at 7,649.71 points. The Nasdaq declined 2.19% to 26,128.13 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55% at 51,891.77 points. Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by communication services, down 2.52%, followed by a 2.38% loss in information technology. The S&P 500 was set for its steepest weekly loss since January, and the Nasdaq was heading for its sharpest weekly fall since June. Third-quarter earnings season shifts into gear next week with reports from Tesla, Meta Platforms and Procter & Gamble. Analysts on average see quarterly earnings surging over 30%, driven by AI-related megacaps, according to LSEG data. While the S&P 500 remains up about 12% in 2026, most of that gain has come from AI-related tech stocks, and the index’s median component has climbed only about 6%, year to date. About 185 S&P 500 stocks have lost ground in 2026. Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week showed price pressures were extending beyond energy commodities. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Oct 16 voiced optimism about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been “hanging in there” during a lingering energy shock and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation. Markets increasingly expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged in October. Barclays now expects 25-basis-point hikes each in December and January. Tesla dropped 2.5% after the electric-vehicle maker unveiled a redesigned Roadster, powered by rocket-style thrusters, developed in collaboration with SpaceX. Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer on Oct 15. Its shares were down 2.9%. Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.3-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 19 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 49 new highs and 263 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: Canberra businesses battling 'multi-agency maze' to stay open, report finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Businesses affected by Civic construction received 'insufficient' financial relief, committee report finds Ongoing construction in Canberra's city centre has seen a reduction in turnover for businesses in the area. ( ABC News: Lily Nothling ) An ACT Legislative Assembly committee investigating the city's night life has accepted reports that "insufficient" relief has been given to businesses affected by light rail and car park construction. The country's peak hospitality advocacy body has welcomed the committee's 28 recommendations to improve the ACT's night-time economy. The recommendations include establishing an ACT Night-Time Economy Commissioner and offering "stronger temporary relief" for affected businesses. The ACT government should consider stronger relief for businesses affected by construction work and establish a dedicated night-time economy commissioner, a review of Canberra's night life has found. Restaurants and other businesses would be forced to shut their doors without more action to address car park access and construction disruptions, according to findings from the ACT Legislative Assembly committee tasked with investigating the city's night-time economy. Chris Gatfield of the Australian Hotels Association has welcomed the committee's recommendations, but says he doubts they will all be delivered. ( Supplied: Chris Gatfield ) The committee's report, made public on Friday, made 28 recommendations to improve what the Australian Hotels Association (AHA) said was "a little bit of a struggle" for the industry. "The general economic climate is really, really tough for the hospitality industry," AHA ACT branch general manager Chris Gatfield said. "That's not necessarily just related to the various infrastructure projects that are going on in the city. But the committee accepted that there had been "insufficient" relief for businesses affected by light rail and car park constructions. It recommended the ACT government "consider offering stronger temporary relief measures for businesses adversely affected by ongoing disruptions associated with major infrastructure works in the city, such as means-tested rent relief". Charcoal Restaurant owner Anna Gray says financial assistance is the only way to ensure her business survives the construction works. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) Anna Gray, the owner of Charcoal Restaurant in the Melbourne building in Civic, said her turnover had reduced by 50 per cent since parts of London Circuit closed in 2024. "Customers don't want to come because there's no parking," she said. Mr Gatfield said businesses need cash flow, but he doubted they would get it. "This will be a decision for government and so far I'm not convinced that they would be in a position to offer that kind of financial support," he said. "You really want the people who are suffering right now to be there to reap the benefits when construction is finished and people return to the city." The committee also found businesses were battling a "multi-agency maze" of red tape to stay open. Josh Dotta, the owner of Fiction nightclub (pictured), told the committee he routinely had to interact with 10 seperate government agencies. ( Facbook: Fiction Club ) Fiction Nightclub operator Josh Dotta gave evidence that he routinely interacted with 10 separate government agencies, while other stakeholders criticised the "silos" and "disconnected sections of government". "Anyone who's ever dealt with a government agency would recognise that sometimes it's very hard to get the person that you actually need to talk to on the phone," Mr Gatfield said. Although the ACT has a dedicated minister for the night-time economy, the committee said a night-time economy commissioner would support that role. The commissioner would consult the industry before major decisions, establish progress metrics, develop a more streamlined red-tape system, support culturally and linguistically diverse workers and take advice from a dedicated advisory group, the recommendations said. "We think it has legs in Canberra and if it works in other places there's absolutely no reason why it wouldn't work here too," Mr Gatfield said. Late-night venues such as Squeaky Clean, pictured during a performance by Citizen Kay, pay significantly more for a liquor licence than similar NSW venues. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) Evidence from the AHA also found liquor licence fees in the ACT were significantly higher than other jurisdictions, prompting a recommendation for a review, especially for larger venues that can host more than 350 people.

events.title: Coral overharvesting on Great Barrier Reef investigated by Fisheries Qld
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Aquarium industry investigated for overharvesting of coral on Great Barrier Reef Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Fisheries Queensland has confirmed it has investigated the overharvesting of coral in the Great Barrier Reef. Coral harvesters are permitted to take up to 190 tonnes from the reef annually. Fisheries Queensland does not intend to release the findings from the investigation. Fisheries Queensland has confirmed it recently investigated an overharvesting of coral on the World Heritage-listed Great Barrier Reef, but has declined to share the outcome. In the 2025-2026 fishing season the harvest of Pocillopora grandis , known as antler coral, was overfished by 30 per cent according to FishNet data. Coral harvesting is the process of collecting coral from the ocean. Harvesters are permitted to take up to 190 tonnes from the reef annually, with much of this destined for the global aquarium trade. Bright colours and interesting shapes are highly prized by 'reefers', who drive demand. But coral catch quotas have been breached several times in recent years, while some operators have been charged with fishing offences. There are quotas within the coral harvesting fishery on the Great Barrier Reef. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito ) The ABC understands an internal investigation has now been completed into this year's exceeded quota. When questioned by the ABC, Fisheries Queensland would not send through the information about the investigations findings. Coral reef ecologist Dr Morgan Pratchett said while this particular species is not under threat, any overharvesting event is of concern. "It sends a bad message given the overwhelming international scrutiny on how this industry is being managed," Dr Pratchett said. Dr Morgan Pratchett is a reef ecologist. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) There are two quotas within the coral harvesting fishery on the Great Barrier Reef, known as individual transferrable quotes (ITC) and prescribed commercial catch (PCC) quotas. Individual quotas are where fishers are given a set amount to fish individually. Breaking these quotas can result in prosecution. PCC quotas, or competitive quotas, are where an amount is set and fishers essentially race to harvest until the quota is exhausted. Harvested coral in tanks for shipping overseas. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito ) According to Fisheries Queensland, this can sometimes result in going over the competitive quota for a coral species, which they say is not "uncommon or unreasonable." A 2024 assessment of the Queensland coral fishery noted that despite efforts to control overharvesting, some species continue to have their catch limits exceeded. It said fisheries would consider "trip limits, increased notifications, and more individual quotas if this issue continues." Do you know more? Email angelaheathcote@protonmail.com or contact her on signal: @angeh.36 At present, several Australian coral species are banned from being imported into the EU due to sustainability concerns. Simon Miller, from the Australian Marine Conservation Society, said he was concerned catch limits are not set at the right levels. "So when you see fishers in a race to fish to go out there where they're competing against each other to catch these corals as quickly as possible, and seeing this overrun of quotas, that's really concerning," Mr Miller said. "They're meant to be some kind of precautionary catch limit yet we keep seeing them overshoot year after year." Simon Miller from the Australian Marine Conservation Society. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) The coral harvesting industry has faced ongoing compliance issues. One recent case of alleged illegal coral harvesting being pursued by the Queensland Director of Public Prosecutions involved coral collector Jardini. The case included Jardini's director Jason Coe, who currently holds five licences in the Queensland coral fishery. Coe has not yet entered a plea. Earlier in 2024, Monsoon Aquatics lead diver and skipper Tim Green was prosecuted by Western Australia Police for offences related to the collection and recording of coral and fish while harvesting on behalf of Monsoon within the Western Australian coral fishery. He was found guilty and fined almost a quarter of a million dollars. Tim Green was found guilty of offences related to the collection of coral in 2024. ( Image: Facebook ) ASIC documents show Tim Green continues to be a shareholder at Monsoon.

events.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
events.summary: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Iran-backed militias sending money back to cash-starved IRGC, U.S. says
events.summary: Iran-backed militias in the region have been sending money back to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to relieve the economic pressure it's under after nine months of war , U.S. CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said Friday. Why it matters: While the U.S. military has been preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran, the Trump administration continues to put immense pressure on the regime with its naval blockade and severe sanctions. U.S. officials say the economic chokehold is causing serious difficulties for Iran and its security forces, while making the regime frustrated and aggressive. The White House hopes the pressure will induce Iran to make a deal that includes nuclear concessions. But so far, that hasn't happened. Driving the news: Cooper said the naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in lost oil revenue. Additionally, CENTCOM and the Treasury Department have managed in recent weeks to freeze $350 million that Iran had in cryptocurrency. Behind the scenes: In a video message released Friday, Cooper revealed that Iran-backed groups such as Hezbollah, Hamas and Shia militias in Iraq — which have been funded by the IRGC for years — now have to give the money back. "The financial strain on Iran's military has become so significant that there are reports about Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments for their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also isn't paying its troops," he said. Cooper said the Iranian government is withholding salaries, pensions and benefits from public sector workers, including the internal security forces and the IRGC. State of play: Cooper attributed the significant increase in Iranian attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz to "desperation" within the IRGC. Despite those attacks, he said that the Strait of Hormuz is still open — with 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moving through it over the last week. Yes, but: In recent weeks, CENTCOM has almost completely stopped conducting strikes against Iranian anti-ship missiles and attack drone launchers in the area of the strait. The pause in strikes, which was ordered by the White House to avoid escalating the war ahead of the midterm elections, made Iran more confident about launching attacks, a U.S. official said. Consequently, CENTCOM is concerned that the increase in ship attacks will cause shipping companies to think twice about transiting the strait — resulting in less oil coming out and a spike in oil prices. U.S. officials say Iran is also attacking more ships to try to raise oil prices and ratchet up pressure on Trump ahead of the midterms. What to watch: The White House and Qatari mediators are still waiting to hear back from Iran about a U.S. counterproposal to end the war. "It's still in internal deliberations in Tehran," a U.S. official said. Regional mediators told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in recent days that Iran shouldn't wait until after the midterms to give its response, a regional source with direct knowledge said. The regional mediators told Iran there's no guarantee that Trump will be more conciliatory after the midterms — on the contrary, he might be more aggressive.

events.title: Thune enjoys surprisingly clear path back to GOP leader despite Trump's attacks
events.summary: The News John Thune took criticism from President Donald Trump, agitated online conservatives, and occasionally frustrated some of his own members this year. Yet his next leadership election is looking smooth compared with the past couple of bouts to lead the Senate GOP. In fact, Thune may actually run unopposed this year, regardless of how the midterms go. “I’m not aware of anyone who wants the job. I certainly don’t,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., told Semafor. “I don’t envy the leader’s task.” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who challenged Thune in 2024 and Mitch McConnell in 2022, told Semafor there’s “no wiggle room; I am not running for leader” this cycle. He said Thune is “probably the only person that’s going to run. But I always want to say if other people run and someone comes up with better ideas, you’ve got to listen to them. But I’m not running.” Know More The biggest headache for Thune was the Save America Act, a voter ID bill that lacked a strategy to become law in the Senate. Trump repeatedly leaned on Thune to kill the filibuster in order to pass it, and other senators wanted Thune to try to force Democrats to pull off a talking filibuster to block the bill. Eventually, though, the effort and outrage over its stalled status faded away. With Democrats favored to win the House and potentially even take the Senate, the fight over killing the filibuster is back on ice. That’s all good news for Thune, who says he’ll likely run for another term regardless of whether Republicans lose the Senate. If no one challenges him, it would be the first unanimous GOP leadership election since 2020. Notably, Johnson had backed Scott in previous leadership races. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told reporters on Thursday that Thune “will get elected pretty resoundingly.” “Do I think he’s got broad support? Yes. I don’t think there’s an insurgent movement that’s against him,” Moreno said. “There’s not a single Republican running nationally that’s saying, ‘Hey, if you elect me, I’ll vote against John Thune as leader.’” Several Democratic candidates say they won’t support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for another term as leader of their caucus. But no one is indicating they are looking to challenge Schumer, either, which means those could just be protest votes. Former Democratic leader Harry Reid received a handful of “no” votes in his leadership race after losing control of the Senate in 2014. Republicans will have their leadership election on Nov. 10; Senate Democrats are likely to have theirs in early December, although the date isn’t set yet. The midterm results remain an X factor for both Thune and Schumer’s futures. Notable Thune told us in June he’d probably run again. Scott said in September he wasn’t committed to supporting Thune.

events.title: FAA equity talks raise questions about the agency's legal authority
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration’s pursuit of an equity stake in a private company that uses AI to manage air traffic is raising questions about whether it has clear legal authority to strike such a deal. The Trump administration has negotiated stakes in dozens of other companies, but none through the FAA. The agency’s interest in owning part of Air Space Intelligence, first reported by Politico , is too “premature” for there to be specifics, a person familiar with the matter told Semafor. Talks so far have been limited to a handful of internal conversations, the person added. One possible statutory underpinning for a deal: Existing law authorizes Transportation Department financial help for state or local governments to “acquire an interest” in some public transportation companies. That argument, like other agencies’ , would be a stretch. “It’s further proof that the administration doesn’t have a ‘plan’ or ‘strategy,’” said Tad DeHaven, who tracks the stakes for the Cato Institute . — Eleanor Mueller and Shelby Talcott

events.title: Copper thefts leave Perth roads in darkness and cost taxpayers millions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts This section of Tonkin Highway en route to Ellenbrook has been without working street lighting for years. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) Major roads and paths across Perth remain dark because widespread copper theft has left street lighting out. This week, police charged three people with stealing copper wire, and police are increasingly scrutinising scrap metal recyclers. The WA government has allocated nearly $12 million in the 2026-27 state budget to replace stolen street lighting cable and upgrade security. More than 100 kilometres of major roads and paths across Perth remain unlit, some for years, because of widespread copper theft. This week, police charged three people with stealing copper wire, which is lucrative on the black market. Police said they arrested and charged a 31-year-old man who allegedly stole more than 190 metres of telecommunication cable from Gidgegannup, before selling the recovered copper to a scrap metal recycler. That theft allegedly occurred over the King's Birthday long weekend in September from a Telstra site, where about 500 kilograms of copper was pulled out of the ground. Roads across Perth's metro area are in darkness at night due to the theft. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) "This had a significant impact on the Gidgegannup and surrounding areas," Mundaring sergeant Tony Signal told 102.5 ABC Perth. Sergeant Signal said police were increasingly scrutinising scrap metal recyclers. "They're obliged by law to record any second-hand dealing of copper at the moment and we find that that's slipping through the cracks," he said. Col Blanch says organised crime groups would find illegal ways to get away with breaking the rules. ( ABC News: Kenith Png ) Police Commissioner Col Blanch previously told the ABC organised crime sought to circumvent those rules when offloading stolen metal. "We know that some scrap metal dealers are doing the wrong thing and doing a lot of business under the table … that's what [the] police's job is to stamp out," he said. "However, when they can't sell it to a second-hand dealer, scrap dealer here, they will put it in a container and they will send large amounts of scrap metal overseas." It's far from an isolated incident involving telecommunications infrastructure , with detectives charging a man with stealing around 50 metres of copper cabling from an exchange site in Wattleup last month. A Telstra spokesperson said copper theft widely impacted service companies and that the telco's copper theft prevention team works closely with police agencies across Australia. Streetlights don't work when the underground copper wiring is removed. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) "We encourage anyone seeing any suspicious activity near our facilities to contact police immediately," the spokesperson said. Street lighting also continues to be targeted, with police arresting a 41-year-old man and a 50-year-old woman this week, after a member of the public reported suspicious activity along Tonkin Highway in Ellenbrook. Police stopped a vehicle in the vicinity a short time later and allege they found a significant amount of stolen insulated copper wiring. Copper thieves taking exceptional risks Demolition sites are being stripped for copper at an escalating rate, according to a Perth demolition contractor, risking electrocution and asbestos exposure to sell the scrap metal on the black market. Main Roads WA said as of October 2, more than 1,400km of cable had been stolen from its network, taking more than 100km of street lighting and nearly 30km of pedestrian/cycle paths lighting offline. "Since cable theft became a widespread issue, Main Roads have replaced 480km of copper roadway and PSP lighting cable as well as re-cabling and re-energising over 500 individual poles," a spokesperson said. "Currently, Kwinana Freeway, Tonkin Highway and Reid Highway are the three priority routes that Main Roads is focusing on for cable replacement and anti-theft treatments. "Works are also planned in key locations along Forrest Highway, Great Northern Highway, Mitchell Freeway, Roe Highway, Albany Highway, Ennis Avenue, Mandurah Road and Armadale Road." The WA government has allocated nearly $12 million in the 2026-27 state budget for street lighting cable theft replacement and security upgrades but still faces an uphill battle. Main Roads director of metropolitan operations James Pinnington said he expected the program to take several years.

events.title: Tariffs pose a risk to US-India relationship
events.summary: President Donald Trump faces a deadline Sunday to decide whether to impose certain penalties on other countries under a bipartisan sanctions law he signed last month. Any move by him to waive sanctions on Russian individuals or entities will be met with criticism, as would a decision not to impose tariffs on China for buying Russian gas. But Washington is hoping he’ll spare at least one country: India. “Both the United States and India should not buy Russian oil and gas, but I don’t think simply imposing big tariffs on India is the way to get them to” reduce their purchases, said Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security. Punishing India for its reliance on Russian energy “would deal a body blow to the US-India relationship,” argued Sadanand Dhume, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. The US and India are currently locked in trade negotiations, which more tariffs would surely disrupt. Fontaine said it is “100%” possible that the Trump administration uses the sanctions law to pressure India to give in to its demands in those discussions. Trump had previously hiked tariffs on India over its Russian energy purchases, but later removed them as trade talks progressed. Asked whether Trump had made a decision on which sanctions, if any, to impose at the deadline, a White House official said that he “signed the act and the administration will comply with the act’s requirements.” The bill gives the president broad power to waive penalties if he deems it in the US interest. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: From kitsch decor to extinct chains, new book revisits classic eateries
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts New book Old Vintage Melbourne, A Culinary Chronicle captures the dining institutions of yesteryear Stalactites in Lonsdale Street has been a Melbourne institution since 1978. ( Supplied: Nicole Konstandakopoulos/Stalactites. Most of the photos featured in this article appear in Old Vintage Melbourne, A Culinary Chronicle, published by Scribe. ) From a sophisticated 70s restaurant with hot-pink light shades, to a St Kilda cake shop and the all-you-can eat smorgasbords of the suburbs, Chris Macheras's latest coffee table book is brimming with Melbourne's culinary history. But the book's beginnings are also quintessentially Melbourne — or at least Melbourne as we knew it in 2020. Stuck at home during COVID-19, the lawyer and artist kicked off an Instagram account featuring vintage photos of the city and suburbs. The page took off, spawning two books and, now, a third: Old Vintage Melbourne: A Culinary Chronicle. Chris Macheras's lockdown project has now led to a third book. ( Supplied: Meghan Lawson ) "It's still crazy to have an idea that was just something that I was sitting there in lockdown, depressed, and then to think that it's created this community and people have found each other via my Instagram page," the author says. But Mr Macheras is clearly someone who thrives creatively in trying times. He produced his latest book while battling Hodgkin lymphoma — a type of blood cancer. "Whilst I was recovering and doing chemo and everything, my brain needed to do something," the 36-year-old says. "They give you a lot of steroids … whilst your body is tired, your mind is very up." The Club Grill restaurant, at the Southern Cross Hotel, was originally for men only. ( Courtesy: Athol Shmith, Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales/Tourism Australia ) He began piecing the book together from home, contacting a large number of restaurants and trawling the archives of the state library, Museums Victoria and the public record office for old images. "I couldn't physically go to the library because I was recovering," he says. "So everything was what I could get by email, and who could send me photos." The late Nick Tsiligiris pictured inside his beloved Olympic Doughnuts van in Footscray. ( Courtesy: Gina Hasapis ) The result is a collection of photos and stories from about 120 food joints, from Marios and Kingsland Chinese Restaurant , to Coles Cafeteria, Glo Glo's, Smorgy's, fresh produce markets and one very popular Footscray donut van. The Olympic Doughnuts van was a landmark for almost 40 years. ( Courtesy: Gina Hasapis ) A Greek grandfather who loved Melbourne Mr Macheras says his grandfather, who emigrated to Melbourne from Greece in 1955, instilled in him a love of history. "We would talk about sort of the difficult life they had as migrants, and that we should really love Australia and love Melbourne because this is a land that gave us the opportunity to leave war-torn Europe, where they were from," he says. The author says the book celebrates Australia's restaurant capital at a time when many people are craving a sense of nostalgia. Melbourne's dine-in Pizza Huts, which began to disappear in the 1990s, are captured in the book. ( Courtesy: Fremantle Media ) Mr Macheras grew up in Preston and Eltham, and remembers eating at places like Jim's Greek Tavern in Collingwood, which is still going strong. "As a kid, we were always going to things that were familiar for an immigrant family," he says. "And then those family restaurants. Dine-in Pizza Hut is super nostalgic for me, going and getting some of that big trough with chocolate mousse, soft serve and jelly." The dessert bar at Pizza Hut lives on in the memories of many a 1980s and 1990s child. ( Courtesy: Claire Sullivan and Rob Breslin ) The story behind the famous Stalactites ceiling A Greek institution on Lonsdale Street in the city is one of many legendary eating establishments featured in the book. Stalactites — named after the handmade structures that grace its ceiling — opened in 1978, when the area was a hub for Melbourne's Greek community, Stalactites operated for 24 hours a day for years, with many daytime and late-night diners eating under its distinctive ceiling. ( Facebook: Stalactites ) "It was a place where all the Greek migrants could come, and they could eat Greek food and speak Greek and maintain that connection," says Nicole Konstandakopoulos, whose parents and grandparents were the original owners of the famous restaurant. "But over time, the Greeks moved out of the city, and they went to suburbs like Oakleigh." The Lonsdale Street institution seen from the outside.

events.title: Invasive fire ants return to organic farms not treated for 14 months
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Invasive fire ants are believed to have spread from organic farms left without treatment options for more than a year. ( Supplied: Scotty Yang ) Treatment on export-certified organic farms was paused in August 2025 after genetically modified ingredients were discovered in baits. The National Fire Ant Eradication Program (NFAEP) says there is evidence some areas have been reinfested from properties that did not have a treatment option for 14 months. A new treatment option has been found, but it requires direct nest injection, making it more labour-intensive than previous methods. Red imported fire ants have re-infested organic farms in Queensland, leaving them without options to control the pest for 14 months. Treatment was suspended in August last year on some export-certified properties in the south-east Queensland suppression zone after genetically modified ingredients were identified in baits used on nests. The National Fire Ant Eradication Program confirmed parts of a 1,110-hectare zone spanning the Lockyer Valley, Scenic Rim and Somerset agricultural hubs were re-infested, though the extent is yet to be determined. Fire ants can fly up to five kilometres, making their spread difficult to control. "We do have evidence of reinfestation of areas from properties that haven't been treated [since the suspension]," senior director of operations Robbie Wilson said. The genetically modified ingredients found in fire ant bait cannot be used on organic farms. ( Supplied: Johan Augustin ) He acknowledged organic farmers could not use ant-killing bait containing genetically modified (GM) corn and oil without risking their organic status. Fire ant treatment suspended on organic farms Fire ant treatments have been suspended on organic farms, and alternatives sought, after baits containing genetically modified soybean oil and corn grit were found to have been unwittingly distributed. "We've been working with (peak body) Australian Organic Limited … about how we support them in the eradication and limitations of infestation, which has been quite positive." Mr Wilson said the affected areas made up a small part of the 30,000 hectares identified as having gaps in treatment across the wider control area. "But that treatment may already be scheduled," he said. He said approving a treatment suitable for organic farmers was the "first phase" of bringing those properties back into the eradication program, which aims to eliminate fire ants by 2032. On Monday, the federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry announced it had granted a permit for a product using concentrated cinnamaldehyde, the organic compound that gives cinnamon its flavour and odour, for use in Queensland. "This treatment product has been assessed as compliant with the National Standard for Organic and Bio-Dynamic Produce," the department said. The tiny fire ants spread quickly and are easy to overlook. ( Supplied: National Fire Ant Eradication Program ) The permit requires application "by direct nest injection and/or as a nest drench" by people authorised by the NFAEP. Mr Wilson said the first shipment of the product from New Zealand was awaiting customs clearance at Brisbane port. "It is an organic product that can be used on certified organic properties," he said. Organic farmer Di Fyson welcomed the new treatment option. ( Supplied: Di Fyson ) But the labour-intensive method could not replace broadscale baiting, which Mr Wilson said authorities continued to work on for larger organic operations. Scenic Rim organic farmer Di Fyson welcomed the new treatment, but questioned why it took so long. Ms Fyson, who grows domestically certified organic leafy greens and pumpkins, received treatments during the suspension. But she said she would be willing to try the new product. "Definitely, particularly if that's going to be the only option," she said. Invasive fire ants detected in Sydney's inner west Specialist fire ant detection dog teams have been deployed to the site in Sydney's Enfield and a nearby area with no other nests having been discovered. Reece Pianta, advocacy director at the Invasive Species Council, which lobbies for better funding for eradication and prevention programs, said he was concerned that substitute treatments were taking too long to deploy "at mass scale." "I'm concerned about the lack of organic farm treatment alternatives creating gaps in fire ant eradication," he said. "We know from past experience when there have been gaps in fire ant treatments, that is when fire ants have spread." "The success of eradication is reliant on keeping those treatment gaps closed.

events.title: Zacharia's rocky stint as press secretary ends
events.summary: Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after less than one week on the job. An administration official told Semafor that Zacharia will be “transitioning out” of her role, which began on Monday and quickly descended into a series of stumbles, culminating in Fox News pressing her earlier today on whether she regretted not being clearer about her failure to pass the bar exam. Moments before news broke of her departure from the role, President Donald Trump said he told Zacharia “ you don’t have to do this ,” but suggested he’d give her the decision to stay or leave. One source familiar with the situation emphasized to Semafor that Trump remains a fan of hers, adding that Zacharia and her family are planning to dine with Vice President JD Vance and his family at his residence tonight. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: State Department warns travelers to China they risk “wrongful detention”
events.summary: The State Department is updating its travel advisory for mainland China to include an increased risk level for wrongful detention, according to a new plan seen by Semafor. The State Department’s move comes after two US citizens were labeled as wrongfully detained earlier this year, and at a complex moment in the relationships between the two most powerful countries in the world. Despite a personally warm relationship between the presidents, the countries’ deep differences from the Taiwan Strait to trade to artificial intelligence remain. A person familiar with the situation told Semafor the department’s change is connected to the continued detentions of the two Americans, Min Zin and Youlin Chen. Zin is a Myanmar scholar who was detained in June and accused of endangering China’s national security. Chen is a seismologist detained in 2024 and charged with espionage. Both are US citizens. The travel advisory as a whole remains at a Level 2, which urges Americans to “Exercise Increased Caution” when traveling to China, but the department is adding a “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention. Previously, the travel advisory for mainland China had an “O” risk indicator, which meant that there were “other potential risks not covered” by the department’s specific risk categories. “The U.S. Department of State has determined that Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China,” a State Department spokesman said in a statement to Semafor. “The D risk indicator means the State Department has determined Americans are at risk of wrongful detention by the government of the country.” A group of bipartisan senators introduced a resolution last month pushing the department to add the wrongful detention indicator to its travel advisory, citing the two detained citizens. The spokesman added that wrongful detention is determined by a variety of factors, including having US citizenship or a connection to the US. This is the latest update to the State Department’s China travel advisory — in early September, the department added stronger warnings about wrongful detention, the “arbitrary enforcement of local laws,” and the usage of exit bans. Asked why the travel advisory remains at a Level 2 given the new wrongful detention label, the spokesman said it “identifies a specific risk of wrongful detention” and that “the overall Travel Advisory level reflects a broader assessment of safety and security conditions.”
